title: Assume that each character code consists of bits. The number
subject: Computer Networks
text: Assume that each character code consists of 8 bits and the asynchronous serial line uses binary signaling, one start bit, two stop bits, and no parity bit. The number of complete characters that can be transmitted per second at 2400 baud is:
solution:
Concept: In asynchronous serial transmission, each data character occupies a complete frame. The frame length equals the data bits plus start, stop, and parity bits. Baud counts signal elements per second; with binary signalling, each signal element carries one bit, so 2400 baud provides 2400 bit-times per second.

Application:

  1. Find the frame size: 8 data bits + 1 start bit + 2 stop bits + 0 parity bits = 11 bit-times per character.

  2. Convert the line rate: binary signalling makes 2400 baud equal to 2400 bit-times per second.

  3. Divide the available bit-times by the frame size: 2400 / 11 = 218.18 characters per second.

  4. Count only complete frames: floor(218.18) = 218 complete characters per second.

Cross-check: 218 frames require 218 × 11 = 2398 bit-times, which fits within 2400. By contrast, 219 frames require 219 × 11 = 2409 bit-times, which exceeds the available capacity. Therefore the maximum number of complete characters is 218.

optionFeedback.html: At 109 complete characters per second, the corresponding allocation is 2400 / 109 ≈ 22.02 bit-times per character.
At 216 complete characters per second, the corresponding allocation is 2400 / 216 ≈ 11.11 bit-times per character.
At 218 complete characters per second, the corresponding allocation is 2400 / 218 ≈ 11.01 bit-times per character.
At 219 complete characters per second, the corresponding allocation is 2400 / 219 ≈ 10.96 bit-times per character.

title: Benefits of network do not include
subject: Computer Networks
text: Benefits of a network do not include
solution:
Concept

A computer network connects multiple devices so they can communicate and share resources. Its classic advantages fall into three buckets: sharing information/data, sharing hardware (peripherals like printers and storage), and centralised management of users and resources. These are the benefits a network is built to deliver.

Application

The question asks which listed item is NOT a benefit. Checking each against the cost/benefit reality of running a network:

  • Improved information sharing — a core purpose: connected machines exchange files and data freely, so this IS a benefit.

  • Better monitoring of worker performance — central servers and logs let an administrator track usage and activity, so this IS a benefit.

  • Sharing of peripherals — one printer, scanner or storage device can serve many users over the network, so this IS a benefit.

  • Low maintenance cost — a network adds cabling/hardware, security, backups and ongoing administration; it raises maintenance effort and cost rather than lowering it. This is NOT a benefit.

Cross-check

Three of the four items are textbook reasons organisations install networks, while increased setup and upkeep cost is a well-known drawback of networking. So the item that does NOT belong among the benefits is “Low maintenance cost.”

optionFeedback.html: This is a real networking benefit: connected devices can exchange files and data directly, so it does belong in the benefits list — not the exception the question asks for.
Central servers and activity logs do let an administrator track usage and performance, so this is a genuine benefit and therefore not the odd one out.
Letting many users share one printer, scanner or storage device is a standard reason to build a network, so this is a benefit — not the item being sought.

Networks add cabling, security, backups and continuous administration, which raises upkeep effort and expense. Reduced upkeep is therefore not something a network provides — this is the item that is NOT a benefit.

title: Is set of formal operating rules, procedure or conventions that
subject: Computer Networks
text: A .......... is a set of formal operating rules, procedure or conventions that govern a given process.
solution:
A protocol is a set of formal operating rules, procedures, or conventions that govern a given process. In networking, protocols define how data is transmitted and received between devices. They ensure compatibility and standard communication across different systems.

This definition aligns with the concept of a protocol, which establishes the rules for interaction. Other terms like routing or switching refer to specific actions or layers within a network architecture, rather than the governing rules themselves.

optionFeedback.html: Routing refers to the process of selecting paths for data to travel across networks. It focuses on direction and path determination rather than the formal rules themselves. The definition provided specifically describes conventions governing a process, which distinguishes it from the act of routing data packets.

A protocol defines the set of formal operating rules and conventions that govern communication or processes. It ensures that different systems can understand each other by following agreed-upon standards. This matches the description of governing rules and procedures provided in the question statement.

A layer typically represents a level in a hierarchical structure, such as the OSI model. It organizes functions into groups rather than defining the specific operating rules or conventions. The question asks for the rules themselves, not the structural levels where they might apply.

Switching involves the movement of data between network nodes or devices. It is an action taken based on rules, but it is not the set of rules itself. The definition focuses on conventions and procedures, which is distinct from the forwarding mechanism of switching.

title: The main aim of which of the following is to
subject: Computer Networks
text:
The main aim of which of the following is to make a network work as a single computer?

(i) Distributed computing
(ii) Parallel computing
solution:
Concept

Distributed computing coordinates autonomous computers connected by a network so that communication, resource sharing, and services can be presented as one coherent system. Parallel computing divides a computation into simultaneous tasks to reduce execution time; it may use processors within one machine and does not by itself define a network-wide single-system view.

Application

Distributed computing coordinates networked machines and presents their resources through a coherent system view. Parallel computing decomposes a workload for simultaneous execution to reduce elapsed time. Therefore the distributed-computing statement, rather than the parallel-computing statement, describes the aim in the stem.

Contrast

  • Distributed computing alone identifies the system-wide coordination aim without assigning it to workload decomposition.

  • Parallel computing alone identifies workload decomposition for speed rather than a network-wide system view.

  • Both paradigms would treat system coordination and simultaneous execution as the same defining aim.

  • Neither paradigm would deny that distributed coordination supplies a coherent service view across networked machines.

Therefore, the applicable statement is distributed computing alone, and the answer value is Only (i).

optionFeedback.html: This choice assigns system transparency to distributed coordination and execution speed to parallel decomposition. Message exchange and shared services hide distributed resources, while simultaneous workers shorten one computation.

This choice assigns system transparency to parallel decomposition and execution speed to distributed coordination. Parallel workers shorten one computation, while autonomous nodes coordinate through messages and shared services.
This choice assigns system transparency to both distributed coordination and parallel decomposition. The mechanisms can coexist because a distributed service may execute internal work in parallel.

This choice assigns system transparency to neither distributed coordination nor parallel decomposition. The mechanisms remain distinct: one coordinates independent nodes, and the other runs workload parts simultaneously.

title: Which of the following options is an example of full-duplex
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following options is an example of a full-duplex transmission device?
solution: The correct option is C (Telephone). A full-duplex transmission device allows data to be transmitted simultaneously in both directions over a single channel. A telephone network is a classic example because both communicating parties can speak and listen at the same time without any interruption.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Radio broadcasting operates in simplex mode, where data transmission is strictly unidirectional; the transmitter sends the signal, and the audience can only listen.
Incorrect. A walkie-talkie operates in half-duplex mode, meaning both parties can communicate, but only one person can transmit data or speak at a time while the other listens.
Correct. Telephones leverage bidirectional link sharing to establish full-duplex communication, allowing instantaneous, concurrent data flow from both ends of the connection.
Incorrect. Television transmission is an example of simplex communication. The broadcast station transmits video and audio signals downstream to your receiver unit with no reverse channel option.

title: Which of the following option is example of half-duplex communication
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following devices is an example of half-duplex communication?
solution:
Concept

A communication mode is classified by whether information can travel in one or both directions and, if it travels both ways, whether the two directions can be active simultaneously. In half-duplex communication, both ends can transmit and receive, but only one end transmits at a time.

Application

Walkie-talkies use a shared push-to-talk channel. One user presses the transmit button and speaks while the other user listens; the users then exchange roles to reply. Thus communication is bidirectional but not simultaneous.

Contrast and cross-check

  • Radio broadcasting has a one-way station-to-receiver path, so it illustrates simplex communication.

  • A conventional telephone call permits simultaneous two-way speech, so it illustrates full-duplex communication.

  • Broadcast television has a one-way station-to-viewer path, so it illustrates simplex communication.

  • Walkie-talkies permit both users to transmit, but turn-taking prevents simultaneous transmission; this matches the half-duplex rule.

Therefore, walkie-talkies are the half-duplex device among the given choices.

optionFeedback.html: Radio broadcasting carries audio from a station to receivers over a one-way path.
A conventional telephone call carries speech in both directions at the same time.
Broadcast television carries audio and video from a station to receivers over a one-way path.
A walkie-talkie channel uses push-to-talk turn-taking between users.

Concept

Transmission mode classifies a communication link by the permitted direction and timing of data flow. It is independent of the physical medium or signalling service used by the link.

Transmission mode

Direction and timing

Simplex

One endpoint always sends; the other endpoint always receives.

Half-duplex

Either endpoint may send, but the endpoints do not send simultaneously.

Full-duplex

Both endpoints may send simultaneously.

  2. Read the qualifier “solely input”: during the described operation, data travels from the remote terminal to the central computer, and no reverse transfer is required.

  • “All of the above” would require every listed choice to establish the required one-way mode, which the medium and band descriptions do not do.

Therefore, the remote input-only operation requires simplex lines.

title: Which of the following statement is correct regarding point-to-point connection
subject: Computer Networks
text:
Which statement is correct regarding a point-to-point connection in data communication?

I. It provides a dedicated link between two devices.

II. It is a time-shared connection.
solution:
Concept

A point-to-point configuration connects exactly two endpoints through a dedicated physical or logical link.

Time-sharing allocates a common communication resource among multiple users or devices at different times; it describes shared use rather than an exclusive endpoint-to-endpoint link.

For example, a direct link between two routers remains point-to-point even when packets are sent at different moments: the deciding issue is that the link capacity belongs to those two endpoints, not whether transmission is continuous.

Application

  1. Statement I identifies a dedicated link between two devices, which matches the definition of a point-to-point connection.

  2. Statement II calls the connection time-shared. That would require a communication resource shared over time, which conflicts with the dedicated two-endpoint arrangement.

Cross-check and contrast

  • Only II reverses both evaluations by rejecting the dedicated-link statement and accepting the time-sharing statement.

  • Both I and II keeps the time-sharing statement even though shared use conflicts with the defining dedicated link.

  • Neither I nor II rejects the dedicated-link statement even though that statement gives the defining property.

  • Only I retains the dedicated-link statement and rejects the time-sharing statement.

Result

Therefore, statement I is true and statement II is false; the answer is Only I.

This is a two-statement combination grouping statements I and II, the inclusive case in a two-statement classification.
This is a zero-statement combination grouping neither statement, the empty case in a two-statement classification.

title: Which of the following statement(s) is/are true regarding Data Communication?
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are true regarding Data Communication? Statements: I. Half duplex communication is multidirectional communication. II. Full duplex communication is bidirectional communication.
solution:
Concept: Data-communication modes are classified along two independent axes: how many directions data can flow over a link, and whether both directions can be active at the same time. A two-endpoint link has exactly two possible flow directions (end A to end B, and end B to end A) — so the accepted direction-count terms in this classification are only “unidirectional” (one-way) and “bidirectional” (two-way). There is no separate “multidirectional” category in this taxonomy, because a single channel between two ends cannot carry more than two directions in the first place.

  • Simplex: one direction only (unidirectional) — e.g., keyboard to computer.

  • Half-duplex: two-way (bidirectional), but the two ends take turns — only one transmits at a time (e.g., a walkie-talkie).

  • Full-duplex: two-way (bidirectional) and simultaneous — both ends transmit at the same time (e.g., a telephone call).

Applying this to the two statements: Statement I calls half-duplex “multidirectional communication.” Under the taxonomy above, half-duplex is bidirectional — not multidirectional; “multidirectional” is not a term this classification uses for any of the three modes, so Statement I's wording does not match the accepted description and is false. Statement II calls full-duplex “bidirectional communication.” Full-duplex is indeed two-way (it additionally happens to be simultaneous, which is a separate property), so describing it as bidirectional is accurate, and Statement II is true.

Cross-check — the “multi means more than one, so it must include two” objection: “Multidirectional” is not a defined technical term anywhere in the simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex taxonomy — it is simply the wrong word for this classification, not an overly-broad synonym for “bidirectional.” The reason is structural, not a matter of degree: a link between two endpoints only ever has two possible directions (A→B and B→A), so there is nothing “more than two” for a duplex mode to have. Standard networking terminology (and the exam's own answer key) therefore describes the direction axis using only “unidirectional” and “bidirectional”; the alternating-vs-simultaneous distinction is handled separately by the terms “half-duplex” and “full-duplex” themselves, not by direction-count words. Reading “multidirectional” as a valid label for half-duplex mixes these two axes and does not match how the field defines the term.

Answer: Only Statement II is correctly worded, so “Only II” is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Keeping Statement I here requires “multidirectional” to be a valid direction-count label — but a two-endpoint link only ever has two possible flow directions (end A to end B, and end B to end A), so no duplex mode can exhibit a third, “multi” direction. Re-examine whether that label genuinely applies to half-duplex before keeping this statement — and check this pairing’s treatment of Statement II against the same single-axis classification.

This pairing correctly excludes Statement I: “multidirectional” cannot apply to any duplex mode, since a two-endpoint link only ever has two possible flow directions (end A to end B, and end B to end A). It also correctly keeps Statement II: full-duplex’s two-way, simultaneous transfer is exactly what “bidirectional” denotes, independent of timing.

Keeping Statement I here requires “multidirectional” to be a valid direction-count label — but a two-endpoint link only ever has two possible flow directions (end A to end B, and end B to end A), so no duplex mode can exhibit a third, “multi” direction. Re-examine whether that label genuinely applies to half-duplex; that is the specific issue with keeping both statements in this pairing.

Dropping Statement II here treats full-duplex’s two-way, simultaneous transfer as not qualifying for “bidirectional” — but two-way transfer between the two ends is exactly what that term denotes, independent of timing. Re-examine whether full-duplex fits that definition; that is the specific issue with dropping both statements in this pairing.

title: What is the primary purpose of tunneling in internetworking?
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the primary purpose of tunneling in internetworking?

options.html: To encrypt data between two different networks
To connect two similar networks through a dissimilar intermediate network
To increase the bandwidth of a WAN connection
To prevent unauthorized access to the Ethernet frames

solution:
Concept

A network tunnel creates a logical point-to-point link by encapsulating an original packet inside a packet of another protocol. The outer protocol carries the packet across an intermediate network, and the tunnel endpoint removes the outer header.

Application

Here, the two endpoint networks use the same inner networking protocol, while the intermediate network uses a different protocol or infrastructure. Encapsulation lets that intermediate network transport the original packets without needing to interpret their inner protocol, so the tunnel connects the two similar networks across the dissimilar network.

Contrast

  • Encrypting data protects confidentiality; it is an optional security property of some tunnels, not the defining purpose of tunneling.

  • Increasing WAN bandwidth changes link capacity; encapsulation instead adds a header and usually adds a small overhead.

  • Preventing unauthorized access is an access-control or link-security function; tunneling by itself does not authorize users or devices.

  • Connecting similar networks through a dissimilar intermediate network describes the logical link created by encapsulation and decapsulation.

Cross-check

RFC 2473 defines a tunnel as a virtual link between endpoints: one endpoint encapsulates the original packet and the other decapsulates it. That mechanism directly matches connecting compatible endpoint networks across a different transit network.

Therefore, the primary purpose is to connect two similar networks through a dissimilar intermediate network.

optionFeedback.html: Encryption protects the confidentiality of data between endpoints. A tunnel may use a security protocol such as IPsec, but encryption and packet encapsulation are separate properties.
A logical link can carry packets between endpoint networks by placing each original packet inside an outer packet for the intermediate network; the far endpoint then removes the outer header.
WAN bandwidth is the physical or provisioned transmission capacity of a link. Encapsulation adds protocol headers and therefore consumes a small part of that capacity.
Access control limits which users or devices may reach Ethernet traffic. Authentication, authorization, filtering, or link-security mechanisms enforce that restriction.

title: Physical topology of FDDI is?
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the physical topology of FDDI?
solution:
Concept

The physical topology of a network describes the actual arrangement of its nodes and links.

In a ring topology, nodes form a closed loop. A dual-ring design adds a second counter-rotating path to improve fault tolerance.

Application

FDDI uses two counter-rotating token rings. Under normal operation, traffic uses the primary ring. After a link or station failure, the rings can wrap to maintain a continuous path.

Contrast

  • A bus uses one shared linear backbone rather than a closed loop.

  • A star places a hub or switch at the center rather than connecting nodes around a loop.

  • The defined FDDI arrangement is represented by one of the named topologies.

Cross-check

The ability of the secondary path to restore a loop after a fault is characteristic of a dual-ring design.

Result

Therefore, the physical topology of FDDI is Ring.

optionFeedback.html: A bus topology places devices on a shared linear backbone, with transmissions propagating along that common medium.
A ring topology connects devices in a closed loop, with frames traveling from one neighboring node to the next.
A star topology connects each device to a central hub or switch, so links radiate from one central point.

title: Which topology is least affected by single cable failure
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which topology is least affected by a single cable failure ?
solution: Mesh topology provides the highest redundancy because every node is connected via dedicated point-to-point links. If a single cable fails, only the communication between those two specific nodes is affected; data can easily be rerouted through alternative paths. Therefore, the correct option is A.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Due to its fully or partially interconnected redundant paths, a single link failure has minimal impact on the overall network performance and communication remains uninterrupted.
Incorrect. In a standard single-ring topology, a single cable break breaks the loop, disrupting communication for the entire network unless a dual-ring setup is used.
Incorrect. While a peripheral cable failure only disconnects that single node, a failure in the central hub/switch cable or the central device itself brings down the whole network.
Incorrect. Bus topology relies on a single central coaxial backbone cable. If this main backbone cable fails or breaks anywhere, the entire network goes down instantly.

title: Which network topology is typically used in local area networks
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which network topology is typically used in local area networks ?
solution: Star topology is the most common topology used in modern Local Area Networks (LANs), such as Ethernet networks. It connects all devices to a central hub or switch. This layout offers high reliability, easy troubleshooting, and scalability. Therefore, Option B is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Bus topology uses a single backbone cable. It is obsolete in modern LANs due to single-point failure and difficult troubleshooting.
Correct. Modern LANs heavily rely on star topology using central switches because a failure in one cable doesn't bring down the entire network.
Incorrect. Ring topology connects devices in a circular loop. It is rarely used in typical modern LANs because a single node failure breaks the entire loop.
Incorrect. Mesh topology connects every device to every other device. It provides high redundancy but is too complex and expensive for standard LAN deployment.

title: Linear LAN architecture in which transmissions from various stations on
subject: Computer Networks
text: A linear LAN architecture in which transmissions from various stations on the network are reproduced over the length of the medium and are accepted by all other stations on that network is known as
solution:
Concept

A network topology describes how stations and communication links are arranged. In a shared-medium topology, every station attaches to the same communication path, so a signal injected by one station travels through that common path and can be observed by the other attached stations.

A linear shared-medium LAN uses one backbone cable with stations connected along its length. This differs from layouts built from dedicated point-to-point links or from a central switching device.

Application

  1. The stem specifies a linear LAN, so the physical communication path is a single line rather than a collection of independent links.

  2. It says transmissions are reproduced over the length of the medium, which identifies one shared backbone carrying the signal past the attached stations.

  3. It also says the other stations accept those transmissions, which is the broadcast behavior of a bus topology. Therefore, the described architecture is Bus Topology.

Contrast

  • Mesh Topology uses several point-to-point links and can provide multiple routes between stations.

  • Star Topology gives each station a separate link to a central hub or switch.

  • Cell Topology divides wireless coverage into geographic cells served by base stations.

Cross-check

Replacing the shared backbone with a central hub would make the layout star-shaped, while adding dedicated interconnections would make it mesh-like. Keeping one common linear backbone preserves the bus structure.

Result

The linear shared-medium LAN described in the question is Bus Topology.

optionFeedback.html: Mesh Topology connects stations through multiple point-to-point links, often providing alternate paths between pairs of stations.
Bus Topology connects stations to one shared backbone, along which a transmitted signal propagates through the common medium.
Star Topology connects every station by an individual link to a central hub or switch that handles communication between stations.
Cell Topology divides wireless coverage into geographic cells, with each cell normally served by a base station.

title: LAN physical topology with end points on the network converging

solution: The correct option is B: Star topology. In a star topology, all devices are connected to a central controller (hub/switch) via dedicated point-to-point links. If a device wants to send data, it goes through the central hub, preventing direct traffic between endpoints.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. In a mesh topology, every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device on the network, rather than connecting to a central hub.
Correct. This matches the exact definition where all endpoints converge at a central hub or switch using point-to-point cables.
Incorrect. In a ring topology, each device is connected to exactly two neighboring devices, forming a circular data path rather than converging at a central switch.
Incorrect. Cell topology is mostly used in wireless networks (cellular networks) to define geographic regions or sectors, not a standard wired LAN physical hub layout.

title: What is the name of the topology which has bidirectional
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the name of the network topology in which every pair of nodes has a bidirectional link?
solution:
Concept

Network topology describes how nodes and communication links are arranged. In a full mesh, every distinct pair of nodes has a dedicated point-to-point link; a bidirectional link permits communication in either direction.

For n nodes, the number of physical links in a full mesh is n(n − 1)/2 because each link joins one distinct pair. This pairwise-connectivity rule distinguishes a full mesh from hub-based or hierarchical layouts.

Application

The stem states that every pair of nodes has a bidirectional link. That is the defining connectivity rule of a full mesh, so the required topology is Mesh topology.

Contrast and cross-check

  • Star topology connects peripheral nodes through a central hub or switch rather than directly connecting every pair.

  • Tree topology arranges nodes in parent-child branches across hierarchical levels.

  • “None of these” would apply only if none of the named topology categories described the stated link arrangement.

  • With four nodes, a full mesh has 4(4 − 1)/2 = 6 links, one for each node pair, which cross-checks the definition.

Result

The topology is Mesh topology.

optionFeedback.html: Star topology uses a hub-and-spoke structure: each peripheral node has a point-to-point link to one central device.
Tree topology uses a hierarchical branching structure, with parent-child links joining multiple levels.
The phrase “None of these” rejects all of the named topology categories rather than naming a network structure of its own.
Mesh topology distributes connectivity across inter-node links instead of requiring one central hub; this design provides path redundancy.

solution: Star topology is the correct answer because all devices connect to a central hub or switch. This design allows for easier troubleshooting and isolation of network failures compared to other topologies.

optionFeedback.html: Devices are connected in a closed loop, where each device has exactly two neighbors. Data travels in a single direction around the ring from one machine to the next.
All devices share a single, central backbone cable (the bus) with terminators at both ends. Data travels along the cable, and each device checks to see if the data is addressed to them.
Star topology connects devices to a central hub.

solution: The correct answer is C (Star). In a star network topology, all peripheral nodes (computers/devices) are connected directly to a central networking device, such as a switch or a hub. All data transmission passes through this central controller.

title: In which of the following network topologies, failure of one
subject: Computer Networks
text: In which of the following network topologies can the failure of one individual node break the entire communication path of the network?
solution:
Answer: C (Ring)

  • In a standard ring topology, nodes form a closed loop. Data is passed from one node to the next.

  • Because each node is part of the forwarding path, failure of one individual node can break the loop and disturb the whole network communication.

  • In a bus topology, the important distinction is that the backbone cable can affect the whole network. Failure of one attached node is different and usually does not stop the remaining nodes.

So the topology asked in the question is Ring, not Bus.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. In a tree topology, failure of a leaf node usually disconnects only that node or branch. It does not necessarily break the entire network path.

Incorrect. In a bus topology, the common backbone cable is the major single point of failure. If an attached individual node fails, the other nodes can usually continue to communicate through the backbone.
Correct. In a standard ring topology, each node forwards data to the next node in a closed loop. Failure of one individual node can break the loop and disturb communication across the network.
Incorrect. Mesh topology has redundant paths. If one node or link fails, communication can often continue through alternate paths.

text: Which of the following network topology has more complex structure?
solution: A Hybrid topology integrates two or more different standard topologies (such as Star, Bus, or Ring) into a single network. Managing, troubleshooting, and configuring the diverse architectures, hardware interfaces, and distinct complex routing rules makes its structure the most complex. Therefore, Option D is correct.

Incorrect. While a full mesh topology has a high count of redundant point-to-point connections, it follows a homogeneous structural pattern. It is less architecturally complex than a heterogeneous hybrid integration.

title: Example of fibre distributed data interconnect (FDDI) is
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following best describes the network arrangement used by Fibre Distributed Data Interface (FDDI)?
solution:
Concept

A token-passing network grants transmission permission through a control token that circulates among stations. Ring arrangements provide a closed path for this circulation; a dual counter-rotating ring adds resilience when one path is disrupted.

Application

FDDI carries data over optical fibre at 100 Mbps and uses token passing on two counter-rotating rings. The primary ring normally carries traffic, while the secondary ring provides an alternate path during a fault.

Contrast

  • Token Bus uses a shared physical bus with a logical token-passing order.

  • Star topology connects all outer stations through one central hub or switch.

  • Mesh topology uses many direct point-to-point links between stations.

  • Token ring circulates transmission permission around a closed ring, matching FDDI's token-passing dual-ring design.

Result

Therefore, among the given choices, FDDI is best described as Token ring.

optionFeedback.html: Stations share one physical backbone, while transmission permission moves in a logical sequence that can differ from their physical placement.
Each outer station has one point-to-point link to a central hub or switch, which relays traffic between the outer stations.
Multiple point-to-point links connect the stations; in the full form, each station has a direct link to every other station.
Stations form a closed path, and transmission permission circulates with a control token around that path.

title: What is the drawback of using BUS topology?
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the drawback of using a BUS topology?

options.html: Only a pair of nodes can be connected
Performance degrades as additional computers are added or on heavy traffic

solution:
Concept

A bus topology connects every node to a single shared backbone cable, which acts as one common broadcast medium. Because the medium is shared, only one device can transmit successfully at a time; access to the cable is governed by a media-access / collision-handling scheme, and the cable's total bandwidth is split among all active senders.

Applying it here

  • Every computer taps into the same backbone, so all of them compete for the one channel.

  • Adding more computers, or sending more traffic, increases contention for that single shared cable.

  • More simultaneous attempts to transmit mean more collisions, which force retransmissions and add delay.

  • The fixed cable bandwidth is now divided among more active nodes, so each node's effective throughput and response time get worse.

So the defining weakness is that throughput and responsiveness fall as the number of computers grows or as traffic rises — the network does not scale well under load.

Why the other choices fail

  • "Only a pair of nodes can be connected" — false; a bus's whole purpose is to let many nodes share one cable, not just two.

  • "There are no drawbacks" — false; the contention, collisions, and single-cable point of failure are exactly its well-known weaknesses.

  • "Very slow data rates" — a bus is not inherently slow; under light load it performs fine. The problem is degradation as load and node count rise, not a low baseline rate.

optionFeedback.html: A bus does not restrict connectivity to two nodes — its defining feature is letting many nodes share one backbone cable. Limiting connections to a single pair describes a point-to-point link, not a bus, so this is not its drawback.

On a single shared backbone, every node competes for one channel; as computers are added or traffic rises, contention and collisions grow and the fixed bandwidth is split further, so throughput and response time degrade. This poor scaling under load is the bus's hallmark weakness.

This is a blanket claim that no weaknesses exist, which cannot hold for any real topology — every design carries trade-offs. A bus in particular relies on one continuous backbone cable, so a single break or fault on that cable can disrupt the whole segment. Asserting zero drawbacks simply ignores such limitations.

A bus's signaling speed is set by the cabling and the standard it runs, not by the topology being inherently "very slow" — the same medium can carry the same nominal data rate as other layouts. Labelling the data rate itself as the defining fault mischaracterizes the medium's normal speed.

title: For devices in network, number of duplex-mode links are required
subject: Computer Networks
text: For n devices in a network, how many full-duplex point-to-point links are required in a full mesh topology?
solution:
Concept

In a full mesh topology, every unordered pair of distinct devices has one direct point-to-point link. A full-duplex link carries traffic in both directions, so the same device pair needs one physical link, not two directional links.

Application

  1. Each of the n devices is incident to n − 1 links, giving n(n − 1) link-ends in total.

  2. Every physical link has two ends and is therefore counted once from each endpoint.

  3. Dividing the link-end count by 2 gives n(n − 1)/2 physical full-duplex links.

Cross-check

For n = 4, the unordered pairs are {1,2}, {1,3}, {1,4}, {2,3}, {2,4}, and {3,4}: six links. The formula gives 4 × 3 / 2 = 6.

Result

Therefore, a full mesh of n devices requires n(n − 1)/2 full-duplex point-to-point links.

optionFeedback.html: Multiplying n by its successor produces an even integer; for n = 4, the value is 20.
Multiplying n by its predecessor produces an even integer; for n = 4, the value is 12.
Half the product of n and its successor gives the nth triangular number; for n = 4, the value is 10.
Half the product of n and its predecessor gives the binomial coefficient C(n, 2); for n = 4, the value is 6.

Correct. In a star topology each device is connected to a central node (hub, switch, or router) by a dedicated point-to-point link; the central node manages and forwards communication.

title: Which of the following statement(s) is/are not true about star
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are not true about star topology? I. Failure of the central computer shuts down the entire network II. Connection of additional computers increases the communication time
solution:
Concept: In a star topology every node connects to the network through a single central connecting device (a hub or switch) over an independent, dedicated point-to-point link — this is the standard model assumed for star topology in networking exams. Two structural consequences follow from this design: (a) the central device sits on every path between two nodes, so it is the network's single point of failure, and (b) each link's own transmission time depends primarily on that link and the central device's forwarding capacity, not on the sheer count of other nodes attached — merely attaching another device does not, by itself, add traffic onto an existing link.

Application: Applying this to the two statements —

  • Statement I: true. Because every node's path to every other node runs through the one central device, that device failing disables all communication — this is precisely the single-point-of-failure consequence above.

  • Statement II: not true, as a general/inherent claim. Because each device's link to the central device is dedicated and independent, simply connecting more computers attaches more such independent links rather than adding traffic onto an existing one, so it is not automatically or inherently true that communication time rises. (In practice, heavier aggregate traffic or a central device nearing its forwarding capacity can still slow things down, but that is a function of load and hardware capacity, not an unavoidable consequence of merely adding devices — which is the sweeping claim statement II makes.)

Cross-check: This lines up with the general contrast between switched and shared-medium topologies: in a shared-medium arrangement such as a bus, or a hub used purely as a signal repeater sharing one collision domain, every device does contend for the same channel, so adding devices reliably slows communication down. A star's dedicated links remove that automatic contention — delay can still grow if overall traffic or the central device's own capacity becomes a bottleneck, but that is a conditional, load-dependent effect, not the blanket "more devices, more delay" rule statement II states.

Therefore, only statement II is not true about star topology.

optionFeedback.html: This option's combination doubts the central-device claim while accepting the additional-computers claim without question. Of the two, the central-device claim follows directly from how a star topology is wired — every node's traffic passes through one shared connecting device, so a central failure is not the sort of consequence that depends on load or circumstance. The additional-computers claim, by contrast, is a general claim about scaling behaviour, which is exactly the kind of claim that needs its own check rather than automatic acceptance.

This option's combination matches how a star topology actually behaves: every node's path runs through one shared central device, so that device failing does disable the whole network, while each node's link to that device is dedicated and independent, so simply connecting more computers does not, by itself, add traffic onto an existing link or automatically raise its communication time — which is exactly why the additional-computers claim, taken as a general rule, is the one that does not hold.

This option's combination extends the same doubt to the central-device claim as well. But that claim does not vary with load or circumstance the way a scaling-behaviour claim can — a star topology's defining feature is that every path between two nodes runs through one shared central device, so doubting that particular claim conflicts with the topology's own basic wiring rather than with some conditional detail.

This option's combination accepts both claims exactly as stated, treating neither as needing a second look. But these two claims are of different kinds — one is a structural claim built into how a star topology is wired, and the other is a general claim about how communication scales as devices are added — and a claim of that second kind does not earn the same automatic acceptance as the wiring-based one; it needs to be checked on its own terms rather than waved through together with the first.

title: Which of the following is true for Circuit Switching handling
subject: Computer Networks
text: Using “path” to mean an end-to-end reserved circuit or channel (not necessarily a separate cable), which statement best describes how circuit switching handles multiple simultaneous connections?

options.html: A single path is used and shared for all data
It encodes all data into a single channel
Separate physical paths are allocated for each channel
All connections are multiplexed into a single channel

solution:
Concept

Circuit switching is connection-oriented: before data transfer begins, the network establishes an end-to-end circuit and reserves transmission resources for that connection until the circuit is released.

A circuit is a dedicated channel through the network. A physical link may carry several circuits in fixed time or frequency slots, but each connection retains its reserved share instead of contending for capacity packet by packet.

Application

For several simultaneous connections, the reservation rule is applied independently to each connection. If N connections are active, the network maintains N separately reserved circuits or channels through the switching fabric.

Cross-check and contrast

  • A single shared path for all data describes pooled use of one transmission resource without a dedicated circuit for each connection.

  • Encoding all data into one channel is a signal-combining operation, not the connection-reservation rule used by a switching network.

  • Multiplexing all connections into one channel describes stream sharing; circuit switching may use fixed multiplexing on a link, but the resulting circuits still have separately reserved resource shares.

  • Question not attempted is a response-state label rather than a statement about circuit switching.

Therefore, among the offered statements, the best description is that separate physical paths are allocated for each channel. Here “paths” means separately reserved circuits or channels; it does not require a different cable for every connection.

optionFeedback.html: A single shared path pools unrelated data streams onto one common transmission resource.
Encoding all data into one channel combines streams through a signal-processing or transmission method.
Separately allocated paths reserve a distinct transmission resource for each connection.
Multiplexing interleaves several streams on a shared transmission resource, such as by time or frequency.
Question not attempted records the absence of a selected networking assertion.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q70
subject: Computer Networks
text: When an e-mail is sent over a network, the message is broken into smaller pieces called:
solution:
Concept

Packet-switched communication divides application data into manageable transmission units before sending it.

Each unit carries a payload and control information so intermediary devices can forward it and the receiver can reassemble the data.

Application

An e-mail message is application data. During transmission over a packet-switched network, the message is divided into packets.

Contrast

  • Bytes are groups of eight bits used to represent digital data; they are not the delivery units named by the question.

  • Digits are symbols used to write numbers; in binary notation, those symbols are 0 and 1.

  • A process is a running instance of a program managed by an operating system.

  • Packets are formatted units that carry payload and delivery-control information across a network.

Result

Therefore, the message pieces are called packets.

optionFeedback.html: Within network data, a byte groups eight payload bits and measures the amount of encoded information.
Within a binary representation, a digit records one 0-or-1 symbol used to encode the payload.
Within the sending system, a process is the running e-mail client or service that hands data to the networking stack.
In network formatting, a packet contains a payload plus a header with addressing and protocol-control fields.

solution:
X.21 is an ITU‑T standard used for connecting data terminal equipment (DTE) to a circuit‑switched network. Key points: It is an ITU‑T recommendation that defines the physical, electrical and procedural characteristics of the interface between terminal equipment and a circuit‑switched network.

title: Match the following:
subject: Computer Networks
text: Match the following:
solution:
Correct matching and brief explanations:

  1. Network Layer — Feedback messaging (ICMP). The network layer reports network-level errors and diagnostics using protocols such as ICMP.

  2. Transport Layer — Segmentation and Reassembly. The transport layer breaks large application data into segments for transmission and reassembles them at the receiver.

  3. Data Link Layer — Access Control. The data link layer manages access to a shared physical medium (MAC-level control) using protocols such as CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA, Token Passing, etc.

  4. Session Layer — Dialogue Control. The session layer establishes, manages, and terminates sessions and controls dialog modes (full-duplex or half-duplex) between applications.

  5. Presentation Layer — Encoding & Translation. The presentation layer translates and encodes data formats so the receiving application can interpret the information (e.g., character encoding, encryption, compression).

  6. Physical Layer — Transmission Modes. The physical layer defines the physical signaling and transmission modes such as simplex, half-duplex, and full-duplex.

Therefore the correct matching is: 1 → Feedback messaging; 2 → Segmentation and Reassembly; 3 → Access Control; 4 → Dialogue Control; 5 → Encoding & Translation; 6 → Transmission Modes.

Segmentation and reassembly are performed by the Transport Layer: the transport layer breaks application data into segments and reassembles them at the receiver. The Network Layer is responsible for network-level functions such as routing and feedback/diagnostic messaging (e.g., ICMP).

Correct. Network Layer is responsible for feedback/diagnostic messages (e.g., ICMP). Transport Layer handles segmentation and reassembly. Data Link Layer controls access to the shared medium (MAC-level access). Session Layer provides dialogue control (manages sessions and duplex mode), Presentation Layer handles encoding/translation (formats, encryption, compression), and Physical Layer defines transmission modes (simplex, half-duplex, full-duplex).

This mapping places access control incorrectly for some layers and places dialogue control and transmission modes incorrectly. Access control (control of who can use a shared link) belongs to the Data Link Layer, not the Transport or Presentation layers. Dialogue control belongs to the Session Layer. Transmission modes (simplex/half-duplex/full-duplex) are properties of the Physical Layer. Review each layer’s primary responsibility to correct the mapping.

title: The physical layer is responsible for (Physical Layer)

title: In SDN architecture, what is the primary role of the
subject: Computer Networks
text: In SDN architecture, what is the primary role of the control plane?

options.html: To forward packets based on routing tables
To manage flow rules and make decisions about where traffic should go

solution:
Concept — The work a network does splits into planes. The control plane is the decision layer: it builds a view of the network, computes paths and writes the forwarding entries that devices will use. The data (forwarding) plane is the execution layer: it moves each arriving packet out of a port by looking those entries up. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) pushes this split further by lifting the control plane out of the individual devices into a logically centralised controller.

Application — In an SDN network the controller keeps a global view of the topology, decides which path traffic should take, and installs the resulting flow rules into every switch’s flow table over a southbound interface such as OpenFlow. The primary role of the control plane is therefore to manage flow rules and decide where traffic should go, while each switch is left with the fast lookup-and-forward job.

Cross-check — Each activity below belongs to a different part of the system:

Activity

Where it belongs

Forwarding a packet against installed table entries

Data (forwarding) plane inside the switch

Managing flow rules and choosing traffic paths

Control plane, centralised in the SDN controller

Physically connecting devices

Cabling, connectors and physical-layer hardware

Encrypting data before transmission

Security protocols such as IPsec or TLS

Result — The control plane manages flow rules and makes the decisions about where traffic should go.

optionFeedback.html: Forwarding packets by matching them against installed routing or flow-table entries is the per-packet execution work carried out by the data (forwarding) plane inside each switch or router.
Managing flow rules and choosing the path traffic takes is the network-wide decision work carried out by the control plane, which in SDN is centralised inside the controller.
Physically connecting devices is the job of cabling, connectors and port hardware at the physical layer, which simply carries bits between the endpoints it joins.
Encrypting data before transmission is a confidentiality service supplied by security protocols such as IPsec or TLS, which act on the payload as it crosses the network.

title: In the OSI model, which layer is responsible for end-to-end
subject: Computer Networks
text: In the OSI model, which layer is responsible for end-to-end error recovery and flow control ?
solution: The correct answer is the Transport layer. In the OSI model, the Transport layer (Layer 4) is specifically designed to manage end-to-end communication between source and destination hosts. Its primary responsibilities include ensuring reliable data delivery through error recovery mechanisms, such as retransmitting lost packets, and managing flow control to prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver. While the Data link layer handles error detection and flow control, it operates only between adjacent nodes on the same network segment (hop-to-hop), not end-to-end across the entire path. The Network layer focuses on routing and logical addressing, while the Session layer manages dialog control between applications. Therefore, because it guarantees complete data integrity and regulates transmission rates across the entire network path, the Transport layer is the definitive answer for end-to-end error recovery and flow control.

optionFeedback.html: The Network layer handles routing and logical addressing, not end-to-end error recovery.
The Transport layer manages end-to-end communication reliability and flow control between source and destination hosts.
Session layer manages dialog control between applications.
Data link layer handles error detection and flow control, it operates only between adjacent nodes on the same network segment (hop-to-hop), not end-to-end across the entire path.

title: Which of the following is not related to data link
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following is not related to data link layer?
solution:
Concept: The OSI model assigns framing, error control, and medium access control (including MAC addressing) to the Data Link Layer (Layer 2) — all single-hop responsibilities between two directly-connected nodes. Congestion control, by contrast, regulates the overall volume of traffic flowing across a network that spans multiple links and routers, so it is a Network Layer function (reinforced at the Transport Layer), not a Data Link Layer one.

Application: Checking each listed function against the data link layer's scope:

  • Framing: encapsulates packets received from the network layer into discrete frames by adding header/trailer boundaries, which are then transmitted as a bit stream — a Data Link Layer function.

  • Error control: detects and corrects bit errors introduced during transmission over a single link — a Data Link Layer function.

  • MAC addressing: uses physical hardware addresses to deliver frames to the correct node sharing that link — a Data Link Layer function.

  • Congestion control: manages traffic load across the entire network path, involving multiple routers and links — NOT a Data Link Layer function.

Note the distinction the question is testing: flow control (pacing transmission to match a receiver's capacity on a single link, e.g. via sliding-window protocols) IS performed at the Data Link Layer, but congestion control (preventing network-wide overload across many links and routers) is not — the two are often confused, but only flow control belongs to Layer 2.

Cross-check: Framing, error control, and MAC addressing are covered in every standard treatment of the Data Link Layer, while congestion-avoidance mechanisms (leaky bucket, token bucket, RED, TCP congestion control) belong to the Network/Transport Layer chapters. Of the four functions listed, congestion control is the one not related to the data link layer.

optionFeedback.html: Congestion control refers to traffic-shaping mechanisms such as leaky-bucket and token-bucket, along with TCP's slow-start, congestion-avoidance, and fast-retransmit algorithms that respond to signals like packet loss, delay, or explicit congestion notification (ECN) marks.

Error control refers to techniques such as checksum computation, cyclic redundancy check (CRC), parity bits, and automatic repeat request (ARQ) schemes like stop-and-wait or sliding-window retransmission, used to detect and recover from corrupted bits.

Framing refers to techniques such as byte stuffing, bit stuffing, and flag/delimiter patterns (for example HDLC's 01111110 flag byte) used to mark where each transmitted unit begins and ends within a continuous bit stream.

MAC addressing refers to the use of a device's hardware identifier assigned to its network interface — typically a manufacturer-assigned 48-bit address, though it can also be locally administered or changed — used to identify the intended device for frame delivery on the shared link; ARP is used separately to resolve a network-layer (IP) address to this link-layer address.

title: In TCP/IP stack, which layer is equivalent to transport layer
subject: Computer Networks
text: In TCP/IP stack, which layer is equivalent to transport layer of OSI model?
solution:
Concept

A protocol stack layer is identified by the SERVICE it provides, not only by its name. The OSI Transport layer (Layer 4) provides end-to-end delivery between two hosts: segmentation, end-to-end flow control, and error control, using port-based connections.

Mapping to the TCP/IP model

In the classic four-layer TCP/IP (DoD/ARPANET) reference model, the layer that performs exactly this end-to-end host-to-host job is the Host-to-Host layer (also written as the Transport layer in modern descriptions). It is where TCP and UDP live, providing port-addressed, end-to-end communication between processes on two hosts.

Why the other layers do not match

  • The Internet layer carries IP packets and does logical addressing and routing — that is the OSI Network layer (Layer 3), not Transport.

  • The Application layer of TCP/IP rolls together the OSI Application, Presentation and Session layers (Layers 5-7) — well above Transport.

Conclusion

The end-to-end, TCP/UDP-bearing layer is the Host-to-Host layer, so it is the TCP/IP equivalent of the OSI Transport layer. Note: "Host-to-Host" and "Transport" are two names for the SAME layer; since the option set offers "Host-to-Host Layer" and not a literal "Transport layer" choice, "None of these" is not required — Host-to-Host is the matching layer.

optionFeedback.html: The Host-to-Host layer is where TCP and UDP run, providing port-addressed end-to-end delivery between two hosts — exactly the role of the OSI Transport layer, so this is the matching layer.
The Internet layer handles IP logical addressing and packet routing, which maps to the OSI Network layer (Layer 3), not the Transport layer.
The TCP/IP Application layer combines the OSI Application, Presentation and Session layers (Layers 5-7), which sit well above the Transport layer.

"None of these" claims the TCP/IP architecture provides no layer for the OSI Transport layer's job — end-to-end delivery, flow control and error control between two communicating endpoints (the home of TCP and UDP). That function is a standard, defined part of the TCP/IP model, so the claim is false and this choice is incorrect.

title: If you use either Telnet or FTP, which is the
subject: Computer Networks
text: If you use either Telnet or FTP, which is the highest layer you are using to transmit data?
solution:
Concept

The OSI reference model organises network communication into seven layers, from the lowest (Physical) up to the highest (Application). The Application layer is the top layer — it is the one that interacts directly with end-user network services and the programs a person actually runs. A protocol's place in the stack is fixed by what job it does, not by the data it happens to carry.

Applying it here

Both Telnet (remote terminal access) and FTP (file transfer) are end-user network services: a user invokes them directly to do useful work over the network. Services that users invoke directly live at the very top of the stack — the Application layer. So whichever of the two you use, the highest layer you are operating at is the Application layer.

Why the other layers are not the answer

  • Transport delivers byte streams or datagrams between endpoints (the job TCP/UDP do). FTP and Telnet sit on top of TCP and use it, so Transport is below them — not the highest layer in use.

  • Session manages dialogue setup, checkpointing and synchronisation between two sides; it is one layer below the top and does not itself house the user-facing service.

  • Presentation handles data representation, encoding and encryption for the layer above it; it serves the Application layer rather than being the topmost layer the user drives.

The topmost layer involved when running Telnet or FTP is therefore the Application layer.

optionFeedback.html: In the OSI model the Application layer is the top layer, where end-user network services and the programs a person runs reside. That makes it the highest layer involved here.
The Presentation layer handles data representation, encoding and encryption. It is an intermediate layer in the stack, not the top one.
The Session layer manages dialogue setup, synchronisation and checkpointing between the two sides. It is an intermediate layer in the stack, not the top one.
The Transport layer (TCP/UDP) provides end-to-end delivery of data between hosts. It is one of the lower layers in the stack, well beneath the top.

title: In OSI network architecture, the dialogue control and token management
subject: Computer Networks
text: In OSI network architecture, dialogue control and token management are the responsibilities of which OSI layer?
solution:
Concept

Dialogue control, token management and synchronization are three closely-related session-management functions. Dialogue control governs whose turn it is to send, which matters in half-duplex exchange where only one side may transmit at a time; token management enforces this by passing a control token so that only the token-holder may send, preventing both ends from sending at once; synchronization inserts recovery checkpoints into the conversation.

In the seven-layer OSI model these three duties together define one specific layer: the Session layer (Layer 5), which establishes, manages and terminates the dialogue between two communicating applications.

Applying it here

The question lists exactly two of these defining functions — dialogue control and token management. Both are textbook duties of the Session layer, so the responsibility lies with the Session layer.

How the other layers differ

  • Network layer — its job is logical addressing and routing of packets across networks (choosing the path), not coordinating whose turn it is to send between applications.

  • Transport layer — its job is reliable process-to-process delivery: segmentation, end-to-end flow control and error recovery between endpoints, not passing dialogue control tokens.

  • Data link layer — its job is framing bits and node-to-node delivery with error and flow control over a single physical link, not managing application conversations.

Cross-check: dialogue control, sessions and synchronization are the textbook hallmarks of Layer 5, which confirms the Session layer.

optionFeedback.html: This layer's role is session management between two applications: dialogue control (deciding whose turn it is to transmit), token management (passing a control token that grants that turn), and synchronization.
This layer's role is logical addressing and routing of packets across networks — selecting the path from source to destination.
This layer's role is reliable process-to-process delivery between endpoints — segmentation, end-to-end flow control and error recovery.
This layer's role is framing bits and node-to-node delivery over a single physical link, with link-level error and flow control.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q151
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for routing?
solution:
The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) reference model divides network communication into seven layers, each with a distinct, non-overlapping job. Selecting a path for data across multiple interconnected networks — using logical addressing and routing tables — is the responsibility defined for Layer 3, the Network Layer, in the OSI specification.

The question asks which layer moves data across separate, interconnected networks by choosing a path between them — this is exactly the Network Layer's defined role, so the Network Layer is the layer being asked about.

  • Data Link Layer (Layer 2) handles delivery of frames between two directly connected nodes on the same network segment, using physical/MAC addressing — a different scope than moving data between separate networks.

  • Transport Layer (Layer 4) handles end-to-end delivery of data segments between processes on the source and destination hosts, assuming a network path already exists between them.

  • Application Layer (Layer 7) provides the interface through which user software accesses network services, operating above the layers concerned with choosing a network path.

Because selecting a path for data across interconnected networks is uniquely defined as the Network Layer's job in the OSI model, Network Layer is the correct answer.

title: Why was the TCP/IP model designed with fewer layers than
subject: Computer Networks
text: Why was the TCP/IP model designed with fewer layers than OSI?
solution:
The OSI Approach (Theoretical): The Open Systems Interconnection model was built as an academic exercise. The designers mapped out every conceivable service a network could offer and isolated them into 7 strict boundaries. Because the model was built before the software existed, some layers turned out to be nearly empty or highly redundant in actual practice.

The TCP/IP Approach (Pragmatic): The TCP/IP suite was engineered by programmers who were actively building working network nodes. They grouped tasks based on how software functions are naturally implemented in an operating system's protocol stack.

optionFeedback.html: This option is incorrect because increasing protocol overhead would reduce efficiency. TCP/IP was designed to be simpler and more practical, not to add unnecessary complexity.

The OSI model was designed by a committee (ISO) as a highly detailed, theoretical framework before the actual protocols were written. Conversely, the TCP/IP model was developed based on working hardware and software (ARPANET). It consolidated functionalities (like merging session, presentation, and application into a single layer) because, in real-world software engineering, separating them created unnecessary complexity and slowed down data processing.

While the US Department of Defense (DoD) funded the initial research for ARPANET (which birthed TCP/IP), the model's structural design with fewer layers was a technical engineering decision to create a robust, fault-tolerant network, not an attempt to enforce bureaucratic or legal government regulations.

This describes the OSI model, not the TCP/IP model. The OSI model prioritized strict theoretical completeness, giving every distinct sub-task its own dedicated layer (7 layers total). TCP/IP completely rejected this rigid academic approach in favor of what was practical and fast to code into operating system kernels.

title: In slotted ALOHA with G-stations attempting to transmit in one
subject: Computer Networks
text: In a slotted ALOHA with G-stations attempting to transmit in one slot, the throughput is equal to –
solution:
In slotted ALOHA, a station may start a transmission only at the beginning of a fixed-length time slot, so every attempt in a given slot is synchronized with every other attempt. If stations together offer G transmission attempts per slot on average, the number of attempts landing in any one slot follows a Poisson distribution with mean G: P(exactly k attempts in a slot) = (Gᵏ × e⁻ᴳ) / k!. Throughput is the probability that a slot carries exactly one attempt (k = 1), since zero attempts wastes the slot and two or more attempts collide and destroy each other.

Applying the Poisson formula for a successful (collision-free) slot:

  1. Write the general Poisson probability of exactly k attempts in a slot: P(k) = (Gᵏ × e⁻ᴳ) / k!.

  2. A slot is successful only when exactly one attempt lands in it, so set k = 1: P(1) = (G¹ × e⁻ᴳ) / 1!.

  3. Simplify the factorial and the exponent: P(1) = G × e⁻ᴳ.

  4. Throughput S is this success probability, so S = G × e⁻ᴳ.

As an independent check, differentiate S with respect to G and set the result to zero: this locates the maximum at G = 1, giving S = 1 × e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368. That matches the well-known textbook result that slotted ALOHA peaks at about 36.8% throughput — exactly double pure ALOHA's peak of about 18.4% — which confirms the formula.

So the throughput of slotted ALOHA is S = G × e⁻ᴳ.

optionFeedback.html: This is exactly the Poisson probability of a slot carrying just one transmission attempt — P(1) = G¹ × e⁻ᴳ / 1! = G × e⁻ᴳ — which is the slotted-ALOHA throughput expression.

This is the well-known throughput expression for pure (unslotted) ALOHA, where a station may begin transmission at any instant rather than only at the start of a fixed slot. Slotted ALOHA imposes that slot-boundary synchronization instead, so this continuous-time model's expression is not the right one for the slotted case.

This flips the sign on the exponent, so the expression grows without bound as attempts increase. Throughput is a probability, so it must stay between 0 and 1 and must fall back toward zero once a slot is heavily contended — a positive exponent cannot produce that behaviour.

This doubles the coefficient in front of the exponential term instead of doubling the exponent. The factor of two that separates pure ALOHA from slotted ALOHA belongs inside the exponent, arising from the wider vulnerable period, not as a multiplier on the leading G.

subject: Computer Networks
text: The throughput of pure ALOHA is given by:
solution:
Concept: Throughput S of a random-access protocol equals the offered load G multiplied by the probability that a transmitted frame survives without a collision — i.e. S = G × P(no collision). In pure ALOHA a station transmits the instant it is ready, with no time-slotting, so any two transmissions that overlap even partially collide.

  1. A frame with transmission time Tt sent at time t0 collides with any other frame whose transmission begins in the interval (t0 − Tt, t0 + Tt); this vulnerable period therefore has length 2Tt — twice the frame time (in slotted ALOHA, slot alignment shrinks the vulnerable period to just Tt).

  2. Frame arrivals are modelled as a Poisson process with average rate G frames per frame-time, so the number of arrivals k in an interval spanning τ frame-times has probability P(k) = (Gτ)ᵏ e−Gτ / k!.

  3. A frame survives only if zero other frames arrive during its own vulnerable period, τ = 2. Substituting k = 0, τ = 2 gives the success probability P(0) = e−2G.

  4. Multiplying the offered load by this success probability gives the throughput: S = G · e−2G.

Cross-check: Differentiating S = G·e−2G with respect to G gives dS/dG = e−2G(1 − 2G); setting this to zero gives G = 0.5, and substituting back gives Smax = 0.5 × e−1 ≈ 0.184 — the well-known 18.4% peak efficiency of pure ALOHA, confirming the derived formula. (The analogous derivation for slotted ALOHA drops the factor of 2 in the vulnerable-period length, giving S = G·e−G with a higher peak of 36.8% at G = 1 — consistent with slotting halving the vulnerable period.)

solution: CSMA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access) relies on the ability of nodes to detect collisions on a shared medium. title: Assume that and are only active stations on an ethernet.
subject: Computer Networks
text: Assume that A and b are only active stations on an ethernet. Both have a steady queue of frames to send. To get the control on the channel they use a binary exponential algorithm. Both are attempting to transmit the frame. The probability that both are successfully allowed to send the frame on the 4th round and in earlier attempts both A and B collides is ________. (Upto 2 decimal places)
solution:
Key idea: compute the probability of collision in each round, then multiply the probabilities that collisions happen in the first three rounds and that no collision happens in the fourth round.

  • 1st round (window size = 1): both must transmit immediately, so collision probability = 1.

  • 2nd round (window size = 2): each picks a slot uniformly from 2 slots; collision occurs if they pick the same slot, so collision probability = 1/2.

  • 3rd round (window size = 4): collision probability = 1/4 (they pick the same slot among 4).

  • 4th round (window size = 8): probability of no collision is 1 minus the probability they pick the same slot, so no-collision probability = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.

Multiply the probabilities: P = 1 × 1/2 × 1/4 × 7/8 = 7/64 ≈ 0.109375

Final answer (rounded to 2 decimal places): 0.11

title: What is the minimum frame size (in Mbits) required in
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the minimum frame size (in Mbits) required in a CSMA/CD network with bandwidth of 1 Gbps and one-way propagation delay of 40 ms?
solution:
Key idea: the minimum frame must be long enough that the sender is still transmitting when a collision signal can travel to the sender (i.e., at least one round-trip propagation time of the link).

  • Compute the round-trip time: 2 × one-way propagation delay = 2 × 40 ms = 80 ms.

  • Convert bandwidth to bits per second: 1 Gbps = 1 × 10^9 bits/s.

  • Minimum frame size (in bits) = round-trip time × bandwidth = 80 ms × 1 × 10^9 bits/s = 0.08 s × 1 × 10^9 bits/s = 80 × 10^6 bits.

  • Convert to Mbits: 80 × 10^6 bits = 80 Mbits.

Answer: 80 Mbits (which lies within the provided acceptable range of 78–82 Mbits).

solution:
Key formula: For CSMA/CD the round-trip propagation delay must be no greater than the frame transmission time.

  • Convert frame size to bits: 20 KB = 20 × 8 × 10^3 = 160,000 bits (using decimal kilo for clarity).

  • Compute transmission time: 160,000 bits / 10,000,000 bps = 0.016 s.

  • Solve for distance: distance ≤ (transmission_time × propagation_speed) / 2 = (0.016 s × 15 km/s) / 2 = 0.12 km = 120 m.

  • Case 2 (if the question actually meant 10 Kbps): transmission_time = 160,000 / 10,000 = 16 s, so distance ≤ (16 s × 15 km/s) / 2 = 120 km.

text: Determine the efficiency of CSMA/CD if the maximum cable length for transmitting data at a rate of 80 Kbps is 16 KM. The signal speed in the cable is 8 * 105 m/s and the frame size is 1264 bits.

  • Compute efficiency: 1 / (1 + 5.65 × 1.2658) ≈ 0.1227 = 12.27%.

text: Suppose two nodes, A and B are attached to opposite ends of the cable with propagation delay of 12.5 μs. Both nodes attempt to transmit at time t = 0. Frames collide and after first collision, A draws k = 0 and B draws k = 1 in the exponential back off protocol. Ignore the jam signal. Then at what time (in seconds) is A’s packet completely delivered at B in μs, if Bandwidth of the link is 10 Mbps and packet size is 1000 bits
solution:
Key data: packet size = 1000 bits; bandwidth = 10 Mbps; one-way propagation delay = 12.5 μs; k for A = 0, k for B = 1.

  1. Compute transmission time for the packet: transmission time = packet size / bandwidth = 1000 bits / (10 × 10^6 bps) = 100 μs.

  2. Collision detection and backoff: both nodes start at t = 0 and detect the collision when the other node's signal reaches them, at 12.5 μs. After that, A uses k = 0 and B uses k = 1.

  3. When can A retransmit? Both nodes stop transmitting as soon as they detect the collision (at 12.5 μs). The last transmitted signal fragments still propagate for another one-way delay (12.5 μs), so the medium becomes idle at 12.5 + 12.5 = 25 μs. With k = 0, A can start retransmission immediately when the medium becomes idle, i.e., at 25 μs.

  4. Check B's retransmission: the slot time here equals the round-trip propagation (2 × 12.5 μs = 25 μs). B waits one slot after collision detection and will attempt at 12.5 + 25 = 37.5 μs, so A's retransmission (starting at 25 μs) proceeds without further collision.

  5. Compute completion time at B: A finishes sending at 25 + 100 = 125 μs. The last bit then needs one-way propagation (12.5 μs) to reach B, so the packet is completely delivered at B at 125 + 12.5 = 137.5 μs.

Final answer: 137.5 μs.

Note: the original solution used the same reasoning but was provided as an image. This text version clarifies why 25 μs is added (medium remains busy until in-flight signals clear) and shows each timing step explicitly.
