title: With each successive collision in CSMA/CD Protocol
subject: Computer Networks
text: With each successive collision in CSMA/CD Protocol
solution:
Answer: Collision probability decreases exponentially.

Reason: CSMA/CD uses a binary exponential backoff. After the x-th collision, each station chooses a random backoff K uniformly from 0 to 2^x - 1 (in practice this range is often capped after a maximum number of attempts).

  • For two stations both at the same backoff stage x, there are 2^x possible choices for each station, so total ordered pairs of choices = 2^x × 2^x = 2^(2x).

  • A collision occurs when both stations pick the same K. There are 2^x such matching pairs.

  • Therefore probability of collision = (number of matching pairs) / (total pairs) = 2^x / 2^(2x) = 1 / 2^x.

  • Example: x = 1 → probability = 1/2; x = 2 → probability = 1/4; x = 3 → probability = 1/8. The probability falls by a factor of two for each additional backoff stage, i.e., it decreases exponentially.

  • Note: In real implementations there is a maximum backoff stage (a cap), so the exponential decrease holds until that cap is reached.

optionFeedback.html: The protocol uses a binary exponential backoff, which means the range of possible backoff slots doubles after each collision. Saying "backoff time increases two times" is ambiguous: the contention window doubles, which reduces the chance of repeated collisions, but the better statement about successive collisions is that collision probability falls (not that backoff time simply "increases two times").

This is incorrect. The collision probability does not increase exponentially with successive collisions. Instead, CSMA/CD uses an exponential backoff that expands the range of random backoff choices, which reduces the chance that nodes pick the same slot again, so collision probability decreases.

Correct. CSMA/CD uses a binary exponential backoff: after the x-th collision each node picks a random backoff K uniformly from 0 to 2^x - 1 (often capped at a maximum stage). For two contending stations at the same backoff stage x, the probability both choose the same slot is 1/2^x, which decreases exponentially as x increases.

This is incorrect. The backoff range grows (it doubles each step in binary exponential backoff), it does not decrease exponentially. The larger backoff range is what lowers collision probability over successive attempts.

L = 10,000 bits

L = 10,000 / 8 = 1250 Bytes

The minimum frame size required for this network is 10,000 bits (or 1250 bytes).

title: In computer network using CSMA/CD, the minimum frame size for
subject: Computer Networks
text: In a computer network using CSMA/CD, the minimum frame size for reliable collision detection is 1500 bytes. What will be the data transfer speed in this network over a 1 Km cable, if the signal speed in the cable is 250000 Km/sec and no repeaters are used in this network?
solution:
In CSMA/CD, a sending station must still be transmitting when a collision signal from the far end of the link returns, otherwise it cannot detect the collision. This is only guaranteed when the frame transmission time is at least twice the one-way propagation delay of the link (the round-trip time for a collision signal), giving the governing relation: Bandwidth = Frame size (in bits) / (2 x Propagation delay).

  1. Convert the minimum frame size to bits: 1500 bytes x 8 = 12,000 bits.

  2. Find the one-way propagation delay for the 1 Km cable at a signal speed of 250000 Km/sec: Propagation delay = distance / speed = 1 Km / 250000 Km/sec = 4 microseconds.

  3. Double the propagation delay to get the round-trip (collision-detection) time: 2 x 4 microseconds = 8 microseconds.

  4. Since 1500 bytes is stated as the minimum frame size, apply the relation at equality: Bandwidth = Frame size / round-trip time = 12,000 bits / 8 microseconds = 1.5 x 109 bps = 1.5 Gbps.

Check: at 1.5 Gbps, transmitting a 12,000-bit frame takes 12,000 / (1.5 x 109) = 8 microseconds, exactly matching the round-trip time above -- confirming that 1500 bytes is indeed the minimum frame size for reliable collision detection on this 1 Km link, at a data rate of 1.5 Gbps.

100 Mbps is a familiar, commonly-seen network data rate, but it does not follow from the frame size, cable length, and signal speed actually given in this problem -- rework the propagation-delay and round-trip-time calculation from the numbers stated here rather than picking a familiar round value.
This value results from mixing the frame-size unit and the round-trip-time unit inconsistently -- recheck that both quantities feeding your division are in the same, correctly derived units.

Converting the 1500-byte frame to 12,000 bits, and computing the one-way propagation delay for the 1 Km cable at 250000 Km/sec gives 4 microseconds; for CSMA/CD's minimum-frame-size condition, the round-trip time is twice this -- 8 microseconds -- so the data rate is 12,000 bits divided by 8 microseconds, i.e. 1.5 x 109 bits per second = 1.5 Gbps.

title: Which of the following is true? Hidden terminal can be
subject: Computer Networks
text:
Which of the following is true?

S1: Hidden terminal can be handled using RTS/CTS

S2: RTS/CTS exchanges help to reduce collisions but it uses the more channel resources and not efficient use of channel resources .
solution:
Answer: Both statements are correct.

Explanation:

  • Statement S1 (hidden terminal): RTS/CTS can mitigate the hidden terminal problem. The sender issues an RTS and the receiver replies with a CTS; nodes that hear the CTS know to defer, which prevents collisions caused by transmitters that cannot hear each other.

  • Statement S2 (overhead and efficiency): RTS/CTS reduces collisions but introduces additional control frames (RTS and CTS) and timing overhead, which consumes channel resources. This extra overhead can make RTS/CTS inefficient for small data frames or in low-contention environments.

Practical note: Use RTS/CTS when the risk of costly collisions is high (large frames or many hidden terminals). Skip RTS/CTS when frames are small or contention is low to avoid unnecessary overhead.

optionFeedback.html: Choosing the answer that only says S1 is incomplete. Statement S1 is correct: RTS/CTS can mitigate the hidden terminal problem by having the sender issue an RTS and the receiver reply with a CTS so nearby nodes defer transmission. However, Statement S2 is also correct: RTS/CTS reduces collisions but introduces extra control frames and delays, using more channel resources. Therefore the best answer is that both statements are true.

Choosing the answer that only says S2 is incomplete. Statement S2 is correct: RTS/CTS exchanges reduce collisions but add overhead (extra control frames and timing), making channel use less efficient in some cases. However, Statement S1 is also correct: RTS/CTS is specifically used to handle the hidden terminal problem. So the correct conclusion is that both statements are true.

Correct. Both statements are true. RTS/CTS helps handle the hidden terminal problem by coordinating transmissions (sender sends RTS, receiver replies CTS, neighbors hearing CTS defer). At the same time, using RTS/CTS adds control-frame overhead and extra waiting time, so it reduces collisions but uses more channel resources and can be inefficient for short frames or low-contention scenarios.

Choosing 'none of the above' is incorrect. Both statements are true: RTS/CTS does help mitigate the hidden terminal problem, and RTS/CTS exchanges reduce collisions but add overhead and use more channel resources, which can be inefficient in some situations.

title: Network Allocation Vector (NAV) is associated with which of the
subject: Computer Networks
text: Network Allocation Vector (NAV) is associated with which of the following MAC technologies?
solution:
Concept

In an IEEE 802.11 medium-access system, carrier sensing has physical and virtual components. Physical sensing observes radio energy, while virtual sensing uses timing information carried in frames.

The Network Allocation Vector (NAV) is the virtual-sensing countdown. A station updates it from the Duration/ID field and treats the medium as reserved while the countdown remains positive.

Application

  1. Suppose a station overhears an IEEE 802.11 frame whose Duration/ID field reserves the medium for 500 microseconds.

  2. The station loads that interval into its NAV and defers a new transmission while the timer counts down.

  3. This virtual carrier-sensing procedure is part of the IEEE 802.11 MAC used by Wi-Fi, alongside CSMA/CA.

Cross-check and contrast

  • CSMA/CD belongs to the classic shared-Ethernet collision-detection procedure rather than this wireless reservation timer.

  • Bluetooth uses its own short-range radio access procedures and is not the IEEE 802.11 MAC family.

  • Ethernet names the IEEE 802.3 family; classic shared Ethernet senses and detects collisions instead of maintaining this IEEE 802.11 reservation state.

  • Question not attempted describes a response state, not a MAC technology.

Therefore, the MAC technology associated with NAV is Wi-Fi.

optionFeedback.html: CSMA/CD senses a shared wired medium before transmission and detects collisions after transmission begins; a collision triggers backoff and retry.
Bluetooth coordinates short-range radio access through scheduled time slots and adaptive frequency hopping; connected devices follow its link-controller scheduling.
Wi-Fi implements the IEEE 802.11 MAC; its virtual carrier-sensing state is maintained as a countdown from Duration/ID information in overheard frames.
Classic shared Ethernet coordinates medium access through carrier sensing and collision detection; a detected collision triggers backoff and retransmission.
Question not attempted records a response state rather than a medium-access technology; it supplies no protocol mechanism for classification.

title: If the packet size is bits, the rate of channel
subject: Computer Networks
text: If the packet size is 5000 bits, the rate of channel is 4 kbps and distance between the hosts is 20 km. Speed of propagation over the transmission media is 200 m/s. Calculate the link utilization for stop and wait flow control mechanism.
solution:
Given: packet size = 5000 bits; channel rate = 4 kbps (4000 bps); distance = 20 km (20000 m); propagation speed = 200 m/s.

Transmission time (Tt): Tt = 5000 bits / 4000 bps = 1.25 s.

Propagation time (Tp): Tp = 20000 m / 200 m/s = 100 s.

Stop-and-wait utilization formula: U = Tt / (Tt + 2·Tp) = 1 / (1 + 2a), where a = Tp / Tt.

  • Compute a: a = Tp / Tt = 100 / 1.25 = 80.

  • Compute utilization: U = 1 / (1 + 2·80) = 1 / 161 ≈ 0.00621.

text: Consider a system with link utilization is 50%, R.T.T = 50μs and bandwidth is 10 Mbps. what is the data size (in bytes) ___________
solution:
Given: link utilization (efficiency) = 0.5, RTT = 50 μs, bandwidth = 10 Mbps. Find the data size.

  • Let S = data size in bits. Transmission time T = S / 10×10^6 seconds.

  • For stop-and-wait, utilization = transmission time / (transmission time + RTT). So:

  • 0.5 = (S / 10×10^6) / ( (S / 10×10^6) + 50×10^-6 )

  • Multiply numerator and denominator by 10×10^6 to simplify:

  • 0.5 = S / (S + 500)

  • Solve: 0.5(S + 500) = S → 0.5S + 250 = S → 250 = 0.5S → S = 500 bits.

  • Convert to bytes: 500 bits ÷ 8 = 62.5 bytes.

Answer: 62.5 bytes (500 bits).

title: Calculate the link utilization (throughput) for the stop-and-wait flow control

text: Calculate the link utilization (efficiency) for the stop-and-wait flow control mechanism if the frame size is 4800 bits, bit rate is 9600 bps, and the distance between the devices is 2000 km. Given propagation speed is 200000 km/s.
solution:
Concept: In stop-and-wait flow control, the sender transmits one frame and then waits idle for its acknowledgement before sending the next. Link utilization (also called efficiency) is the fraction of time the link actually carries data, given by Tt / (Tt + 2Tp), where Tt is the transmission time and Tp is the one-way propagation time. The factor 2Tp accounts for the round trip the frame and its acknowledgement travel. This is a pure dimensionless ratio between 0 and 1 — it is not the throughput in bits per second.

Application: Substitute the given values step by step.

  1. Transmission time Tt = frame size / bit rate = 4800 / 9600 = 0.5 s.

  2. Propagation time Tp = distance / propagation speed = 2000 / 200000 = 0.01 s.

  3. Efficiency = Tt / (Tt + 2Tp) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 2 × 0.01) = 0.5 / 0.52 = 0.9615.

Cross-check: Because the transmission time (0.5 s) is much larger than the round-trip propagation overhead (2 × 0.01 = 0.02 s), the sender stays busy almost the whole time, so the efficiency must be close to 1 — and 0.9615 ≈ 0.96 confirms this. (For reference, the actual data throughput would be 0.96 × 9600 ≈ 9231 bps; the utilization asked here is the ratio 0.96, not this bps value.)

Result: The link utilization is approximately 0.96.

title: The selective repeat protocol is similar to Go back except
subject: Computer Networks
text: The selective repeat protocol is similar to Go back N except in the following way

options.html: Frame Formats are similar in both the protocols
The sender has a window defining maximum number of outstanding frames in both the protocols
Both uses piggybacked acknowledgements where possible and does not acknowledge every frame explicitly.

solution:
Correct selections: the statements concerning piggybacked acknowledgements and the practice of acknowledging the most recently received frame represent the exception (difference) between selective repeat and Go-Back-N.

Key differences (why those statements are the exceptions):

  • Acknowledgement behavior: Go-Back-N uses cumulative acknowledgements that effectively acknowledge the highest in-order frame received (it does not send an individual acknowledgement for every received frame). Selective Repeat, by contrast, acknowledges each frame individually so the sender knows exactly which frames were received and which need retransmission.

  • Retransmission and buffering: Go-Back-N discards out-of-order frames at the receiver and the sender retransmits from the missing frame onward. Selective Repeat allows the receiver to buffer out-of-order frames and only retransmits the specific missing frames.

  • Piggybacking: both protocols can use piggybacked acknowledgements when the receiver has data to send back. However, piggybacking does not change the fundamental difference in acknowledgement granularity described above.

Why the other statements are not the exceptions:

  • Frame format similarity: both protocols use similar frame structures because both are sliding-window protocols; this is a similarity, not the distinguishing feature.

  • Sender window: both protocols use a sender window to limit outstanding frames. That is a shared characteristic of sliding-window schemes, not the exception asked for.

Summary: The main exception (difference) is in acknowledgement and retransmission behavior: Go-Back-N uses cumulative acknowledgements and retransmits multiple frames after a loss, while Selective Repeat uses individual acknowledgements and retransmits only the missing frames.

This statement is correct as a similarity: both protocols use a sender window that limits the maximum number of outstanding (unacknowledged) frames. This is common to sliding-window protocols and is not the key difference.

This statement mixes two ideas. Both protocols can use piggybacked acknowledgements when a return data frame is available, but they differ in acknowledgement semantics. Go-Back-N typically uses cumulative acknowledgements and may not acknowledge every individual frame explicitly, whereas Selective Repeat sends acknowledgements for individual frames (so it can acknowledge out-of-order frames). This difference in acknowledgement behavior is one of the key distinctions between the protocols.

Piggybacking as a technique can be used by both protocols, but the phrase about acknowledging the most recently received frame describes cumulative acknowledgement behavior (acknowledging the highest in-order frame) which applies to Go-Back-N, not to Selective Repeat. title: How many check bits are required for bit data word
subject: Computer Networks
text: How many check bits are required for a 16-bit data word to detect 2-bit errors and correct single-bit errors using a Hamming code (SEC-DED)?
solution:
A Hamming code built only for single-error correction (SEC) needs the smallest check-bit count r satisfying 2r ≥ m + r + 1 for an m-bit data word. To also detect double-bit errors (SEC-DED), one further overall parity bit is added on top of that SEC code, so the total check-bit count p must instead satisfy 2(p−1) ≥ m + p.

  1. For a 16-bit data word, m = 16. Testing p = 5 in the SEC-DED inequality: 2(p−1) = 24 = 16, and m + p = 16 + 5 = 21; since 16 is less than 21, 5 check bits do not satisfy the inequality.

  2. Testing p = 6: 2(p−1) = 25 = 32, and m + p = 16 + 6 = 22; since 32 is at least 22, the inequality is satisfied.

  3. Since p = 5 fails and p = 6 is the smallest value that satisfies the inequality, 6 is the minimum number of check bits required.

Independent check: build the SEC-DED code from a plain SEC Hamming code. For m = 16, the smallest r satisfying 2r ≥ m + r + 1 is r = 5, since 25 = 32 ≥ 16 + 5 + 1 = 22, while 24 = 16 does not cover 16 + 4 + 1 = 21. Adding the one extra overall parity bit needed for double-error detection gives 5 + 1 = 6 total check bits, matching the result above.

So a 16-bit data word needs 6 check bits for a SEC-DED Hamming code, which matches the official ISRO 2013 Computer Science answer key.

optionFeedback.html: With 5 check bits added to a 16-bit data word, the total transmitted codeword is 21 bits long.
With 6 check bits added to a 16-bit data word, the total transmitted codeword is 22 bits long.
With 7 check bits added to a 16-bit data word, the total transmitted codeword is 23 bits long.
With 8 check bits added to a 16-bit data word, the total transmitted codeword is 24 bits long.

title: Which sublayer of DLL is responsible for error detection?
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which sublayer of DLL is responsible for error detection?
solution:
Concept. Handling errors on a link is two separate jobs, and the IEEE 802 model places them in two different sublayers of the data link layer. Detection answers one question — are the bits that arrived the bits that were sent? — and is answered by a redundancy check carried inside every frame. Error control, or recovery, is what happens afterwards: acknowledging frames, keeping them in sequence and retransmitting whatever did not survive.

Applying the split to the data link sublayers:

  1. The sending station’s Media Access Control sublayer runs a cyclic redundancy check over the frame’s fields and writes the result into the frame check sequence, the trailer that closes every IEEE 802.3 frame.

  2. The receiving Media Access Control sublayer recomputes that same CRC over the bits it actually received and compares the result with the frame check sequence it was handed. A mismatch means the frame is damaged, and the frame is discarded. This recompute-and-compare step is precisely what “error detection” names.

  3. Logical Link Control, IEEE 802.2, sits above it and defines no check field of its own. Its acknowledged and connection-mode services number frames, acknowledge them and retransmit the missing ones — that is error control and recovery, which can only run after some other mechanism has already detected the damage.

Cross-check against the standards and the other candidates:

  • IEEE Std 802 lists among the Media Access Control sublayer’s functions “protection against errors, generally by means of generating and checking frame check sequences”, and IEEE 802.3 assigns frame check sequence generation and validation to that sublayer while stating that it provides no error recovery.

  • The physical layer moves an unstructured stream of bits and defines no frame fields at all, so there is nothing there to compute a check over.

  • The application layer operates on user-level messages several layers above the link between two directly connected stations.

A word on the exam shorthand. IEEE 802 is often summarised in one line as “LLC — flow control and error control; MAC — media access”, and that line is what makes Logical Link Control look attractive here. It is a statement about error control — the acknowledgement-and-retransmission machinery. The step that actually detects a corrupted frame is the frame check sequence, and that field is generated and verified by the Media Access Control sublayer.

Answer: MAC.

optionFeedback.html: Logical Link Control (LLC) is the upper sublayer of the data link layer, standardised as IEEE 802.2. It presents one uniform interface to the network layer and identifies which upper-layer protocol a frame is carrying. It is also the sublayer whose connection-mode and acknowledged services define the sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmissions exchanged between the two link endpoints.

Media Access Control (MAC) is the lower sublayer of the data link layer. It defines the hardware address that identifies a station on the link and the rules by which stations share the medium, such as CSMA/CD on classic Ethernet. It is also the sublayer that assembles and disassembles the frame itself, whose fields include those hardware addresses, the payload and the frame check sequence trailer.

The physical layer is the OSI layer immediately below the data link layer. It specifies voltage levels, bit timing, connectors, cabling and modulation, and it carries an unstructured stream of bits across the medium, leaving frame boundaries and the meaning of individual frame fields to the layer above it.

The application layer is the topmost layer of the OSI model. It defines the protocols through which user programs reach network services - HTTP, SMTP, FTP and DNS among them - and it works on user-level messages, several layers removed from the link between two directly connected stations.

title: The main function of Data link layer is
subject: Computer Networks
text: The main function of Data link layer is
solution:
Concept: In the OSI reference model, each layer is assigned its own distinct set of responsibilities so that node-to-node link handling stays separate from end-to-end network and application concerns. The Data Link layer's mandate covers framing (dividing the bit stream into frames), physical (MAC) addressing between adjacent nodes, medium access control, flow control on the link, and — the responsibility most emphasized in standard curricula — error control: detecting bit errors introduced by the physical medium and recovering from them, using detection methods such as CRC/parity together with correction mechanisms such as Hamming/Reed–Solomon codes or ARQ-based retransmission.

Application: Among the given options, only “Error detection and Correction” matches this mandate: the Data Link layer both detects errors (CRC/parity) and recovers from them, either via a forward error-correcting code (e.g., Hamming) or by having the sender retransmit the frame after a NAK/timeout (ARQ) — so “correction” here does not require the receiver to always fix bits itself; requesting a clean retransmission is itself a standard, textbook form of error correction at this layer. This is why the reported concern (“only detection, not correction”) does not hold: correction is achieved through retransmission-based ARQ (the common case) and, on some links (e.g., wireless/satellite), through FEC codes as well — both are documented Data Link layer mechanisms, not just detection.

Cross-check — why the other options do not fit:

  • Routing selects a path for data across multiple interconnected networks using logical (IP) addressing; this is a Network layer function, operating beyond a single physical link.

  • Encryption is generally provided at higher layers (e.g., TLS, IPsec) or as an optional feature of specific link technologies; it is not this layer's principal, defining responsibility.

  • “None” is ruled out because this layer does have well-documented responsibilities of its own — framing, physical addressing, flow control, and media access, in addition to error control.

Result: The main function among the options offered is “Error detection and Correction.”

optionFeedback.html: Routing is the process of selecting a path for data across multiple interconnected networks, based on logical (IP) addressing, carried out using routing tables and routing protocols (such as OSPF or BGP) that operate between routers.

Error detection and correction refers to identifying bit errors introduced on a transmission medium — typically using techniques such as CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) or parity — and recovering from them, either through error-correcting codes (e.g., Hamming codes) or by requesting retransmission of the affected frame (ARQ), using node-level (MAC) addressing on a single physical link.

Encryption transforms data to protect its confidentiality from unauthorized access, carried out through cryptographic protocols such as TLS or IPsec that operate at the transport, network, or application layers, or optionally as a link-level feature on some specific link technologies.

This option asserts that no distinct set of responsibilities — such as dividing the bit stream into frames, assigning node-level (MAC) addresses for each hop, medium access control, and flow control on the link — exists at this layer, treating all such tasks as absent or delegated entirely to other layers.

title: Which of the following methods is used to detect double
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following methods is used to detect double errors?
solution: To detect double errors effectively, one must use a method that can identify changes in multiple bits simultaneously. Parity schemes like Odd or Even Parity are limited because they only check if the total number of set bits is odd or even. If two bits flip, the parity remains unchanged (e.g., an even number of errors preserves even parity), making single-bit error detection the maximum capability for these methods. In contrast, Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) employs polynomial division to generate a checksum that is highly sensitive to multiple bit errors. This mathematical approach ensures that even if two bits are corrupted during transmission, the resulting checksum will differ from the expected value, allowing for reliable detection. Therefore, CRC is the superior choice among the options provided for detecting double errors.

optionFeedback.html: Parity schemes typically detect single-bit errors. Flipping two bits preserves the parity state, making double errors undetectable.
Parity schemes typically detect single-bit errors. Flipping two bits preserves the parity state, making double errors undetectable.
CRC uses polynomial division to generate a robust checksum capable of detecting multiple bit errors, including double errors.
XOR-based checksums often fail to detect errors where an even number of bits flip, as the changes cancel out.

title: Communication system is designed using the following three bit words

text:
A communication system is designed using the following three 5 bit words as the only valid codewords and uses error correction using hamming distance.

During operation, receiver gets the word 01000. What would the system conclude?

options.html: It will be unable to correct the error

solution:
Concept

In minimum-distance (nearest-neighbour) decoding, a received word is corrected to the valid codeword that lies at the smallest Hamming distance from it. The Hamming distance between two equal-length bit strings is the number of positions in which they differ. A correction is committed only when exactly one valid codeword is strictly closest; if two or more valid codewords share that smallest distance, no unique nearest codeword exists and the error cannot be resolved unambiguously.

Application

Compute the Hamming distance from the received word 01000 to each valid codeword by counting the differing bit positions:

Codeword

Bits

Differing positions vs 01000

A

position 2

The smallest Hamming distance is 1, and it is achieved by two different valid codewords, 00000 and 11000. Because the minimum distance is shared rather than held by a single codeword, there is no unique nearest codeword to decode to.

Cross-check

For the decoder to commit a correction, the winner must beat every other codeword strictly. Here the closest distance (1) ties between two codewords while the third (01110) sits farther away at distance 2. A tie at the minimum violates the strict-uniqueness requirement, so the system reports that it is unable to correct the error.

title: BLOCK PARITY is

solution: The primary reason block parity (Longitudinal Redundancy Check) was invented was to catch burst errors (where multiple consecutive bits are corrupted during transmission). title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 2
subject: Computer Networks
text: In order that a code is ‘\(t\)’ error correcting, the minimum Hamming distance should be :
solution:
Concept: For a code to correct up to t bit errors, the minimum Hamming distance between any two valid codewords must satisfy d_min ≥ 2t + 1. This follows from the nearest-codeword decoding rule: every valid codeword defines a sphere of radius t (all words reachable by at most t bit-flips from it), and decoding is guaranteed to recover the correct codeword only when no two such spheres overlap.

Application: Applying this rule to the item:

  1. Let C1 and C2 be any two valid codewords, decoded by nearest-codeword matching.

  2. First check that a distance of only 2t is NOT enough: if d(C1, C2) = 2t exactly, construct a received word W that agrees with C1 in t of the differing positions and with C2 in the other t differing positions. Then d(C1, W) = t = d(C2, W), so a single t-bit error pattern produces a W equidistant from both codewords — decoding is ambiguous, so 2t cannot guarantee correction.

  3. Now check that d(C1, C2) ≥ 2t + 1 IS enough: if C1 is transmitted with at most t errors producing W, then d(C1, W) ≤ t.

  4. By the triangle inequality, d(C1, C2) ≤ d(C1, W) + d(W, C2), which rearranges to d(W, C2) ≥ d(C1, C2) − d(C1, W) ≥ (2t + 1) − t = t + 1.

  5. Since d(W, C2) ≥ t + 1 > t ≥ d(C1, W), the received word W is always strictly closer to C1 than to C2, so nearest-codeword decoding always recovers C1 correctly. So 2t + 1 is both necessary (step 2) and sufficient (steps 3–4), i.e. the minimum Hamming distance of the whole code must satisfy d_min ≥ 2t + 1.

Cross-check: The well-known (7, 4) Hamming code has d_min = 3 and is documented to correct exactly 1-bit errors (t = 1). Substituting into the derived relation: 2t + 1 = 2(1) + 1 = 3, which matches d_min = 3 exactly — confirming the relation independently.

Result: The minimum Hamming distance required for a code to be t-error-correcting is 2t + 1.

text: If the data frame to be transmitted is 1101011011 and the CRC generator polynomial used for the checksum is x4 + x + 1, what is the transmitted frame?
solution:
CONCEPT: A degree-r CRC generator is represented by an (r + 1)-bit divisor. The sender appends r zero bits, performs modulo-2 division, and replaces those zeros with the r-bit remainder.

A valid codeword has zero remainder when the entire transmitted frame is divided by the same generator, because the appended remainder cancels the message remainder.

  1. APPLICATION: The polynomial x4 + x + 1 has coefficients 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, so its binary divisor is 10011 and r = 4.

  2. Append four zeros to the data: 1101011011 becomes 11010110110000.

  3. Apply XOR with 10011 at each leading 1. The working states are:

    1. Start: 11010110110000.

    2. After the first aligned XOR: 01001110110000.

    3. After the next aligned XOR: 00000010110000.

    4. After the third aligned XOR: 00000000101000.

    5. After the final aligned XOR: 00000000001110; the last four bits give remainder 1110.

  4. Replace the appended zeros with 1110: 1101011011 + 1110 = 11010110111110.

CROSS-CHECK: Dividing 11010110111110 by 10011 gives syndrome 0000. Dividing the nearby candidate 11010110111011 by the same generator gives syndrome 0101, so the zero-syndrome check distinguishes the constructed frame.

Result: the transmitted frame is 11010110111110.

title: Which of the following is true?
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following is true?

options.html: CRC can detect all double-bit errors provided the divisor contains at least two logic 1’s.
CRC can detect any odd number of errors provided the divisor is a factor of x.
CRC cannot detect burst error of length less than the degree of the polynomial.

solution:
Answer: CRC can detect all single-bit errors.

Explanation: A single-bit error corresponds to the polynomial x^k. A valid CRC generator polynomial has a nonzero constant term (it is not divisible by x), so it cannot divide x^k. Hence any single-bit error produces a nonzero remainder and will be detected.

  • Double-bit errors: Detection is not guaranteed simply by the number of 1s in the divisor. Two-bit errors separated by k bits correspond to the polynomial x^i + x^j = x^j(x^{i-j}+1). A double-bit error will be undetected only if the generator polynomial divides x^{i-j}+1. So the correct test is divisibility by x^k+1 for the separation k, not a plain count of ones.

  • Odd number of bit errors: All odd numbers of bit errors are detected if and only if the generator polynomial has (x + 1) as a factor. If G(x) is divisible by x+1, then any error polynomial with an odd number of 1s will leave a nonzero remainder.

  • Burst errors: If the generator polynomial has degree r, then any burst error of length less than or equal to r is guaranteed to be detected. This is because such a burst corresponds to a polynomial of degree at most r-1, which cannot be divisible by the degree-r generator; for bursts longer than r detection is not guaranteed and depends on divisibility.

Summary: The statement that CRC detects all single-bit errors is correct. The other properties depend on specific divisibility conditions: double-bit detection depends on divisibility by x^k+1, odd-number detection requires (x+1) as a factor, and burst errors up to length r (degree of generator) are always detected.

This statement is misleading. Detection of two-bit (double-bit) errors depends on whether the generator polynomial divides x^k + 1 for the separation k between the two error bits. It is not guaranteed simply by counting the number of ones in the divisor. In practice, many well-chosen generator polynomials avoid dividing x^k + 1 for likely separations and thus detect most double-bit errors, but the precise condition is divisibility by x^k + 1, not the number of 1s alone.

title: Which of the following are true?
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following are true?

options.html: CRC can detect all errors in a message
We need more hamming distance to correct error as compared to error detection
If a single parity bit is added, then the minimum hamming distance of code words will be 2

solution:
Final answer: The true statements are the ones about needing more Hamming distance for correction and the effect of adding a single parity bit.

  • We need more hamming distance to correct error as compared to error detection — True. A code with minimum Hamming distance D can detect up to D−1 bit errors and can correct up to floor((D−1)/2) bit errors. Thus correcting t errors requires D ≥ 2t+1, which is a stronger (larger) requirement than detecting the same number of errors.

  • If a single parity bit is added, then the minimum hamming distance of code words will be 2 — True. An overall parity bit forces all valid codewords to have even parity. Any single-bit change in a valid codeword produces an invalid codeword, and two distinct valid codewords must differ in at least two bit positions, so the minimum distance is 2.

Why the other statements are false:

  • CRC can detect all errors in a message — False. CRC schemes detect many common errors (e.g., bursts shorter than the generator polynomial length and many random errors) but cannot guarantee detection of every possible error pattern. Certain error patterns that are exact multiples of the CRC generator polynomial will leave the CRC unchanged and go undetected.

  • Ethernet uses CSMA/CA for access control — False. Wired Ethernet uses CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection). CSMA/CA (Collision Avoidance) is used by wireless technologies such as Wi‑Fi.

Summary: The correct statements are the one about Hamming distance requirements for correction versus detection, and the one about adding a single parity bit producing minimum Hamming distance 2. The CRC and Ethernet statements are incorrect for the reasons given above.

Correct. The minimum Hamming distance D of a code determines both detection and correction capability: a code can detect up to D-1 bit errors and can correct up to floor((D-1)/2) bit errors. Therefore, to correct t errors you need D >= 2t+1, while to detect s errors you need D >= s+1, so correcting requires a larger minimum distance than mere detection.

Any single-bit flip will change parity and produce an invalid codeword, so single-bit errors are detectable. title: The message is to be transmitted using the CRC polynomial
subject: Computer Networks
text: The message 1001 is to be transmitted using the CRC polynomial x³ + x + 1 to protect it from errors. The message that should be transmitted is –
solution:
Concept: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) detects transmission errors using binary (mod-2) polynomial division. For a generator polynomial of degree r, the sender appends r zero bits to the message, divides the result by the generator's binary bit pattern using XOR (mod-2, no-borrow) division, and replaces the appended zeros with the resulting remainder — the Frame Check Sequence (FCS) — to form the transmitted frame. The receiver divides the received frame by the same generator; a zero remainder confirms that no error altered the frame in transit.

Application: For this message, the generator polynomial x3+x+1 corresponds to the binary bit pattern 1011 (coefficients of x3, x2, x1, x0), so its degree is r = 3.

  1. Append r = 3 zero bits to the message 1001, forming the augmented dividend 1001000.

  2. Divide 1001000 by 1011 using mod-2 (XOR) division: the leading 4 bits 1001 XOR 1011 = 0010; bring down the next bit (0) to get 0100.

  3. The leading bit of 0100 is 0, so no XOR is applied; bring down the next bit (0) to get 1000.

  4. 1000 XOR 1011 = 0011; bring down the last bit (0) to get 0110.

  5. The leading bit of 0110 is 0, so the division stops; the final 3 bits give the remainder = 110.

  6. Replace the 3 appended zero bits of the augmented dividend with this remainder: 1001 followed by 110 gives the transmitted message 1001110.

Cross-check: A correctly formed frame divides evenly (remainder 000) by the generator. Dividing 1001110 by 1011 using the same mod-2 process leaves remainder 000, confirming 1001110 is the valid transmitted message.

title: Bit stuffing refers to
subject: Computer Networks
text: Bit stuffing refers to

options.html: inserting a 0 in user stream to differentiate it with a flag
inserting a 0 in flag stream to avoid ambiguity
appending a nibble to the flag sequence
appending a nibble to the user data stream

solution:
Bit stuffing is a data-link-layer framing technique that guarantees transparency: it prevents a bit pattern that matches the reserved flag sequence (typically 01111110) from occurring by accident inside the user's own data.

Applying this to the frame content here, the sender scans the outgoing user data stream and, whenever it detects five consecutive 1 bits, inserts a single extra 0 bit immediately after them, regardless of what bit follows. This guarantees the stream can never accidentally contain six 1s in a row, so it can never be confused with the flag pattern. On the receiving side, the destuffing process removes that inserted 0 after every run of five 1s, exactly reversing the operation and recovering the original data. This is precisely the bit-stuffing definition: inserting a 0 into the user stream to keep it distinguishable from a flag.

Each other option changes either the wrong stream or the wrong unit of insertion:

  • Targeting the flag stream (rather than the user data) would mean altering the one fixed, pre-agreed marker both ends rely on to detect frame boundaries — the flag must stay constant, so nothing is ever inserted into it.

  • Appending a nibble (4 bits) to the flag sequence combines both problems: it changes the reserved marker and does so in a coarser, unconditional unit rather than the single conditional bit the technique actually adds.

  • Appending a nibble to the user data stream applies the right target (the data) but the wrong unit and the wrong trigger: a fixed 4-bit block added regardless of context is not equivalent to a single bit inserted only after five consecutive 1s.

optionFeedback.html: This is the exact bit-stuffing rule: after five consecutive 1s in the user data stream, the sender inserts a single 0 bit, which forces the receiver to strip that inserted 0 back out during destuffing rather than misreading the run as the start of the reserved flag pattern (01111110).

The flag sequence is a reserved bit pattern known in advance to both sender and receiver; modifying it during transmission would remove the very landmark receivers rely on to detect frame boundaries, so protocols never touch the flag itself — the technique operates elsewhere in the transmission and follows a specific triggering condition rather than being applied here.

Beyond targeting the flag sequence, which must remain a fixed, recognizable marker, a four-bit nibble is a much coarser unit than what framing techniques manipulate bit by bit; padding a fixed control marker with extra bits would break every receiver's ability to recognize it consistently.

A nibble is a fixed four-bit group; adding one regardless of the data content would alter the message length whether or not a flag-like run actually appears, which is wasteful and does not match how the technique conditions its action on a specific bit pattern appearing in the stream.

title: Which of the following functions of the Data Link layer
subject: Computer Networks
text:
Which of the following functions of the Data Link layer are correct?
1.Framing: Framing is a function of the data link layer. It provides a way for a sender to transmit a set of bits that are meaningful to the receiver. This can be accomplished by attaching special bit patterns to the beginning and end of the frame.

2.Physical addressing: After creating frames, Data link layer adds physical addresses (MAC address) of sender and/or receiver in the header of each frame.

3.Error control: Data link layer provides the mechanism of error control in which it detects and retransmits damaged or lost frames.

4.Flow Control: The data rate must be constant on both sides or else the data may get corrupted thus, flow control coordinates that amount of data that can be sent before receiving an acknowledgement.

5.Access control: When a single communication channel is shared by multiple devices, MAC sub-layer of the data link layer helps to determine which device has control over the channel at a given time.
solution:
All five statements are correct. Brief explanations of each function follow:

  • Framing: The Data Link layer organizes raw bits into frames and marks frame boundaries so the receiver can identify meaningful units.

  • Physical addressing: The Data Link layer adds MAC (physical) addresses to frame headers to identify the sender and/or receiver on the local network.

  • Error control: The layer detects corrupted frames and can request retransmission to provide reliable delivery over a noisy link.

  • Flow control: Flow control regulates the rate of frame transmission so the sender does not overwhelm the receiver.

  • Access control: When multiple devices share a medium, the MAC sublayer decides which device may use the channel at a given time (e.g., CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA).

optionFeedback.html: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: framing and physical addressing are functions of the Data Link layer. However, the Data Link layer also provides error control, flow control, and access control, so selecting only statements 1 and 2 is incomplete.

Statements 3 and 4 are correct: error control and flow control are functions of the Data Link layer. However, framing (statement 1), physical addressing (statement 2), and access control (statement 5) are also functions, so selecting only statements 3 and 4 is incomplete.

Statements 4 and 5 are correct: flow control and access control are functions of the Data Link layer. But framing, physical addressing, and error control are also functions, so selecting only statements 4 and 5 leaves out important responsibilities of the layer.

All five statements are correct. Framing organizes data into frames; physical addressing adds MAC addresses to frames; error control detects and retransmits damaged or lost frames; flow control regulates the rate of transmission so the receiver is not overwhelmed; access control (MAC sublayer) decides which device may use a shared channel at a given time.

  • Access Control (AC) field is available in data frames as well as in token frames: Correct. The AC field is used in both token and data frames to control access and priority on the ring.

  • Frame Status (FS) field not included in CRC calculations: Incorrect. The Frame Status field is part of the frame status information and is not properly characterized as being excluded from frame integrity mechanisms.

  • FS field uses only one set of A & C flags: Incorrect. The Frame Status field conveys Address-recognized and Copy flags and can represent multiple flag combinations rather than a single fixed set.

The other two statements are incorrect: the Frame Status (FS) field is included in the frame integrity considerations and can reflect multiple combinations of Address-recognized (A) and Copy (C) flags.

Not all four statements are correct. The minimum-size restriction and presence of the AC field in token and data frames are correct. The claims that the Frame Status (FS) field is not included in CRC calculations and that FS uses only one set of A & C flags are incorrect: FS is considered in frame integrity mechanisms and can represent multiple A/C flag combinations.

title: Stations Alpha and Zeta are the transmitting on an Ethernet.
subject: Computer Networks
subtopic: Overview and Evolution of Ethernet – IEEE 802.3
text: Stations Alpha and Zeta are the transmitting on an Ethernet. Both Alpha and Zeta attempt to transmit a frame but they collide and Zeta wins the first backoff race. With what probability, Zeta wins the first backoff race?
solution:
A) 0.25

At every attempt to transmit a frame, both Alpha and Zeta chooses value of ‘K’ randomly. Based on the value of ‘K’ we will decide by looking at the backoff time who will win the race. We know that the station having smaller backoff time will win and it will send the frames earlier.

Attempt 1: Value of K is 0 <= K <= 2x-1 (x is the attempt number). Since Zeta won the race that means Zeta must have chosen the smaller number. Now K can be 0 or 1. So Zeta chose 0 and Alpha chose 1.

Total possibilities are (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1).

Probability = Favorable Outcome / Total outcome.

Favorable Outcome = (1,0)

P = 1 / 4 = 0.25

optionFeedback.html: In the first backoff stage, stations choose a slot from {0, 1}. Zeta wins only if its chosen slot is strictly smaller than Alpha's.
This value does not match the calculation for the first backoff race where the contention window is limited to two slots.
This value corresponds to a contention window size used in later collision stages, not the initial attempt.

title: The efficiency of ethernet increases

text: The efficiency of ethernet increases
solution:
Formula: efficiency = 1/(1 + 6.44·a)

Definition: a = Tp / Tt

Where Tp is the propagation delay and Tt is the transmission time (frame transmission duration).

Key insight:

  • Because efficiency = 1/(1 + 6.44·a), reducing the ratio a increases efficiency.

  • To reduce a = Tp/Tt you can either decrease Tp (propagation delay) or increase Tt (transmission time).

Practical implication: decrease propagation delay (for example by shortening cable length or improving propagation speed) or increase frame transmission time (for example by using larger frames) to increase Ethernet efficiency.

Conclusion: Efficiency increases when propagation time decreases and transmission time increases.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q117
subject: Computer Networks
text: Why are IP addresses required even though MAC addresses are globally unique?

options.html: MAC addresses cannot be used for routing across networks

solution:
Concept: In the OSI/TCP-IP layering model, a MAC address is a Layer 2 (Data Link) address burned into a network interface by its manufacturer -- it is globally unique but flat, meaning it carries no information about which network the device sits on. An IP address is a Layer 3 (Network) address with a hierarchical network-plus-host structure, and routers use only that network portion to decide the next hop when forwarding a packet between different networks.

Application: Because a MAC address has no network component, a router receiving a frame cannot tell from the MAC address alone which network, among many separate networks, the destination belongs to. Global uniqueness only guarantees that no two interfaces share the same MAC value; it does not organize interfaces into networks. The IP address's network portion is what lets a router look up a route and forward the packet toward the correct destination network, so IP addressing is required in addition to the MAC address even though the MAC address is already globally unique.

Checking each option against this concept:

  • Routers strip MAC addresses permanently -- at each hop, a router replaces the frame's Layer 2 header with new source and destination MAC addresses for the next physical link; it re-addresses the frame at every hop rather than permanently removing MAC addressing from the network.

  • IP addresses are faster -- address lookups for MAC-based forwarding (switching/ARP tables) and IP-based forwarding (routing tables) both run as hardware-assisted operations at comparable speeds; raw lookup speed is not the property that makes network-layer addressing necessary.

  • MAC addresses expire periodically -- a manufacturer-assigned MAC address is burned into the interface and stays fixed for its lifetime, with no built-in expiry or renewal cycle (software-based MAC randomization for privacy is a separate, optional mechanism).

  • MAC addresses cannot be used for routing across networks -- this matches the concept above: a flat, non-hierarchical Layer 2 address carries no network-membership information, so it cannot serve as the basis for forwarding across separate networks, which is exactly why the hierarchical IP address is needed alongside it.

optionFeedback.html: When a router forwards a packet from one Layer 2 segment onto another, it builds a new frame for the outgoing link using the MAC address of its own outgoing interface and the MAC address of the next-hop device on that segment.

Layer 2 forwarding decisions are made using a switch's MAC address table (populated via ARP/learning), while Layer 3 forwarding decisions are made using a router's routing table keyed by network-prefix entries; each device performs its own table lookup as part of standard packet delivery.
A device's MAC address is programmed into the network interface at the factory by the manufacturer, using an IEEE-assigned vendor prefix (OUI) combined with a device-specific suffix.
A MAC address is a single 48-bit value assigned as one flat block per interface, structured as a vendor-specific OUI prefix plus a per-device suffix, with no additional subdivision.

In computer networking, every device connected to a network must be uniquely identifiable so that data sent across the network reaches the correct destination. This identification is provided by a network address assigned at the Network Layer of the OSI/TCP-IP model, which routers use to locate and route data across interconnected networks.

The Internet is a global network of interconnected networks that runs on the TCP/IP protocol suite. On the Internet, the network-layer address used to route data toward a device is called its Internet Protocol (IP) Address. An IP address (a 32-bit number in IPv4, or a 128-bit number in IPv6) is bound to a device's network interface, and routers use it, hop by hop, to forward packets toward that device. (In practice, a device may sit behind Network Address Translation, NAT, sharing one public IP address with other devices on the same private network, with port numbers distinguishing the individual devices behind that shared address; even so, the IP address remains the network-layer identifier used for Internet-wide routing, which is exactly what this term refers to.)

  • Media Access Control Address: a 48-bit hardware identifier assigned to a network interface card, operating at the Data Link Layer.

  • Specific Address: does not appear in networking standards (IETF, IEEE, IANA) as a named address type; it has no defined bit-length, notation, or assigning authority.

  • Port Address: a 16-bit number that operates at the Transport Layer to distinguish individual processes or applications on a device.

Hence, the network-layer address used to route data to each device on the Internet is its Internet Protocol (IP) Address.

An IPv4 address is a 32-bit value, conventionally written as four decimal numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots (for example, 192.168.1.1); IPv6 extends this to a 128-bit value written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons.

Correct matching: P – 4, Q – 3, R – 1, S – 2

title: IP header checksum must be recomputed in each router before
subject: Computer Networks
text:
IP header checksum must be recomputed in each router before being forwarded to next router, the reasons may be

a. TTL field b. Fragment offset field

c. 16 – bit datagram length field d. 16-bit datagram identification field

Find the correct reasons.
solution:
The IP header checksum covers only the IP header. Routers must recompute this checksum whenever they modify any header fields.

  • TTL (Time To Live): The TTL is decremented by each router, which changes the header and therefore requires recomputing the checksum.

  • Fragment Offset: If a router fragments a datagram, it assigns fragment offsets for the resulting fragments. That modification to the header necessitates updating the checksum.

  • 16-bit Total Length (Datagram Length): When fragmentation occurs, the total length of each fragment differs from the original datagram; routers that create fragments update this field, so the checksum must be recalculated.

  • 16-bit Identification: This field is set by the sender to help reassemble fragments and is not modified by routers. It does not by itself require checksum recomputation.

Conclusion: The header checksum must be recomputed for changes to TTL, Fragment Offset, and the 16-bit total datagram length. The 16-bit identification field is not changed by routers and is not a reason to recompute the checksum.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The header checksum covers only the IP header and must be recomputed when header fields change. The TTL (Time To Live) is decremented by each router, and both the fragment offset and the 16-bit total datagram length are updated when fragmentation occurs. Because these header fields can be modified by routers, the checksum must be recalculated.

Incorrect. While fragment offset and the 16-bit total datagram length can change when fragmentation occurs, the 16-bit datagram identification field is not modified by routers (it is set by the sender and retained to match fragments). Also, the TTL is decremented by each router and should be included as a reason for recomputing the header checksum.

Incorrect. This choice includes the 16-bit datagram identification field, which routers do not modify. The fragment offset is the field that can change during fragmentation and should be listed instead. Also note that TTL is decremented by routers and is a correct reason to recompute the header checksum.

Incorrect. Although TTL and fragment offset are reasons to recalculate the checksum, the 16-bit datagram identification field is not altered by routers and therefore is not a reason. The 16-bit total datagram length is the other field that can change when fragmentation occurs and should be included instead.

title: In IPv4, packet fragmentation and reassembly is handled by IPv4
subject: Computer Networks
text: In IPv4, packet fragmentation and reassembly is handled by –

options.html: using the More Fragments and Fragment Offset Fields

solution:
Concept

Every physical link imposes a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) — the largest payload a single frame on that link may carry. When an IPv4 datagram is bigger than the MTU of the next link, the datagram is split into fragments, and only the destination host puts them back together. IPv4 keeps all of the bookkeeping for that split-and-rejoin inside its own header, in the Identification field, the Flags field (which contains the More Fragments bit) and the Fragment Offset field.

The general rule: fragmentation is a Network layer operation driven by IPv4 header fields, and reassembly happens end to end at the destination, never hop by hop.

Applying it to this question

The stem asks which mechanism actually performs fragmentation and reassembly. The three IPv4 header fields that carry fragmentation state work together like this:

IPv4 header field

What it carries

Job during split and rejoin

Identification (16 bits)

The same value copied into every fragment of one datagram

Groups arriving fragments that belong to the same original datagram

Flags — More Fragments (MF)

Set to 1 on every fragment except the last one

Tells the receiver whether further pieces are still on the way

Fragment Offset (13 bits)

This fragment's position in the original payload, counted in units of 8 bytes

Places each fragment at the correct byte position in the rebuilt datagram

So the mechanism the stem is asking about is "using the More Fragments and Fragment Offset Fields": the MF bit signals that the datagram is still incomplete, and the Fragment Offset says exactly where each received piece belongs. Together they are what lets the destination rebuild the original datagram.

Cross-check against the other mechanisms

  • Header Checksum — a 16-bit check computed over the IPv4 header bytes alone and recomputed at every hop. It detects a header damaged in transit, but it carries no information about how a datagram was divided.

  • Encapsulating packets in larger data frames — a Data Link layer packaging step. A link will not accept a frame larger than its own MTU, so making frames bigger is simply not available as a way to move an oversized datagram.

  • MAC Header — a Data Link layer header holding hardware addresses for one hop only. Each router strips it and writes a fresh one for the next link, so it never reaches the destination and cannot carry reassembly state.

This confirms the reading: reassembly state has to survive the whole path, and only the IPv4 header — through the More Fragments flag and the Fragment Offset — carries it end to end.

optionFeedback.html: The More Fragments flag and the Fragment Offset field both sit inside the IPv4 header. MF is a single bit set on every piece of a divided datagram except the last one, and Fragment Offset is a 13-bit value giving that piece’s position inside the original payload, counted in units of 8 bytes.

The Header Checksum is a 16-bit field computed over the bytes of the IPv4 header alone, and it does not cover the payload. Each router recomputes it from the header of the arriving datagram, and after decrementing the TTL it writes a freshly computed checksum into the header it forwards.

Encapsulating a datagram inside a frame is a Data Link layer packaging step. The size of frame a link will accept is bounded by that link’s own MTU, and the datagram carried inside the frame is handed onward unchanged.

The MAC header is the Data Link layer header carrying the source and destination hardware addresses for a single hop. Each router strips the incoming MAC header and writes a fresh one for the outgoing link, so it is rebuilt at every step of the path.

This choice records that no option was selected on the answer sheet. It names no IPv4 header field, no link-layer structure and no transmission mechanism, so it describes nothing about how a datagram travels across a network.

title: Consider very large network of routers. Sender and receiver are
subject: Computer Networks
text:
Consider a very large network of 6000 routers. Sender and receiver are connected with this network. Sender sends data to receiver and after some time sender receives ICMP time exceeded message for the same transmitted datagram. The maximum number of routers that can be travelled by datagrams when ICMP message reaches back to sender is __________

&Protocols
solution:
Key facts: the TTL (Time To Live) field in an IP header is 8 bits, so its maximum value is 255.

  • Forward datagram: If the sender sets the TTL to 255, the datagram can be forwarded across up to 255 routers. At the 255th router the TTL becomes zero and that router drops the packet and generates an ICMP Time Exceeded message.

  • ICMP reply: The ICMP Time Exceeded message sent by that router can itself use a TTL up to 255. To count the total routers traversed by both the original datagram and the returning ICMP without double-counting, note that the router that generated the ICMP is included in the forward path already.

Calculation: 255 (forward) + 255 (return) - 1 (shared router counted once) = 509.

Answer: 509 (assuming both the original datagram and the ICMP response use the maximum TTL of 255).

title: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is used for (ARP)

text: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is used for —

title: Name the protocol used to find MAC address from IP

text: Which protocol is used to find a MAC address from an IP address?
solution:
Concept

Address resolution links a network-layer protocol address to the link-layer hardware address needed to deliver a frame on a local network.

The direction of the mapping matters: a protocol-address-to-hardware-address lookup is different from a hardware-address-to-protocol-address lookup.

Application

  1. A sender knows the destination IPv4 address but needs a destination MAC address for the local Ethernet frame.

  2. ARP broadcasts a request for the device that owns that IPv4 address.

  3. The matching device replies with its MAC address, which the sender uses in the frame.

Cross-check and contrast

  • RARP begins with a known MAC address and obtains an IP address.

  • ICMP carries IP control and error messages, including ping-related messages.

  • SMTP transfers email at the application layer.

Therefore, the required protocol is ARP (Address Resolution Protocol).

optionFeedback.html: RARP associates a known hardware address with a protocol address, historically helping a host obtain its IP address.
ARP associates a known IPv4 protocol address with a local-network hardware address used for link-layer frame delivery.
ICMP carries control and error information between IP nodes, including Echo Request and Echo Reply messages.

title: What protocol is used to find the hardware address of
subject: Computer Networks
text: What protocol is used to find the hardware address of a local device?
solution:
Concept

Every device on a local network has two addresses: a logical IP address and a physical hardware (MAC) address. Address resolution is the process of discovering the unknown hardware address that corresponds to a device whose IP address is already known, so that a frame can actually be delivered on the local link.

Applying it here

To send data on a LAN, a host knows the destination IP address but must learn the matching hardware address. The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) does exactly this: the sender broadcasts an ARP request asking which device owns a given IP address, and the device that owns that IP replies with its hardware (MAC) address, which the sender then caches. This IP-to-hardware mapping on the local network is precisely what the question asks for.

Contrast with the other choices

  • RARP works in the opposite direction: a diskless host that already knows its own hardware address uses it to obtain its IP address, so it maps hardware to logical, not logical to hardware.

  • IP is a network-layer addressing and routing protocol; it carries packets using logical addresses and performs no hardware-address lookup.

  • ICMP is a diagnostic and error-reporting protocol (used by tools like ping); it reports delivery problems and does not resolve addresses.

optionFeedback.html: This protocol resolves in the opposite direction: a host that already knows its own hardware address uses it to obtain its IP address, mapping hardware to logical rather than logical to hardware.

On a local link this protocol takes a known IP address and resolves it to the corresponding hardware (MAC) address, by broadcasting a request for the owner of that IP and caching the hardware address returned in the reply.
This is the network-layer addressing and routing protocol; it carries packets using logical addresses and performs no hardware-address lookup on the local link.
This is a diagnostic and error-reporting protocol used by utilities such as ping; it signals delivery and reachability problems and carries out no address-to-hardware resolution.

title: What is the primary function of the ARP in an
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the primary function of the ARP in an IPv4 local network?

options.html: To resolve domain names into IP addresses
To determine the MAC address corresponding to an IP address

solution:
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is used in an IPv4 local network to find the MAC (hardware/physical) address that corresponds to a known IPv4 address. Hosts identify each other logically by IP address, but to actually deliver a frame on the same LAN segment they need the destination's Layer-2 MAC address — ARP bridges this gap.

When a host wants to send data to an IP address on the same network and does not have the matching MAC address cached, it broadcasts an ARP request ("Who has IP X? Tell me your MAC."). The host owning that IP replies with a unicast ARP reply carrying its MAC address, which the sender stores in its ARP cache for future use.

Therefore, the primary function of ARP is to determine the MAC address corresponding to a given IP address — i.e., to map an IP (network-layer) address to a MAC (link-layer) address. This makes option (3) correct.

Why the others are wrong: assigning IP addresses dynamically is done by DHCP; resolving domain names to IP addresses is done by DNS; encrypting communication is the job of protocols such as IPsec/TLS; and forwarding packets between different networks is performed by routers (the IP routing/forwarding function).

optionFeedback.html: Dynamically assigning IP addresses to hosts (leasing, renewing, and reclaiming them) is the role of DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), not ARP. ARP works with addresses that already exist; it does not hand out IP addresses.

Translating human-readable domain names (like example.com) into IP addresses is performed by DNS (Domain Name System). ARP does not deal with names at all — it operates only on numeric IP and MAC addresses within a local network.

Correct. Within an IPv4 LAN, a host knows the destination's IP address but needs its MAC address to deliver the frame. ARP broadcasts a request and receives a reply that supplies the MAC address matching that IP — exactly the IP-to-MAC mapping described here.

Encrypting network communication to protect confidentiality is provided by security protocols such as IPsec, TLS/SSL, or WPA, not by ARP. ARP carries plain address information and performs no encryption.

Forwarding packets between different networks is the job of routers using the IP routing/forwarding process. ARP operates within a single local network segment to find hardware addresses; it does not move packets across networks.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q115
subject: Computer Networks
text: How does tunneling enable IPv6 communication over IPv4 networks?
solution:
Tunneling is a transition technique in which packets belonging to one network-layer protocol are wrapped, unchanged, inside the packets of a different network-layer protocol so that they can be carried across a network built for the second protocol.

For IPv6 traffic crossing IPv4-only infrastructure, a dual-stack router or host at the tunnel entry takes the complete IPv6 packet (its own header and payload) and places it as the payload of a new IPv4 packet:

  1. The source generates an ordinary IPv6 packet with a full IPv6 header and payload.

  2. At the tunnel entry point, that entire IPv6 packet is encapsulated as the data portion of a new IPv4 packet, and the IPv4 header's Protocol field is set to 41 to mark the payload as an IPv6 datagram.

  3. The resulting IPv4 packet is forwarded hop by hop through the IPv4-only network using ordinary IPv4 routing, since every intermediate router only ever sees a normal IPv4 packet.

  4. At the tunnel exit point, the IPv4 header is removed, recovering the original, unmodified IPv6 packet, which is then delivered onward on the IPv6 side.

Cross-check: this is distinct from header translation, which rewrites an IPv6 header into an IPv4 header (or vice versa) instead of wrapping the packet, and from dual stack, where a device runs both protocol stacks natively without needing to wrap one protocol inside the other. Per RFC 4213 (Basic Transition Mechanisms for IPv6 Hosts and Routers), encapsulating IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets is exactly how tunneling achieves IPv6-over-IPv4 connectivity.

optionFeedback.html: This choice names header translation — a technique in which a device reads a packet's header fields and writes a new header in a different protocol's format from those fields, so the packet continues its journey carrying that newly written header.

This choice names encapsulation — a technique in which a device wraps a complete packet, header and payload together and unchanged, as the payload of a new outer packet in a different protocol's format, so the packet continues its journey wrapped inside that new outer packet.

This choice names broadcasting — a delivery mode in which a device sends one copy of a packet to every host on its local network segment, addressed to the segment's broadcast address rather than to a single destination.
This choice names a routing-table maintenance action in which a device deletes existing entries from its routing table, changing the set of destinations for which it currently has a known next hop.

title: What is IP class and number of sub-networks if the
subject: Computer Networks
text: Under classful subnetting, the mask 255.224.0.0 extends a default class mask by borrowing host bits. Counting all subnet-number values, which IP class and number of subnets does it represent?
solution:
Concept

In classful IPv4 subnetting, the default network prefix is /8 for Class A and /16 for Class B. A subnet mask longer than the default prefix borrows host bits for subnet numbering.

If n host bits are borrowed, counting all subnet-number values gives 2n subnets. Each decimal mask octet can be converted to binary to count its consecutive leading 1-bits.

Application

  1. The first mask octet, 255, contributes 8 leading 1-bits. The second octet, 224, is 11100000 in binary and contributes 3 more leading 1-bits, so the mask is /11.

  2. Relative to the Class A default /8 prefix, /11 borrows n = 11 − 8 = 3 host bits. A Class B default /16 prefix cannot be extended to the shorter /11 mask by borrowing host bits.

  3. The number of subnet-number combinations is 23 = 8.

Cross-check

The three borrowed bits run from 000 through 111, yielding eight distinct combinations. This agrees with the /11 minus /8 calculation.

Therefore, the mask represents Class A with 8 subnets under the stated classful convention.

optionFeedback.html: This pairing uses the Class A default prefix length of 8 bits and reports three subnet-number combinations.

This pairing uses the Class B default prefix length of 16 bits and reports three subnet-number combinations.

title: In class subnet, we know the IP address of one
subject: Computer Networks
text:
In a class A subnet, we know the IP address of one host and the mask as given below:

IP address: 125.134.112.66
Mask: 255.255.224.0

What is the first address (network address)?
solution:
The network address of a subnetted IP is found by applying (bitwise ANDing) the subnet mask to the address, octet by octet. Wherever a mask octet is neither 255 nor 0, the corresponding address octet must be rounded down to the nearest multiple of that octet's block size, where block size = 256 minus the mask value in that octet.

  1. The mask's first two octets are 255 and 255, so the network address keeps the host's first two octets unchanged: 125 and 134.

  2. The mask's third octet is 224, giving a block size of 256 − 224 = 32 for that position.

  3. The host's third octet is 112. Dividing 112 by 32 gives a quotient of 3 with a remainder of 16, so the octet is rounded down to the block boundary 3 × 32 = 96.

  4. The mask's fourth octet is 0, so the network address's fourth octet is always 0, regardless of the host's value of 66.

  5. Combining the four octets gives the network address 125.134.96.0.

This can be cross-checked with a direct bitwise AND: 112 in binary is 01110000 and 224 is 11100000; ANDing these bit by bit gives 01100000, which is 96 in decimal — the same result obtained from the block-size calculation.

So the first (network) address of this subnet is 125.134.96.0.

optionFeedback.html: 125.134.96.0 shifts the third octet from the host's 112 down to 96 while clearing the fourth octet to 0.
125.134.112.0 keeps the host's third octet value of 112 unchanged and clears only the fourth octet to 0.
125.134.112.66 keeps every octet identical to the host address stated in the question, including the un-cleared fourth octet 66.
125.134.0.0 clears both the third and fourth octets to 0, reaching back to the boundary of the first two octets only.

title: Router outside the organization received packet Consider following steps taken

title: IP currently uses 32-bit addresses, if we could redesign IP
subject: Computer Networks
text:
IP currently uses 32-bit addresses, if we could redesign IP to use the 6-byte MAC address instead of the 32 bit addresses, how many statements are true about the system.

(i) Allows IP addresses to be dynamically allocated when the hardware moves to the different network

(ii) Mapping is necessary to enable indirection from IP address to the MAC address

(iii) As we use static IP addresses, routing will be much less efficient

(iv) No effect on the system
solution:
(i) False: MAC addresses are hardware-specific and static. They do not change when the device moves to a different network. IP addresses, however, can be dynamically allocated (e.g., via DHCP), allowing network flexibility.

(ii) False: If the MAC address is used directly as the address, there would be no need for mapping between an IP address and a MAC address. The whole concept of ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) would be redundant.

(iii) True: Static MAC addresses are not optimized for hierarchical routing as IP addresses are. This lack of structure in MAC addresses would make routing tables larger and routing less efficient, as every address is unique but not structured hierarchically like IP addresses.

(iv) False: Using MAC addresses instead of IP addresses would have significant effects on routing, address allocation, and network management, leading to various inefficiencies and complications.

Only one statement (iii) is true

title: Which technique is used to allow multiple devices to share
subject: Computer Networks

solution: NAT (Network Address Translation) is used to map multiple private IP addresses within a local network to a single public IP address before forwarding the packets to the internet. title: What part of is the Network ID, assuming default subnet
subject: Computer Networks
text: What part of 192.168.10.51 is the Network ID, assuming a default subnet mask?
solution:
Concept

An IPv4 address is split into a Network ID (which network the host belongs to) and a Host ID (which host within that network). With a default classful subnet mask, the class of the address — decided by the first octet — fixes how many leading octets form the Network ID:

  • Class A (first octet 1–126): mask 255.0.0.0 → Network ID = first 1 octet.

  • Class B (first octet 128–191): mask 255.255.0.0 → Network ID = first 2 octets.

  • Class C (first octet 192–223): mask 255.255.255.0 → Network ID = first 3 octets, host = last octet.

Application

  1. Read the first octet of 192.168.10.51 → it is 192, which lies in 192–223, so this is a Class C address.

  2. The default mask for Class C is 255.255.255.0, so the masked (network) portion is the first three octets and the last octet is the host.

  3. Apply the mask: keep the first three octets, zero the host octet → Network ID = 192.168.10 (full network address 192.168.10.0), and the host part is 51.

Cross-check

Reverse it: every address from 192.168.10.1 to 192.168.10.254 shares the same first three octets, so they must share one Network ID — 192.168.10 — confirming the host byte (51 here) is what varies. Hence the Network ID of 192.168.10.51 under the default mask is 192.168.10.

optionFeedback.html: Keeping only the first octet is the Network ID rule for a Class A address (mask 255.0.0.0). For a first octet of 192 the address is Class C, so a single octet is fewer than the masked network portion of this address.

Under the Class C default mask 255.255.255.0 the first three octets are the bits left set by the mask, so they form the network portion of the address and only the final octet (51) lies in the host portion.

A value built from the trailing octets with the leading octets zeroed inverts the mask: it strips out exactly the network bits the default mask keeps, so it represents the host/inside-network view rather than the network portion the question asks for.
The last octet alone is the Host ID under a Class C mask — it identifies the machine inside the network, which is the unmasked host portion rather than the masked network portion.
