title: UGC NET Paper 1 June 2010 Set W — Question 48
subject: Computer Networks
text: At the network layer, a device connected to the Internet is identified for Internet Protocol communication by which type of address?
solution:
Concept

Internet Protocol communication uses logical network-layer addressing. An address at this layer identifies a network interface so packets can be routed across interconnected networks.

Application identifiers and physical-location identifiers serve different purposes and do not replace the network-layer identifier used in an IP packet.

Application

For a device exchanging packets over the Internet, the relevant identifier in the Internet Protocol header is its IP address. Routers use the destination IP address when forwarding the packet toward the receiving network.

Contrast

  • An e-mail address identifies a mailbox for electronic messaging, not a network interface in an IP packet.

  • A street address identifies a physical postal or geographic location, not an Internet Protocol endpoint.

  • An IP address is the logical network-layer identifier carried in IP communication.

  • “None of these options” would apply only if no listed address type served this network-layer role; the list includes IP address.

Result

Therefore, the required identifier is an IP address.

optionFeedback.html: An e-mail address names a mailbox used for sending and receiving electronic messages.
A street address names a physical location used for postal or geographic reference.
An IP address is a logical network-layer address assigned to a network interface for IP communication.
“None of these options” collectively rejects the three listed address types and does not denote an addressing mechanism of its own.

title: In IPv4 addressing, block of address can be define as

text:
(A) In IPv4 addressing, a block of address can be define as x.y.z.t/n in which x.y.z.t define one of the address and /n define the mask
(B) The first address in the block can be found by setting the rightmost 32-n bits to 0s

solution:
Explanation: Evaluate each statement.

  • In IPv4 addressing, a block can be defined as x.y.z.t/n where x.y.z.t is an address and /n is the prefix length (network mask). This is correct (CIDR notation).

  • There are five IPv4 address classes historically (A, B, C, D, and E); this statement is correct. Note that Class D is used for multicast and Class E is reserved.

  • Supernetting combines several networks into a larger network (used with CIDR to aggregate routes). This statement is correct.

Conclusion: The true statements are the ones describing CIDR notation, the rule to compute the first address by zeroing host bits, the existence of five IPv4 classes, and that supernetting aggregates networks. The correct answer is the choice that lists those four true statements.

title: Consider the address and subnet mask Find the subnet id?
subject: Computer Networks
text: Consider the address 141.14.196.46 and subnet mask 255.255.192.0. Find the subnet id?
solution:
Key idea: Apply the subnet mask to the IP (bitwise AND) to get the subnet ID.

  • Convert the mask 255.255.192.0 to binary for the third octet: 192 = 11000000. This mask is /18.

  • Convert the IP's third octet to binary: 196 = 11000100.

  • Perform bitwise AND on the third octet: 11000100 AND 11000000 = 11000000 (which is 192).

  • Set all host bits to zero (the lower 6 bits of the third octet and the entire fourth octet). The subnet ID becomes 141.14.192.0.

Final answer: 141.14.192.0

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The subnet mask 255.255.192.0 is /18, so only the first two bits of the third octet are network bits. Convert the third octet of the IP (196 -> 11000100) and mask (192 -> 11000000). ANDing them gives 11000000 (192). Set host bits to zero in the remaining octets, giving the subnet ID 141.14.192.0.

Incorrect. The value 141.14.1.46 does not zero the host bits according to the given mask. With mask 255.255.192.0 (/18), the third octet must be one of 0, 64, 128, 192. The given IP's third octet (196) falls in the 192 subnet, so the correct subnet ID is 141.14.192.0, not 141.14.1.46.

Incorrect. The candidate 25.255.192.0 has a different first octet than the given IP (141...), so it cannot be the subnet ID for that IP. The subnet ID must share the network portion with the IP; with mask 255.255.192.0 and IP 141.14.196.46 the correct subnet ID is 141.14.192.0.

subject: Computer Networks
text: An organization has a class-C network of 195.32.7.0. It is submitted with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.240. What is the broadcast address of the last but one sub network?
solution:
Key steps: determine subnet size and find the second-to-last block.

  1. Identify the mask: 255.255.255.240 is /28.

  2. Compute block size: 256 (addresses in last octet) ÷ 16 (because /28 leaves 4 host bits → 2^4 = 16) = 16, so subnets increase in steps of 16 in the last octet.

  3. List the final /28 blocks in the /24: 208–223, 224–239, 240–255.

  4. The second-to-last block is 224–239, so its broadcast address (the last address in that block) is 195.32.7.239.

Final answer: 195.32.7.239

optionFeedback.html: 195.32.7.255 is the broadcast address for the whole class-C network when using a /24 mask. With a /28 mask (255.255.255.240) the network is divided into smaller subnets of 16 addresses each, so broadcasts occur at the end of each 16-address block, not at .255 (unless the block happens to end at .255).

195.32.7.223 is the broadcast address for the subnet that ends at 223 (the block 208–223). That subnet is the third-from-last block in the /28 partitioning, not the last-but-one. The last-but-one block ends at 239.

195.32.7.239 is correct. With mask 255.255.255.240 (/28) each subnet has 16 addresses (block size 16). The blocks in the final part of the /24 are 208–223, 224–239, 240–255; the second-to-last block is 224–239, whose broadcast is .239.

195.32.7.254 is a host address within the last /28 block (240–255); it is not the broadcast for any /28 block. For the last /28 block the broadcast is .255, and for the previous block the broadcast is .239.

title: The Direct Broadcast Address of the subnet is the subnet

text: The Direct Broadcast Address of the subnet is 201.15.16.31. W the subnet mask of the network is ___________
solution:
To determine the subnet mask from the direct broadcast address:

  • Convert the last octet (31) to binary: 00011111.

  • Count the consecutive 1s starting from the least-significant bit (the right side): there are 5 ones. These are the host bits.

  • Calculate the prefix length: 32 − 5 = 27, so the mask is /27.

  • Write the subnet mask: /27 = 255.255.255.224.

optionFeedback.html: 255.255.255.240 is a /28 mask (4 host bits, block size 16). The given broadcast 201.15.16.31 corresponds to five host bits set to 1 (binary 00011111), so the correct mask is /27 (255.255.255.224), not /28.

title: How many hosts can be configured using subnet mask
subject: Computer Networks
text: How many hosts can be configured using a subnet mask 255.255.255.248?
solution:
Concept

In IPv4 a subnet mask splits an address into a network portion (the 1-bits) and a host portion (the 0-bits). The number of distinct addresses in a subnet is 2 raised to the number of host bits; of these, two are reserved — the all-zeros address is the network ID and the all-ones address is the broadcast — so the count of usable (configurable) hosts is 2h − 2, where h is the number of host bits.

Application

  1. Write the last octet of the mask in binary: 248 = 11111000. The first three octets are 255 (all 1-bits), so every host bit lies in the last octet.

  2. Count the 0-bits (host bits): 11111000 has three trailing zeros, so h = 3.

  3. Total addresses in the subnet = 23 = 8.

  4. Subtract the two reserved addresses (network + broadcast): usable hosts = 8 − 2 = 6.

Cross-check

This mask is a /29 (32 − 3 = 29 network bits). A /29 is the standard small block that yields 6 usable host addresses — a common allocation for point-to-multipoint links and tiny LAN segments — which confirms the result.

optionFeedback.html: With three host bits the subnet holds 23 = 8 addresses, and removing the network and broadcast addresses leaves 6 configurable hosts — this is the host count for a 255.255.255.248 (/29) mask.
248 is just the value of the mask's last octet itself, mistaken for the number of hosts. The octet figure describes how the address is masked, not how many devices the subnet can hold.

48 corresponds to no quantity in this problem; it appears to come from misreading the mask octet 248. The mask's last octet here is 248, not 48, so this figure is a misread rather than a derived value.

255 is the maximum value a single octet can hold, and it is the value of each fully masked octet — it is being confused with a host count. A mask value is not the same thing as the number of devices a subnet supports.

text: An IPv4 address has first octet 100. A classful network requires at least 80 subnets. Which value should be used in the second octet of the subnet mask to maximize the number of hosts per subnet?
solution:
Concept

In fixed-length classful subnetting, borrowing s bits from the host portion creates 2s subnet identifiers. To maximize hosts while meeting a requirement of N subnets, choose the smallest s for which 2s is at least N. In a mask octet, s borrowed bits appear as s leading 1-bits followed by 0-bits.

Application

The first octet 100 lies in the Class A range 1–126, so the classful default prefix is /8. Apply the minimum-bits rule:

  1. With 6 borrowed bits, 26 = 64, which is fewer than 80.

  2. With 7 borrowed bits, 27 = 128, which is at least 80; therefore 7 is the minimum.

  3. The new prefix is /8 + 7 = /15. Seven leading 1-bits in the second mask octet give 11111110 in binary, or 254 in decimal, so the full mask is 255.254.0.0.

Cross-check

A Class A subnet table lists 7 borrowed bits as 255.254.0.0 (/15), providing 128 subnet identifiers and 131070 usable host addresses per subnet. One fewer borrowed bit gives 255.252.0.0 and only 64 subnet identifiers; borrowing more bits would reduce the host capacity unnecessarily.

Result

The required second-octet value is 254, giving subnet mask 255.254.0.0 (/15).

The mask-octet value 224 is 11100000 in binary and contributes three leading network bits. Borrowing three Class A host bits yields 8 subnet identifiers.
The mask-octet value 248 is 11111000 in binary and contributes five leading network bits. Borrowing five Class A host bits yields 32 subnet identifiers.
The mask-octet value 254 is 11111110 in binary and contributes seven leading network bits. Borrowing seven Class A host bits yields 128 subnet identifiers.

title: The subnet mask for particular network is Which of the
subject: Computer Networks
text: The subnet mask for a particular network is 255.255.31.0. Which of the following pairs of IP addresses could belong to this network?
solution:
To determine if two IP addresses belong to the same network, they must have the exact same Network ID. The Network ID is calculated by performing a bitwise AND operation between the IP address and the Subnet Mask.

1. Analyze the Subnet Mask

The mask is 255.255.31.0.

  • 1st and 2nd Octets (255.255): These are fixed. For two IPs to be in the same network, their first two octets must match exactly.

  • 3rd Octet (31): This is the "interesting" octet. In binary, 31 is 00011111.

  • 4th Octet (0): This is part of the host portion and does not affect the Network ID.

2. Evaluate the Options

Option A: 172.57.88.62 and 172.56.87.23

  • The second octets are 57 and 56.

  • Since the mask is 255.255.x.x, the first two octets must be identical. These are different.

  • Result: Different Networks.

Option B: 10.35.28.2 and 10.35.29.4

  • The first two octets match (10.35). Let's check the 3rd octet (28 and 29) against the mask (31).

  • Binary 28: 00011100

  • Binary 29: 00011101

  • Binary Mask 31: 00011111

  • AND Operation:

    • 28 AND 31 = 28

    • 29 AND 31 = 29

  • The Network IDs are different (10.35.28.0 vs 10.35.29.0).

  • Result: Different Networks.

Option C: 191.203.31.87 and 191.234.31.88

  • The second octets are 203 and 234.

  • Since the mask for the second octet is 255, these must match. They do not.

  • Result: Different Networks.

Option D: 128.8.129.43 and 128.8.161.55

  • The first two octets match (128.8). Let's check the 3rd octet (129 and 161) against the mask (31).

  • Binary 129: 10000001

  • Binary 161: 10100001

  • Binary Mask 31: 00011111

  • AND Operation:

    • 129 AND 31: 10000001 AND 00011111 = 00000001 (1)

    • 161 AND 31: 10100001 AND 00011111 = 00000001 (1)

  • Both addresses result in the same Network ID: 128.8.1.0.

Final Answer

The correct pair is 128.8.129.43 and 128.8.161.55.

optionFeedback.html: The subnet mask fixes the first two octets. These addresses differ in the second octet, so they cannot belong to the same network.

Ensure both addresses share the same network prefix when applying the subnet mask to their third octets. The values 28 and 29 must fall within the same valid block defined by the mask.They are on different network.
The second octets differ (203 vs 234). Since the subnet mask covers the first two octets completely, these addresses belong to different networks.

The third octets differ significantly (129 vs 161). This difference is too large for both addresses to reside in the same network block under this mask.
But they are in the same network. Solution Provided Below.

title: Router uses the following routing table: packet bearing destination address
subject: Computer Networks
text:
A router uses the following routing table:

A packet bearing a destination address 144.16.68.117 arrives at the router. On which interface will it be forwarded?
solution:
Longest Prefix Match (LPM) is the rule a router applies whenever more than one entry in its forwarding table matches a destination address: among all entries whose network and mask actually cover that address, the router picks the entry with the LONGEST (most specific) subnet mask -- not the first match, not the widest match.

An entry only qualifies for this comparison if the destination genuinely falls inside the address range its mask defines; an entry with a longer mask than every other row is excluded outright if the destination lies outside its own range.

Check each entry in the table against the destination address 144.16.68.117:

Interface

Mask (CIDR)

Address range covered

Matches 144.16.68.117?

eth0

255.255.0.0 (/16)

144.16.0.0 to 144.16.255.255

Yes

eth1

255.255.224.0 (/19)

144.16.64.0 to 144.16.95.255

Yes

eth2

255.255.255.0 (/24)

144.16.68.0 to 144.16.68.255

Yes

eth3

255.255.255.224 (/27)

144.16.68.64 to 144.16.68.95

No (117 > 95)

Three rows match -- eth0 (/16), eth1 (/19), and eth2 (/24). Longest Prefix Match selects the entry among these with the most specific (longest) mask: eth2's /24 is longer than both /16 and /19, so eth2 wins.

Cross-check: eth3 actually carries the longest mask of all four rows (/27), longer even than eth2's /24 -- but a longer mask only matters once an entry matches. Since 144.16.68.117 lies outside eth3's 144.16.68.64 to 144.16.68.95 range, eth3 never enters the comparison at all, which is why it is excluded despite its more specific mask.

The router therefore forwards the packet out eth2.

optionFeedback.html: eth0's mask 255.255.0.0 (/16) covers the address range 144.16.0.0 to 144.16.255.255. A /16 mask fixes the network portion to the first two octets, leaving the third and fourth octets as host-identifying bits within that range.

eth1's mask 255.255.224.0 (/19) covers the address range 144.16.64.0 to 144.16.95.255. A /19 mask fixes the network portion through the top three bits of the third octet (the block starting at 64), leaving the remaining third-octet bits and the entire fourth octet as host-identifying bits within that range.

eth2's mask 255.255.255.0 (/24) covers the address range 144.16.68.0 to 144.16.68.255. A /24 mask fixes the network portion to the first three octets, leaving only the fourth octet as host-identifying bits within that range.

eth3's mask 255.255.255.224 (/27) covers the address range 144.16.68.64 to 144.16.68.95. A /27 mask fixes the network portion through the top three bits of the fourth octet (the block starting at 64), leaving the remaining five bits of the fourth octet as host-identifying bits within that declared block.

title: Calculate the broadcast address if the IP address (CIDR) is
subject: Computer Networks
text: Calculate the broadcast address if the IP address (CIDR) is 201.102.77.35/27
solution:
Broadcast address is the last address in the subnet, where all the host bits are made to be 1's. A broadcast address targets all systems on a specific subnet instead of a single host.

Step 1: Use the bitwise AND operator on the binary IP address to the binary CIDR address to get the network address.

11001001.01100110.01001101.00100011 (201.102.77.35)

& 11111111.11111111.11111111.11100000 (/27)

-----------------------------------

11001001.01100110.01001101.00100000 (201.102.77.32)

[201.102.77.32]

Step 2: Next use the bitwise OR operator on the binary network address and the inverted CIDR address to get the broadcast address.

11001001.01100110.01001101.00100000 (201.102.77.32)

(or) 00000000.00000000.00000000.00011111 (inverted /27)

-----------------------------------

11001001.01100110.01001101.00111111 (201.102.77.63)

[201.102.77.63]

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. A /27 subnet has 32 addresses (block size 32). The subnet containing 201.102.77.35 runs from 201.102.77.32 to 201.102.77.63, so 201.102.77.31 is the broadcast address of the previous subnet (201.102.77.0/27), not of the subnet that contains .35.

Correct. With a /27 mask (255.255.255.224) the subnet size is 32 addresses. The network address for the host 201.102.77.35 is 201.102.77.32, and the last address in that block (the broadcast) is 201.102.77.63.
Incorrect. 201.102.77.32 is the network (first) address of the subnet that contains 201.102.77.35. The broadcast is the last address in that subnet, which is 201.102.77.63.
Incorrect. 255.255.255.224 is the subnet mask corresponding to /27, not a broadcast address. For the subnet containing 201.102.77.35, the broadcast address is 201.102.77.63.

Consider the following table

Find the next hop, if the router has the ip address “ 128.114.52.04”
solution:
Key idea: Use the longest-prefix match by applying the /22 mask to the destination IP and compare the resulting network with the routing table.

Step-by-step:

  • Given IP: 128.114.52.02

  • Mask /22 corresponds to 255.255.252.0 (block size of 4 in the third octet).

  • Compare with the routing table entries: the table lists 128.114.56.0/22 and 128.114.60.0/22 (and 192.168.30.0/23). The network 128.114.52.0/22 is not present.

  • Because there is no matching specific route, the packet uses the default route.

Answer: R2 (default next hop)

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The interface labeled I0 corresponds to the network 128.114.56.0/22. The destination IP 128.114.52.02 falls into the 128.114.52.0/22 block (network address 128.114.52.0), not 128.114.56.0/22, so this interface is not used.
Incorrect. The interface labeled I1 corresponds to 128.114.60.0/22. The given IP 128.114.52.02 does not fall in that /22 range, so I1 is not the correct next hop.

solution:

title: Suppose an organisation has CIDR based IP address Organisation decided
subject: Computer Networks
text: Suppose an organisation has CIDR based IP address 215.58.204.10./20, Organisation decided to divide the network into three subnet name as X, Y, Z respectively. Which of the following is a valid IP address of the subnet Y?
solution:
Given: 215.58.204.10/20

Subnet mask: /20 = 255.255.240.0. Compute the network address: third octet 204 & 240 = 192, so the network is 215.58.192.0/20.

The /20 network range is 215.58.192.0 through 215.58.207.255.

One reasonable way to divide this /20 into three subnets is to allocate one /21 and two /22 subnets so the ranges do not overlap and cover the whole /20:

  • Subnet X: 215.58.192.0/21 — covers 215.58.192.0 to 215.58.199.255

  • Subnet Y: 215.58.200.0/22 — covers 215.58.200.0 to 215.58.203.255

  • Subnet Z: 215.58.204.0/22 — covers 215.58.204.0 to 215.58.207.255

Check the candidate addresses:

  • 215.58.201.100/22 falls inside 215.58.200.0–215.58.203.255, so it is a valid address for Subnet Y (and the /22 mask matches that subnet).

  • 215.58.192.12/22 and 215.58.196.254/21 both lie within 215.58.192.0–215.58.199.255 (Subnet X) under this partition, so they are not in Subnet Y.

Therefore the address 215.58.201.100/22 is a valid IP for subnet Y in this partitioning. Note: different valid partitions of the /20 are possible, but the partition above matches the provided correct option.

optionFeedback.html: The address 215.58.192.12/22 lies in the block 215.58.192.0–215.58.199.255 (the portion starting at 215.58.192.0). In the partition used here, that block corresponds to a different subnet (X), so this address is not part of subnet Y.

This is correct. When the /20 network 215.58.192.0/20 is partitioned into one /21 and two /22 subnets, subnet Y can be 215.58.200.0/22, which covers 215.58.200.0–215.58.203.255. The address 215.58.201.100/22 falls inside that range and therefore is a valid address for subnet Y.
The address 215.58.196.254/21 is within 215.58.192.0–215.58.199.255, which corresponds to the larger first subnet (X) in the partition used. Therefore it is not part of subnet Y.
'None of these' is not correct here because 215.58.201.100/22 is a valid address for subnet Y under a reasonable partitioning of the /20 network (see explanation).

title: Router has the following (CIDR) entries in the routing table.
subject: Computer Networks
text:
A router has the following (CIDR) entries in the routing table.

Next-hop for a packet with IP address 138.48.63.10
solution:
Given:

  • Routing table entries: 138.48.56.0/22 → I-0; 138.48.60.0/22 → I-1; 192.150.48.0/23 → R-1; default → R-2.

  • Packet IP: 138.48.63.10.

Key idea: match the packet to the most specific routing entry by checking which subnet contains the IP.

/22 networks have a block size of 4 in the third octet, so:

  • 138.48.56.0/22 covers third-octet values 56–59.

  • 138.48.60.0/22 covers third-octet values 60–63.

Since the packet's third octet is 63, the address 138.48.63.10 falls into 138.48.60.0/22.

Therefore the packet matches the 138.48.60.0/22 route and is forwarded to next-hop I-1.

optionFeedback.html: The route I-0 is 138.48.56.0/22. A /22 covers addresses where the third octet runs in blocks of 4 (56–59 for 138.48.56.0/22). The packet 138.48.63.10 is not in the 56–59 range, so this route is incorrect for that packet.

The route I-1 is 138.48.60.0/22. A /22 covers third-octet blocks of 4, so 138.48.60.0/22 includes addresses with third octet 60–63. The packet 138.48.63.10 falls within that range, so it matches this route — this is the correct next-hop.
The route R-1 is 192.150.48.0/23, which is a completely different major network (192.150.x.x). The packet 138.48.63.10 does not match that network, so this route is incorrect.
R-2 is the default route used when no specific route matches. Since 138.48.63.10 matches the 138.48.60.0/22 route, the default route is not used for this packet.

title: IP address is found to be residing on sub-network with
subject: Computer Networks
text: IP address 172.16.123.213 is found to be residing on a sub-network with the following subnet mask: 255.255.255.240. What is the network address of this subnet?
solution:
Concept

The address of a subnet is obtained by a bitwise AND of a host IP address with its subnet mask. Wherever the mask holds a 1 the bit is a network bit and passes through unchanged; wherever the mask holds a 0 the bit is a host bit and is forced to 0. So the mask splits every address into a fixed network prefix and a host field, and zeroing that host field names the subnet itself rather than any machine on it.

Applying it here

  1. Write the mask in binary: 255.255.255.240 = 11111111.11111111.11111111.11110000. That is 24 + 4 = 28 network bits, so the prefix length is /28.

  2. The first three mask octets are all 1s, so the first three octets of the address survive the AND untouched: 172.16.123.

  3. Only the final octet is split. In binary 213 = 110101012 and 240 = 111100002.

  4. AND them bit by bit. The leading four bits 1101 sit under mask bits of 1, so they are preserved. The trailing four bits 0101 sit under mask bits of 0, so they become 0000. Result: 110100002.

  5. Convert back to decimal: 128 + 64 + 16 = 208.

  6. Network address = 172.16.123.208.

Cross-check with the block-size method

  • Four host bits give a block size of 24 = 16 addresses per subnet, which is also the familiar shortcut 256 - 240 = 16.

  • So every /28 boundary in the final octet is a multiple of 16: 0, 16, 32, ... 192, 208, 224, 240.

  • 213 falls between the boundary 208 (= 13 x 16) and the next boundary 224 (= 14 x 16), so its subnet runs 208-223 and starts at 208 - the same value the AND produced.

  • Note that "network address" means the base of that range. The first usable host would be 209 and the broadcast address would be 223; neither is what the question asks for.

Comparing the offered values

Final octet

Low four bits

Role under /28

213

0101

A host inside its block, not a boundary

240

0000

A /28 boundary (15 x 16), base of 240-255

245

0101

A host inside the block 240-255

208

0000

A /28 boundary (13 x 16), base of 208-223

The value 240 is a genuine /28 boundary, but it is the base of the block 240-255, which does not contain 213; 213 and 245 both carry a non-zero host field, so neither can name a subnet.

optionFeedback.html: The final octet 213 is 11010101 in binary. The /28 mask 255.255.255.240 ends in 11110000, so it splits this value into a leading group 1101 and a trailing group 0101; the trailing group here is non-zero, so 213 is not an exact multiple of sixteen.

The final octet 240 is 11110000 in binary. Dividing it at the four-bit boundary that the /28 mask 255.255.255.240 sets, the leading group is 1111 and the trailing group is 0000; a trailing group of four zeros makes 240 an exact multiple of sixteen.

The final octet 245 is 11110101 in binary. Measured against the four-bit split that the /28 mask 255.255.255.240 imposes, its leading group is 1111 and its trailing group is 0101; a non-zero trailing group means 245 is not an exact multiple of sixteen.

The final octet 208 is 11010000 in binary. The four-bit split imposed by the /28 mask 255.255.255.240 puts 1101 in the leading group and 0000 in the trailing group; four trailing zeros make 208 an exact multiple of sixteen.
This choice is the paper's not-attempted marker rather than an address, so it carries no final octet to split into leading and trailing groups under the /28 mask 255.255.255.240.

title: In IPv4 addressing, what is the purpose of CIDR notation
subject: Computer Networks
text: In IPv4 addressing, what is the purpose of CIDR notation ?

options.html: To specify the address range and subnet mask in a concise format
To facilitate dynamic IP allocation using DHCP

solution: CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation specifies the network prefix length using a slash followed by a number, such as /24. This concise format indicates how many bits define the network portion versus host portion, enabling efficient IP address allocation and routing.

optionFeedback.html: This option is incorrect because CIDR does not relate to Maximum Transmission Unit. MTU refers to the largest packet size a network interface can transmit, which is unrelated to IP address notation.
CIDR notation combines the IP address with a prefix length to define the network portion. This format allows flexible subnetting by specifying how many bits belong to the network versus host.

CIDR notation does not identify reserved IP addresses. Reserved addresses are defined by specific ranges like 10.0.0.0/8 or loopback 127.0.0.0/8, which CIDR can represent but not specifically identify.
CIDR notation is not used for dynamic IP allocation. DHCP handles dynamic assignments, while CIDR defines network boundaries and routing efficiency through prefix notation.

title: An organization is granted the block The administrator wants to

text:

solution:
Final answer: 130.56.255.192 to 130.56.255.255

  1. Start with the given block: 130.56.0.0/16. You need 1024 subnets.

  2. Since 1024 = 2^10, you must borrow 10 bits from the host portion.

  3. New prefix length = 16 + 10 = /26.

  4. Addresses per subnet = 2^(32 - 26) = 64 addresses (62 usable hosts).

  5. Subnets increment by 64 in the last octet. The last subnet index is 1023, so offset = 1023 × 64 = 65472, which corresponds to .255.192 in the last two octets.

  6. Therefore the last subnet's network address = 130.56.255.192 and its broadcast (last address) = 130.56.255.255.

optionFeedback.html: This is incorrect. To create 1024 subnets from a /16 you must borrow 10 bits, producing /26 subnets of 64 addresses each. The last subnet's network address is 130.56.255.192 and its broadcast is 130.56.255.255, not 130.56.0.0–130.56.254.255.

Correct. Reason: 1024 = 2^10 so you borrow 10 bits from the /16, giving a new prefix length of /26. Each subnet has 64 addresses, so the last subnet network is 130.56.255.192 and its broadcast (last address) is 130.56.255.255.

solution: To find the broadcast address, identify the network portion and host portion based on the subnet mask. title: What does the term ‘NAT’ stand for in networking
subject: Computer Networks
text: What does the term ‘NAT’ stand for in networking ?
solution: NAT stands for Network Address Translation. This is a fundamental networking concept used to remap one IP address space into another by modifying network address information in the IP header of packets while they are in transit across a traffic routing device. The primary purpose of NAT is to allow multiple devices on a local network to share a single public IP address when accessing the internet, which conserves IPv4 addresses and adds a layer of security by hiding internal network structures. Option B, Network Access Translation, is incorrect because NAT does not primarily deal with access control or authentication. Option C and D are also incorrect as they refer to 'Node' or 'Application' translation, which do not accurately describe the function of modifying IP addresses at the network layer. Therefore, Option A is the correct definition.

title: Identify the local link address from the following IPv6 addresses:
subject: Computer Networks
text: Identify the link-local address from the following IPv6 addresses:
solution:
Concept

An IPv6 address is classified by the leading bits of its first hextet, which fix its scope and purpose. A link-local unicast address is valid only on a single network link (it is never routed off that link), and by RFC 4291 it lies in the FE80::/10 block. The /10 pins only the first 10 bits to 1111111010, so its first hextet ranges from FE80 to FEBF. The task is to match each address to its reserved prefix and pick the one whose high-order bits fall in that link-local range.

Applying the prefix rules

Address (first hextet)

Reserved prefix

Type / scope

2001:0db8:...

2001:db8::/32

Documentation / global

FE80:...

FE80::/10

Link-local unicast

FF02:...

FF00::/8

Multicast

::1

::1/128

Loopback

2001:4860:4860::...

2000::/3

Global unicast

Only the address whose first hextet is FE80 has high-order bits inside FE80::/10, so it is the link-local address.

Cross-check

Expand the first hextet to bits: FE80 = 1111 1110 1000 0000. Its first 10 bits are 1111111010, which is exactly the FE80::/10 pattern (any first hextet FE80-FEBF shares these 10 bits). None of the other addresses' high-order bits match this pattern, confirming the choice.

optionFeedback.html: An address starting 2001:0db8:abcd falls in 2001:db8::/32, the range reserved for documentation/examples - a routable, global-format address whose scope is the whole internet rather than a single link.
An address starting FE80 has high-order bits inside FE80::/10 (first hextet FE80-FEBF), the block RFC 4291 reserves for link-local unicast - valid only on the local link and never routed beyond it.
An address starting FF02 falls in FF00::/8, the multicast range used for one-to-many delivery to a group of interfaces.
::1 is the loopback address ::1/128, which a host uses to reach itself; its scope is the host alone, not any network link.
An address starting 2001:4860 falls in 2000::/3, the global-unicast range routed across the public internet (here a public DNS resolver).

title: In classful addressing the IP address with 0(zero) as network
subject: Computer Networks
text: In a classful addressing the IP address with 0(zero) as network number:

options.html: refers to broadcast on the local network
refers to the broadcast on a distant network

solution:
Answer: An IP address whose network portion is all zeros refers to the current (local) network in classful addressing.

Key points:

  • This-network convention: A network field of all zeros is interpreted as "this network" (the local network).

  • Broadcast addresses: Broadcasts are indicated by setting the host portion to all ones (for example, 192.168.1.255 for a /24). A zero network number does not mean broadcast.

  • Directed (distant) broadcasts use a specific network number with all host bits set to one; they are not signified by an all-zero network field.

  • Loopback: Loopback addresses are in the 127.0.0.0/8 block (commonly 127.0.0.1), unrelated to the all-zero network convention.

  • Historical note: Early classful IPv4 specifications used the all-zero network convention. Modern practice prefers explicit network numbering to avoid ambiguity.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. In classful addressing, a network field composed of all zeros is used to mean the current (local) network, sometimes called "this network." This distinguishes it from other special uses such as broadcast or loopback.
Incorrect. A broadcast on the local network is indicated when the host portion is all ones (for example, 192.168.1.255 in a /24). An all-zero network number does not denote a broadcast address.
Incorrect. A directed (distant) broadcast targets a specific network by setting that network's host bits to all ones. An all-zero network number does not indicate a broadcast to a remote network.
Incorrect. Loopback addresses are in the 127.0.0.0/8 range (commonly 127.0.0.1). The all-zero network number is unrelated to loopback testing.

title: What is the purpose of routing table?
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the purpose of a routing table?

options.html: To store every address of every node
To know the exact location of destination address
To find most efficient route to the destination

solution:
Concept: A routing table is a data structure stored in a router (or host) that maps destination networks to the information needed to reach them — typically a destination network/prefix, a next-hop address, an outgoing interface, and a metric. Its governing purpose is path selection: for any incoming packet the router looks up the destination and decides the best (lowest-cost) way to forward it onward.

Application: When a packet arrives, the router reads its destination IP, searches the table for the matching entry using longest-prefix match, and forwards the packet to the next hop on the path with the most favourable metric (lowest cost / administrative distance). So the table exists to pick the most efficient route to the destination; it does not store the location of every individual host, and it does not record an exact geographic position.

Contrast: the other purposes describe what a routing table is not for:

  • Storing every address of every node: a routing table holds network prefixes and next hops, not an entry for every host; keeping every node's address would not scale and is not the table's job.

  • Knowing the exact location of the destination: a router only needs the direction of the next hop toward the destination network, not the destination's precise physical location.

  • Flooding the network: flooding sends a packet out on all links and is deliberately inefficient; it is the behaviour routing tables exist to avoid.

Result: the routing table's purpose is to find the most efficient route to the destination.

optionFeedback.html: A routing table records destination networks/prefixes and their next hops, not an individual entry for every node; treating it as a complete host directory mistakes its scope.
A router needs only the next-hop direction toward the destination network, not the destination's exact physical location; this confuses forwarding direction with precise location.
Flooding forwards a packet out on every link and is intentionally inefficient; it is the opposite of what a table-driven router does.
The table maps destination networks to next hops and metrics so the router can select the lowest-cost path and forward the packet that way.

title: Routing information Protocol (RIP) uses
subject: Computer Networks
text: Routing information Protocol (RIP) uses
solution:
Answer: RIP is a distance-vector routing protocol.

Key details:

  • Metric: Uses hop count as its routing metric; a hop count of 16 indicates an unreachable route.

  • Updates: Sends periodic routing updates (typically every 30 seconds).

  • Algorithm and loop mitigation: Implements the distance-vector (Bellman-Ford) approach and uses split horizon, route poisoning, and hold-down timers to help limit routing loops.

  • Versions: RIPv1 is classful; RIPv2 adds support for CIDR (classless addressing) and optional authentication.

  • Limitations: Not suitable for large networks due to slow convergence and the 15-hop limit.

Therefore, the correct characterization is that RIP uses the distance-vector routing method.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Routing Information Protocol (RIP) is a distance-vector routing protocol. It uses hop count as its metric, sends periodic updates (typically every 30 seconds), and treats a hop count of 16 as unreachable. RIP also uses techniques such as split horizon, route poisoning, and hold-down timers to reduce routing loops.

solution:
Final distance vectors (shortest-path distances):

  • From A: to A = 0, to B = 6, to C = 4, to D = 3

  • From B: to A = 6, to B = 0, to C = 2, to D = 3

  • From C: to A = 4, to B = 2, to C = 0, to D = 1

  • From D: to A = 3, to B = 3, to C = 1, to D = 0

Key reasoning and checks:

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q98
subject: Computer Networks
text: How does split horizon help reduce the count-to-infinity problem in distance vector routing?

options.html: Stopping routers from sending updates on all ports
Preventing routers from advertising a route back on the interface

solution:
Concept

In distance-vector routing protocols (such as RIP), each router learns routes from its neighbors and re-advertises them onward. The count-to-infinity problem occurs when a route becomes unreachable but two neighboring routers keep advertising it to each other with steadily increasing hop counts, because each one still believes the other has a valid path. Split horizon is a loop-avoidance rule: a router omits a route from the update it sends out the very interface through which it originally learned that route, since re-advertising it there would just be echoing the neighbor’s own information back to it.

Application

Consider router B, which learns a route to network X from neighbor A on the link between them. Under split horizon, B does not include that route to X in the update it sends back to A on that same link. So if the link between A and X later fails, A does not receive a stale route to X from B claiming a working path via B, which is exactly the false information that would otherwise make A and B keep raising their advertised hop counts to each other toward infinity.

Cross-check

Contrast this with the other offered mechanisms. Suppressing updates on every port (rather than only the interface a specific route was learned on) would stop the router from advertising anything at all, which is not split horizon's selective, per-route, per-interface behaviour. Choosing distance over hop count is a metric-design decision (as in EIGRP), unrelated to which interface an update is withheld from. Turning off periodic updates concerns the update schedule (related instead to triggered updates), not the direction in which a specific route is withheld. RFC 1058 describes exactly this interface-specific withholding behaviour, confirming that preventing a router from advertising a route back on the interface it was learned from is the mechanism that reduces count-to-infinity here.

optionFeedback.html: This describes a router halting its outgoing update transmissions across every one of its ports at once, rather than continuing its normal update schedule.
This describes replacing the hop-count metric with a distance-based measure when routers compare and select among candidate paths.
This describes a router omitting one specific route from the update sent out one specific interface, rather than acting on every route or every interface uniformly.
This describes turning off the router's scheduled, interval-based update transmissions altogether.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q67
subject: Computer Networks
text: Assuming no routing loop is present, which situation would primarily cause a router to select a valid but suboptimal path even though every routing protocol involved continues to run and converge correctly?

options.html: Unequal cost metrics between heterogeneous routing protocols

solution:
A dynamic routing protocol compares the candidate paths it has learned using its own metric and selects whichever candidate has the lowest value of that metric, trusting that value as “best” regardless of whether the number actually reflects real-world path quality. Different protocols compute this metric on different scales: RIP simply counts hops, OSPF derives a cost from link bandwidth, and EIGRP combines bandwidth and delay into a composite value — so a metric value computed by one protocol is not comparable to a metric value computed by another.

When routes learned from one protocol are redistributed into a different protocol, the receiving protocol has no way to translate the original metric onto its own scale, so it must instead assign a seed (default) metric to the redistributed routes. Because that seed metric does not represent the routes' true cost, a router can end up preferring a path that its own metric marks as best even though a different, non-redistributed path is actually shorter or faster — and this happens purely from the metric mismatch, with every protocol involved still converging normally and operating exactly as designed.

The other three situations, by contrast, each describe an actual breakdown in protocol operation rather than a side effect of protocols working correctly:

  • A route-redistribution loop — the case this stem's “no routing loop” premise explicitly rules out — happens when a route is fed back into the very protocol it originated from; the metric keeps inflating (or the route oscillates) until it is discarded, a misconfiguration that breaks correct operation, not an artifact of it.

  • An MTU mismatch on a link used by a link-state protocol typically prevents the two routers from ever completing neighbor/adjacency formation, so the protocol is not functioning correctly once that happens — it simply fails to form a relationship on that link.

  • If link-state packets are never acknowledged, the reliable-flooding mechanism that keeps every router's link-state database synchronized has itself broken down — again a functional failure, not a consequence of correct operation.

So the situation that produces a suboptimal path while every routing protocol continues to run and converge correctly is unequal cost metrics between heterogeneous routing protocols.

optionFeedback.html: Redistributing routes between routing protocols that use different metric systems — for example hop count on one side and a bandwidth-derived cost on the other — requires the receiving protocol to assign a fresh seed metric, since the two numeric scales are not directly convertible into each other.

A redistribution loop happens when a route that originated in one protocol is redistributed into a second protocol and then redistributed back into the first, so the route keeps re-entering the protocol it came from and its metric keeps changing on each pass.

An MTU mismatch means the two routers on a link have configured different maximum packet sizes for that interface; several link-state protocols check for matching MTU values while exchanging their database description packets before an adjacency can complete.

Link-state packets are sent with a reliability mechanism that expects an acknowledgment from the receiving router within an expected interval; when that acknowledgment does not arrive in time, the sending router keeps retransmitting the same packet at that interval until it is acknowledged.

title: What is the term for an endpoint of an inter-process
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the term for an endpoint of an inter-process communication flow across a computer network ?
solution: In computer networking, a socket serves as the fundamental endpoint for inter-process communication (IPC) across a network. It combines an IP address, which identifies the specific machine, with a port number to identify the specific application or service running on that machine. This unique combination allows multiple processes on different devices to communicate reliably over a network connection.\nWhile a port (Option A) is part of the socket definition, it only identifies the application layer service and lacks the network address component necessary to define a complete communication endpoint. A pipe (Option C) is typically used for IPC between processes on the same machine, not across a network. A machine (Option D) refers to the physical or virtual hardware itself rather than the specific communication interface used by software processes. Therefore, a socket is the precise technical term for an endpoint enabling networked inter-process communication.

optionFeedback.html: A port is a numerical identifier (like 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS) used to distinguish different processes running on the same physical machine. A port is an essential component used to build a socket, but the port itself is just a number, whereas the socket is the actual operational endpoint that handles the traffic flow.

It perfectly matches the definition. Network APIs (like POSIX Berkeley Sockets) use sockets to read and write data across a network. It is the programmatic interface where the inter-process communication flow strictly begins and terminates.

While a pipe is an inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism, it is traditionally used for communication between processes running on the same local computer (such as utilizing the | character in a Linux terminal to pass data from one command to another). Standard pipes cannot bridge communication across a computer network.

A machine (or host) refers to the entire physical or virtual hardware node connected to the network. A single machine can host thousands of concurrent, independent communication flows. Therefore, the entire machine is far too broad to be considered an individual "endpoint" of a single IPC flow.

TCP establishes a dedicated connection before data transfer begins. This ensures reliability through acknowledgments and retransmissions for lost packets.

title: In context of OSI model of computer networks, which of
subject: Computer Networks
text:
In the context of the OSI model of computer networks, which of the following statements name a transport-layer protocol?

  • I. Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

  • II. User Datagram Protocol (UDP)
solution:
Concept

The transport layer provides end-to-end communication between application processes. In the Internet protocol suite, TCP and UDP are its two principal protocols.

TCP expands to Transmission Control Protocol and provides reliable, connection-oriented byte-stream service. UDP expands to User Datagram Protocol and provides connectionless datagram service.

Application

  1. Statement I names Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), which operates at the transport layer.

  2. Statement II names User Datagram Protocol (UDP), which also operates at the transport layer.

  3. Therefore, the two statements identify transport-layer protocols.

Contrast and cross-check

  • ‘Only I’ omits UDP even though UDP supplies transport-layer datagram service.

  • ‘Neither I nor II’ excludes both established transport-layer protocols.

  • ‘Only II’ omits TCP even though TCP supplies transport-layer byte-stream service.

RFC 9293 defines TCP, and RFC 768 defines UDP; both belong to the Internet transport layer.

Result

The answer by value is ‘Both I and II’.

optionFeedback.html: ‘Only I’ includes TCP and excludes UDP. RFC 1122 places TCP and UDP together at the transport layer, so this response splits two protocols that share one layer classification.
‘Neither I nor II’ excludes both TCP and UDP. RFC 1122 places TCP and UDP together at the transport layer, so this response places both outside their shared layer classification.
‘Both I and II’ includes both TCP and UDP. RFC 1122 places TCP and UDP together at the transport layer, so this response places both inside their shared layer classification.
‘Only II’ excludes TCP and includes UDP. RFC 1122 places TCP and UDP together at the transport layer, so this response splits two protocols that share one layer classification.

title: Which of the following TCP/IP protocol allows an application program
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following TCP/IP protocol allows an application program on one machine to send a datagram to an application program on another machine?
solution:
Concept: In the TCP/IP suite, the transport layer offers two delivery styles. A connection-oriented byte-stream service (TCP) sets up a reliable, ordered connection before any data flows; a connectionless datagram service hands each self-contained message to the network independently, with no prior handshake. The protocol whose entire purpose is to let one application program ship a single datagram to another application program — addressed by port number, with minimal overhead and no connection setup — is the User Datagram Protocol (UDP).

Application: The defining specification (RFC 768) describes UDP exactly as the question phrases it: a procedure for application programs to send messages (datagrams) to other application programs with a minimum of protocol mechanism. UDP runs over IP, multiplexes to the right program using source and destination ports, and forwards each datagram on a best-effort basis without establishing or maintaining a connection. So the protocol that lets an application on one machine send a datagram to an application on another machine is UDP.

Contrast with the other choices:

  • VMTP — a transport protocol designed for request-response (transaction/RPC) message exchange in distributed systems, not the standard TCP/IP datagram delivery service for ordinary application programs.

  • X.25 — an older packet-switched WAN networking standard (network/data-link layers), not a TCP/IP transport protocol for application-to-application datagrams.

  • SMTP — an application-layer protocol for transferring email between mail servers; it relies on an underlying transport, it does not itself provide the datagram delivery service.

Cross-check: Of the four, only UDP sits at the transport layer with a connectionless, datagram (message) delivery model addressed by ports — matching the description precisely. The correct answer is UDP.

optionFeedback.html: UDP is the TCP/IP transport-layer protocol whose defining role is exactly this: it lets an application program hand a single self-contained datagram to another application program, addressed by port, on a best-effort basis with no connection setup — the minimal-mechanism message service described in RFC 768.

VMTP is a transport protocol built for request-response transaction (RPC-style) messaging in distributed systems. Picking it likely comes from recognising it as a transport protocol while overlooking that the standard TCP/IP service for plain application-to-application datagram delivery is a different, ubiquitous protocol.

X.25 is a legacy packet-switched WAN standard operating at the network/data-link layers, not a TCP/IP transport protocol. Choosing it confuses a wide-area packet-switching technology with the suite's application-to-application datagram transport.

SMTP is an application-layer protocol for moving email between servers; it depends on an underlying transport rather than providing datagram delivery itself. Selecting it mistakes a specific email application service for a general transport-layer datagram protocol.

title: Port address in TCP/IP is bits long.
subject: Computer Networks
text: Port address in TCP/IP is ________ bits long.
solution:
Concept

A port number is the transport-layer address that identifies a specific process or service running on a host. In both the TCP and the UDP segment headers, the Source Port and Destination Port are each stored in a fixed 16-bit field. A field of n bits can encode 2n distinct values, so the size of this field is what fixes how many ports can exist.

Application

  1. The TCP/UDP header reserves a 16-bit field for the port address (one for source, one for destination).

  2. With 16 bits, the number of distinct port values is 216 = 65,536.

  3. These are numbered 0 to 65,535, which is exactly the standard port range used by every operating system.

Cross-check

The well-known fact that valid ports run from 0 to 65,535 is the give-away: 65,535 = 216 − 1, which is only possible if the field holds 16 bits. A 32-bit field would allow over 4 billion ports, and a 48-bit field even more — neither matches the observed 0–65,535 range. Hence the port address is 16 bits long.

optionFeedback.html: 32 bits is the width of an IPv4 address, which lives at the network layer, not at the transport layer where ports are defined. Substituting the host-address size for the port-field size produces this value.

48 bits is the size of a MAC (hardware) address, which belongs to the data-link layer, not to a transport-layer port. Mapping the Ethernet address width onto the port field produces this incorrect value.

The TCP and UDP segment headers define the Source Port and Destination Port as 16-bit fields. Sixteen bits span 216 = 65,536 codes, i.e. the addresses 0 through 65,535 — the exact port range these protocols operate over.

Reaching for "none of the above" reflects an assumption that the port field has some non-standard or undefined width. In reality the TCP/UDP header defines a fixed, well-documented port size, so a catch-all rejection of every numeric choice does not apply here.

title: Which of the following services use TCP? DHCP ii) SMTP
subject: Computer Networks
text:
Which of the following services use TCP?

i) DHCP

ii) SMTP

iii) HTTP

iv) TFTP

v) FTP
solution:
Concept — The transport protocol a service uses depends on what the application needs. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it performs a handshake and uses sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission so that every byte arrives correctly and in order. UDP is connectionless and lightweight: it has no handshake and no built-in reliability, which suits bootstrapping, broadcast, or small low-overhead transfers.

Application — Classify each service by the transport it relies on:

  • SMTP uses TCP: an email message must arrive complete and in order.

  • HTTP uses TCP: a web page and its resources must be delivered reliably.

  • FTP uses TCP for both its control and data connections, so whole files transfer without loss.

  • DHCP uses UDP: a client broadcasts to obtain configuration before it even has an IP address, which fits connectionless UDP.

  • TFTP uses UDP: it is deliberately 'trivial' and carries its own minimal acknowledgement scheme on top of UDP instead of relying on TCP.

Cross-check — Collecting the TCP services gives SMTP, HTTP and FTP, that is items ii, iii and v.

optionFeedback.html: This grouping puts DHCP among TCP services. DHCP exchanges its messages by broadcast before the client even has an IP address, so it operates over connectionless UDP, not TCP.

This grouping lists SMTP, HTTP and FTP as TCP services. Each of these carries data that must arrive complete and in order — full mail messages, web pages, and entire files — so each runs over the connection-oriented TCP transport.

This grouping includes TFTP among TCP services. TFTP is deliberately lightweight and layers its own minimal acknowledgement scheme on top of UDP, so it runs over UDP; DHCP in this grouping is UDP-based as well.
This grouping includes DHCP and TFTP among TCP services. Both are designed for lightweight, low-overhead exchanges and run over UDP rather than TCP.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q153
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following is a connection-oriented protocol ?
solution:
A protocol is connection-oriented when the sender and receiver first establish a session (commonly via a handshake) and maintain state for that session throughout the exchange, so that delivery can be tracked, acknowledged, and reordered if needed. A connectionless protocol instead sends each unit of data independently, with no session setup and no guarantee of delivery or order.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) begins every exchange with a three-way handshake — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — before any application data is sent. Once the connection is open, TCP numbers every byte, acknowledges receipt, retransmits lost segments, and closes the session explicitly at the end. This session-based, stateful behaviour is exactly what defines a connection-oriented protocol, so TCP fits the description in the stem.

Contrasting the other options confirms this:

  • UDP sends each datagram independently with no handshake and no session state, so it is connectionless rather than connection-oriented.

  • IP works at the network layer and forwards each packet on a best-effort basis without setting up or tracking any session between source and destination — also connectionless.

  • HTTP is an application-layer protocol that defines request/response message formats between a client and server; it does not itself establish the transport session — it runs on top of a transport-layer connection (typically TCP).

Hence, among the given options, TCP is the connection-oriented protocol.

optionFeedback.html: UDP is a transport-layer protocol that sends datagrams directly without a prior handshake, so each datagram is delivered independently with no session state maintained between sender and receiver.
IP operates at the network layer, forwarding each packet independently on a best-effort basis without establishing or maintaining any session between source and destination.
TCP is a transport-layer protocol that begins data exchange with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and maintains sequence numbers and acknowledgments for the duration of the exchange.

HTTP is an application-layer protocol that defines request and response message formats between a client and server, and it is typically carried over a separate transport-layer session established beneath it.

title: Is used to connect the smartwatch and wireless headphone to
subject: Computer Networks
text:
"______ is used to connect the smartwatch and wireless headphone to the phone and is a ______ range wireless technology. ______ is used to connect the phone and the laptop to the outside world called the "Internet" and it uses radio waves to allow high-speed data transfer over short distances. ______ is used to connect the phone to countless services via the "Internet" and is a ______ range wireless technology."

Therefore, the correct sequence is Bluetooth, Short, Wi-Fi, 3G/4G/5G, Long.

title: The TCP sliding window
subject: Computer Networks
text: The TCP sliding window

options.html: can be used to control the flow of information
always occurs when the field value is 0
always occurs when the field value is 1

solution: The TCP sliding window mechanism is a fundamental protocol feature designed to manage data transmission rates between sender and receiver. It allows the sender to transmit multiple packets before receiving an acknowledgment, thereby controlling the flow of information and optimizing network utilization. This aligns with standard networking definitions regarding flow control.

optionFeedback.html: The sliding window mechanism allows the receiver to control how much data the sender transmits, preventing buffer overflow. This process is known as flow control.
A window size of zero signals the sender to pause transmission for flow control, but the sliding window mechanism functions with non-zero values during normal data exchange.
The TCP window size adjusts dynamically based on network conditions and receiver capacity, not fixed at a value of 1.

title: An ACK number of in TCP always means that
subject: Computer Networks
text: In TCP, an ACK number of 1000 always means that ______.
solution:
In TCP, the acknowledgement (ACK) number is the next sequence number the receiver expects — a cumulative pointer into the connection's sequence-number space, not a literal count of bytes received. TCP numbers a connection's stream starting from its Initial Sequence Number (ISN), a value each endpoint picks essentially unpredictably per connection (RFC 9293); the SYN itself consumes exactly one sequence number, so the first data byte sits at ISN + 1.

Applying this here: if ACK = 1000, the number of data bytes received so far — counted modulo 2^32, i.e. before the connection's sequence-number space has wrapped around — works out to (1000 − ISN − 1), i.e. 999 − ISN. Because ISN can be any 32-bit value and is not guaranteed to be 0 (or any other fixed number), this expression can equal 999, 1000, 1001, or a value entirely different from all three, depending on the connection.

  • "999 bytes" is the (modulo-2^32) count only when ISN = 0 for that connection.

  • "1000 bytes" is the (modulo-2^32) count only when ISN = −1 (mod 2^32) for that connection.

  • "1001 bytes" is the (modulo-2^32) count only when ISN = −2 (mod 2^32) for that connection.

Since TCP never fixes the ISN to any one of these particular values for every connection, none of the three specific byte counts is entailed by ACK = 1000 in every case — hence the correct choice is that none of the above always holds.

optionFeedback.html: This treats 999 as the byte count ACK = 1000 must always represent; that count only holds for one particular Initial Sequence Number, not for every connection.
This treats 1000 as the byte count ACK = 1000 must always represent; that count only holds for one particular Initial Sequence Number, not for every connection.
This treats 1001 as the byte count ACK = 1000 must always represent; that count only holds for one particular Initial Sequence Number, not for every connection.
Every specific-count option only holds for one particular Initial Sequence Number; since TCP never fixes the ISN, no single byte count is guaranteed by ACK = 1000 for every connection.

title: Checksum field in TCP header is
subject: Computer Networks
text: Checksum field in TCP header is

options.html: ones complement of sum of header and data in bytes
ones complement of sum of header, data and pseudo header in 16 bit words

solution: The TCP checksum is calculated by summing 16-bit words of the header, data payload, and a pseudo-header containing IP information. The final checksum value is the ones complement of this sum.

optionFeedback.html: The TCP checksum calculation is performed using 16-bit words, not individual bytes.
The TCP checksum algorithm sums the header, data payload, and a pseudo-header using 16-bit words.
The TCP checksum is still mandatory in IPv6; only the IP header checksum was removed.
TCP checksums are for error detection, not security. MD5/SHA offer stronger integrity protection.

title: TCP operates over Gbps link. If TCP uses the full
subject: Computer Networks
text: TCP operates over a 40 Gbps link. If TCP uses the full bandwidth continuously, how long would it take the sequence numbers to wrap around completely?
solution:
Key insight: TCP sequence numbers count bytes and the sequence number space is 2^32.

  • Sequence number space: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 bytes.

  • Bandwidth: 40 Gbps = 40 × 10^9 bits/s = 5 × 10^9 bytes/s (8 bits = 1 byte).

  • Time to wrap = sequence number space / bandwidth.

  • Calculation: 4,294,967,296 bytes / (5 × 10^9 bytes/s) ≈ 0.858993459 s ≈ 859 ms.

Therefore the sequence numbers will wrap around in about 859 ms when sending continuously at 40 Gbps.

optionFeedback.html: 962 ms — Incorrect. TCP sequence numbers count bytes and the total space is 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 bytes. At 40 Gbps the link carries 40 × 10^9 bits/s = 5 × 10^9 bytes/s. Time = 4,294,967,296 / (5 × 10^9) ≈ 0.859 s (≈ 859 ms). 962 ms is larger than the correct value.

642 ms — Incorrect. Using the correct calculation: sequence space = 2^32 bytes = 4,294,967,296 bytes. Bandwidth = 40 Gbps = 5 × 10^9 bytes/s. Time = 4,294,967,296 / (5 × 10^9) ≈ 0.859 s (≈ 859 ms). 642 ms underestimates the time needed to exhaust the 32-bit sequence space.

330 ms — Incorrect. This is much smaller than the correct result. Calculate: sequence space = 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 bytes; bandwidth = 40 Gbps = 5 × 10^9 bytes/s. Time = 4,294,967,296 / (5 × 10^9) ≈ 0.859 s ≈ 859 ms, not 330 ms.

859 ms — Correct. Reason: TCP uses 32-bit sequence numbers so the space is 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 bytes. At 40 Gbps = 40 × 10^9 bits/s = 5 × 10^9 bytes/s, so time to wrap = 4,294,967,296 / (5 × 10^9) ≈ 0.85899 s, which is about 859 ms.

title: What are the following different parameters needed to identify the
subject: Computer Networks
text:
What are the following different parameters needed to identify the TCP connections between client and servers in internet of WAN or LAN.  

  1. S.port

  2. D.port

  3. S.IP

  4. D.IP
solution:
To uniquely identify a TCP connection, the following parameters are required:

S.port (Source Port) - Identifies the sending application.
D.port (Destination Port) - Identifies the receiving application.
S.IP (Source IP Address) - Specifies the sender's network location.
D.IP (Destination IP Address) - Specifies the receiver's network location.
Together, these parameters form the "TCP 4-tuple", which uniquely identifies a TCP connection in both WAN and LAN environments.

title: Let TCP operates over 32Gbps Gbps bit per second) link.
subject: Computer Networks
text: Suppose a TCP-like protocol uses a sequence-number field that is 2 bits wider than TCP’s standard 32-bit field and operates over a 32 Gbps link (1 Gbps = 109 bits per second). If it continuously uses the full bandwidth, after how many seconds will the sequence number wrap around? Assume that one sequence number is consumed per byte, and give the answer to two decimal places.
solution:
Concept: For a continuously transmitting link, a byte-oriented k-bit sequence-number field has 2k distinct sequence positions. The wraparound time equals the total sequence space in bytes divided by the transmission rate in bytes per second.

Application:

  1. The standard TCP sequence-number field is 32 bits wide. The stem adds 2 bits, so k = 32 + 2 = 34 bits.

  2. Sequence space = 234 = 17,179,869,184 byte positions.

  3. Link rate = 32 Gbps = 32 × 109 bits per second = (32 × 109)/8 = 4 × 109 bytes per second.

  4. Wraparound time = 234/(4 × 109) = 17,179,869,184/4,000,000,000 = 4.294967296 seconds, which rounds to 4.29 seconds.

Cross-check: With the standard 32-bit field, the exact time would be 232/(4 × 109) = 1.073741824 seconds. Two extra bits multiply the sequence space and time by 22 = 4; using the exact value, 1.073741824 × 4 = 4.294967296 seconds, which again rounds to 4.29 seconds.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The 16-bit checksum field allows the receiving network node to perform a 1's complement sum calculation to detect data corruption occurred during transmission.
Incorrect. An 8-bit size (1 byte) is structurally too small for a TCP checksum. Protocols like IPv4 use 16 bits for error checking, while TCP maintains a matching 16-bit field length.

title: The persist timer is used in TCP to
subject: Computer Networks

options.html: To detect crashes from the other end of the connection

solution: The persist timer in TCP is designed to prevent a deadlock scenario when the receiver advertises a zero window. If window update packets are lost, the sender might wait indefinitely for new data availability. The persist timer ensures periodic probes to check if buffer space has opened up, allowing transmission to resume.

title: Consider the following TCP connection where only control segments are

text:
Consider the following TCP connection where only control segments are exchanged. The TCP follows the same 3-way handshaking procedure as in circuit switching. FIN and SYN have the usual meaning of TCP connections. What are the possible values of X and Y respectively?

&Protocols
solution: The respective values are 7001, 6001. For X, acknowledgement of SYN is sent. As these are control segments, no data is shared. Only 1 sequence number is consumed. Hence 7001, 6001 is the correct answer. For Y, acknowledgement to FIN is sent.

title: When TCP sends SYN with seq Num or FIN with
subject: Computer Networks
text: When TCP sends a SYN with seq Num = X or FIN with seq Num = X, the consequent ACK has acknowledgement = X + 1, i.e. SYNs and FINs each take up one unit in sequence number space. Is this necessary.

options.html: It is essential for a FIN, but matter of convention and consistency for a SYN
It is essential for a SYN, but matter of convention and consistency for a FIN
It is essential for a SYN and FIN
Matter of convention and consistency for a FIN and SYN

solution: In TCP, SYN and FIN flags consume one sequence number in the sequence number space. This is essential for a FIN because it marks the end of data and helps ensure reliable delivery. title: Suppose Host is sending Host large file over TCP connection.
subject: Computer Networks
text:
Suppose Host A is sending Host B a large file over a TCP connection. Then which of the following statements is/are true?

S1: The number of unacknowledged bytes that A sends cannot exceed the size of the receiver buffer.

S2: If the sequence number for a segment of this connection is m, then the sequence number of the subsequent segment will be necessarily (m+1).
solution:
Answer: S1 only

  • Why S1 is true: TCP implements flow control using the receiver’s advertised window (rwnd), which reflects available receiver buffer space. The sender must not have more unacknowledged bytes outstanding than the receiver advertises. In practice the amount of outstanding data is limited by the minimum of the receiver window and the sender's congestion window (cwnd).

  • Why S2 is false: TCP sequence numbers count bytes in the byte stream, not packets. If a segment has sequence number m and carries u data bytes, the next sequence number will be m+u, not necessarily m+1. Examples: if a segment carries 1000 bytes, the next sequence number is m+1000; a SYN consumes one sequence number; a pure ACK with no data does not advance the sequence number.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. TCP uses flow control: the receiver advertises a receive window (rwnd) that reflects available buffer space, and the sender must not have more unacknowledged bytes outstanding than the receiver advertises. In practice outstanding data is limited by the minimum of the receiver's advertised window and the sender's congestion window.

Incorrect. TCP sequence numbers count bytes in the bytestream, not packets. The next segment's sequence number equals the current sequence number plus the number of data bytes sent in that segment. For example, if a segment with sequence number m carries 1000 data bytes, the subsequent sequence number will be m+1000. Also note control flags: a SYN consumes one sequence number and segments with no data do not advance the sequence number.

Incorrect. While the first statement about flow control limiting outstanding data is correct, the second statement is false because TCP sequence numbers count bytes, not packets. solution:
Given: RTT = 10 ms, MSS = 2 KB, receiver window = 24 KB. Slow start begins with a congestion window of 1 MSS and doubles the congestion window each RTT.

  • After 1 RTT (t = 10 ms): cwnd = 2 MSS, send 2 MSS = 4 KB. Cumulative sent = 6 KB.

  • After 2 RTTs (t = 20 ms): cwnd = 4 MSS, send 4 MSS = 8 KB. Cumulative sent = 14 KB.

  • After 3 RTTs (t = 30 ms): cwnd = 8 MSS, send 8 MSS = 16 KB. Cumulative sent = 30 KB, which exceeds the receiver window of 24 KB.

Conclusion: The sender can transmit the full 24 KB receiver window during the third RTT. Time = 3 × 10 ms = 30 ms.

title: Computer on Mbps network is regulated by token bucket. The

text: A computer on a 80 Mbps network is regulated by a token bucket. The token bucket is filled at a rate of 10 Mbps. It is initially filled to capacity with 210 megabits. The time taken for the computer to transmit at the full 80 Mbps is ………… sec.
solution:
Given: initial tokens B = 210 Mbits, token arrival rate r = 10 Mbps, transmission rate C = 80 Mbps.

  • Net token consumption rate while transmitting at full rate = C − r = 80 − 10 = 70 Mbps.

  • Time to exhaust the initial token bucket: t = B / (C − r) = 210 / 70 = 3 s.

  • Verification: bits sent in 3 s = C × t = 80 × 3 = 240 Mbits. Tokens available = initial 210 + r × t = 210 + 10 × 3 = 240 Mbits → matches.

Answer: 3 seconds

title: An SMTP client sends an email of size KB over

text: An SMTP client sends an email of size 500 KB over a TCP connection with MSS = 1 KB. The connection uses slow start, doubling the congestion window every RTT until it reaches 32 KB. If the RTT is 100 ms, calculate the total time (in milliseconds) to send the email.
solution:
Key idea: slow start doubles the congestion window each RTT; with MSS = 1 KB, the window is measured in KB and you send up to cwnd KB each RTT.

  • RTTs to reach a 32 KB window: starting at 1 KB and doubling each RTT, 1 × 2^5 = 32, so it takes 5 RTTs to reach a 32 KB window.

  • Data sent during those 5 RTTs (windows of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 KB): 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 KB.

  • Remaining data after these RTTs: 500 − 31 = 469 KB.

  • With a 32 KB window thereafter, each RTT can send up to 32 KB, so the additional RTTs needed are ceil(469 / 32) = 15 RTTs.

  • Total RTTs = 5 + 15 = 20 RTTs. With RTT = 100 ms, total time = 20 × 100 ms = 2000 ms.

Final answer: 2000 ms.

solution:
Correct answer: 2048 bytes

  1. Maximum sender-window limit = min(congestion window, receiver advertised window) = min(4 KB, 6 KB) = 4 KB = 4096 bytes.

  2. Unacknowledged data = LastByteSent − LastByteAcked = 10240 − 8192 = 2048 bytes.

  3. Currently available/usable sending window = 4096 − 2048 = 2048 bytes.

So 4096 bytes is the maximum limit, while 2048 bytes is the remaining window currently available for sending new data.

title: Which of the following statement is false about UDP.
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following statement is false about UDP.

options.html: UDP is used for management processes such as SNMP
UDP does not have any mechanism for flow control.
UDP is a suitable transport protocol for multicasting.

solution:
Answer: The false statement is "UDP provide congestion control like TCP."

  • UDP is used for management processes such as SNMP — True. SNMP typically uses UDP because it is lightweight and suitable for short request/response exchanges; reliability or retries are handled at the application layer if needed.

  • UDP does not have any mechanism for flow control — True. UDP is connectionless and does not implement flow control or windowing; senders are not paced by receiver feedback.

  • UDP provide congestion control like TCP — False. UDP does not implement congestion-control algorithms such as slow start, congestion avoidance, or retransmission timers. Applications or higher-level protocols built on UDP must implement any needed congestion control themselves.

  • UDP is a suitable transport protocol for multicasting — True. UDP supports sending datagrams to multicast addresses and does not require per-recipient connections, making it appropriate for group communication and streaming scenarios.

Additional note: UDP provides basic error detection via an optional checksum but does not provide acknowledgments, retransmission, or ordering guarantees. Those features, if required, must be implemented by the application or a higher-level protocol.

optionFeedback.html: True. Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) commonly uses UDP because it is lightweight and adds minimal overhead. SNMP transactions are short request/response exchanges and either rely on the application to handle retries or accept occasional packet loss.

True. UDP is connectionless and does not implement flow control or windowing. A sender using UDP will transmit datagrams without coordination with the receiver, so any required pacing or buffering must be handled by the application layer.

False. UDP does not provide congestion control like TCP. It offers no built-in mechanisms such as slow start, congestion avoidance, or retransmission timers. Applications that need congestion-friendly behavior must implement their own rate control (examples include some RTP-based systems or protocols built on top of UDP).

True. UDP is suitable for multicasting because it can send independent datagrams to multicast IP addresses without establishing per-recipient connections. This makes it appropriate for streaming and group communication where a connection-oriented protocol like TCP is not practical.

title: Which of the following field is not part of UDP

text: Which of the following field is not a part of UDP header?
solution:
Correct answer: Window size is not a part of the UDP header.

Key point: UDP uses a fixed 8-byte header composed of four 16-bit fields.

  • Source Port — 16 bits (2 bytes): identifies the sender’s port; included in the UDP header.

  • Destination Port — 16 bits (2 bytes): identifies the receiver’s port; included in the UDP header.

  • Length — 16 bits (2 bytes): total length of UDP header plus payload in bytes.

  • Checksum — 16 bits (2 bytes): used for optional error-checking of the UDP header and data.

Contrast with TCP: Window size is a TCP header field used for flow control and does not exist in UDP, which is connectionless and does not provide flow control.

Window size is not part of the UDP header. Window size is a field in the TCP header used for flow control. UDP has a simple fixed 8-byte header and does not include a window size field, so this choice is correct.
Checksum is part of the UDP header. It is a 16-bit (2-byte) field used for optional error-checking of the UDP header and payload, so this is not the correct answer.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q152
