text: Which protocol is used to send emails?
solution:
Concept

Application-layer protocols in the TCP/IP model are each purpose-built for a specific kind of communication - one for transferring files, one for delivering hypertext, one for remote terminal access, and one for relaying electronic mail between mail servers. The protocol responsible for delivering (sending) email between mail servers is the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), defined in RFC 5321.

Application to this question

Here the question asks which protocol sends emails. SMTP supplies exactly this function: it defines the command sequence (HELO/EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA) that a sending mail server uses to hand a message to a receiving mail server, and it typically runs over TCP port 25 (or 587 for client submission).

Cross-check against the other protocols

  • HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) governs how a browser requests and a web server returns hypertext resources such as web pages; it carries no mail-relay commands.

  • FTP (File Transfer Protocol) governs uploading and downloading files between a client and a file server over separate control and data connections; it has no mail-header syntax.

  • Telnet governs opening an interactive text-based session on a remote host, sending keystrokes and receiving character output over a virtual terminal connection; it carries no email envelope or message-relay semantics.

Since only SMTP defines mail-relay commands between mail servers, SMTP is the protocol used to send emails.

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) defines how a client such as a web browser requests a resource and how a web server returns hypertext content, typically over TCP port 80 or 443.
FTP (File Transfer Protocol) defines commands for uploading and downloading files between a client and a file server, using separate control and data connections, typically over TCP ports 20 and 21.
Telnet defines a way to open an interactive text-based session on a remote host, sending keystrokes and receiving character output over a virtual terminal connection, typically over TCP port 23.

title: Full form of IMAP?
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the full form of IMAP?
solution:
Full-form / acronym-expansion questions on networking protocols test both the exact standard wording and the protocol's underlying role. IMAP (RFC 3501) is one of the two dominant protocols — alongside POP3 — that a mail client uses to retrieve email from a server, and its core idea is letting the client repeatedly access messages that stay stored on the server, rather than downloading and removing them.

Expanding the acronym letter by letter:

  1. I — Internet: it operates over any standard Internet/TCP-IP connection.

  2. M — Message: it manages individual, stored email messages on the server.

  3. A — Access: its defining behaviour is giving the client ongoing access to those messages, not a one-time transfer.

  4. P — Protocol: a formally defined set of client-server communication rules.

Put together, this gives Internet Message Access Protocol. As a cross-check, contrast IMAP with POP3 (Post Office Protocol), which downloads mail and typically removes it from the server — IMAP's whole purpose is enabling multi-device access, which is exactly why an 'access' idea (not a one-time transfer) belongs in its name. This also rules out framings of IMAP as an international governance standard, a live chat/messaging service, an authority-granting mechanism, or a permission system — none of which match what IMAP actually does.

optionFeedback.html: Some test-takers assume unfamiliar internet-standard acronyms must be governed by an international body (drawing an analogy to organisations like ISO or ITU) and default to 'International' as the safe-sounding qualifier. That assumption is a guess based on the word's general connotation, not on IMAP's actual specification or governance.

'Messaging' is often used loosely as a synonym for any electronic communication, leading test-takers to substitute it for the more precise, protocol-specific term used in networking literature. This substitution is a vocabulary-level slip rather than a reflection of what the protocol's RFC actually names.

IMAP's full form follows directly from its job: a client reaches a mail server over the Internet and is given ongoing access to the messages held there — reading, organising, and searching them in place — rather than pulling them down and typically deleting them the way POP3 does.

'Authority' is a familiar word from security contexts (e.g. Certificate Authority), so test-takers pattern-match the syllable onto IMAP by association rather than by checking the protocol's actual defined name.
'Permission' evokes the everyday sense of being granted rights to do something, so test-takers substitute it for the actual defined term based on general usage rather than the protocol's formal name.

title: The cookie of HTTP client are stored at the which
subject: Computer Networks
text: The cookie of a HTTP client are stored at the which side of the system?
solution:
Answer: Cookies are stored on the client-side (in the user's browser).

Explanation:

  • How cookies work: Servers send cookies using the Set-Cookie HTTP header; the browser stores the cookie and automatically includes it with subsequent requests to the matching domain and path.

  • Cookies vs sessions: The cookie itself is stored client-side. Session data is typically stored server-side (in memory, files, or a database). The server usually issues a session identifier to the client via a cookie so it can link requests to the server-side session.

  • Types of cookies: Session cookies are deleted when the browser closes; persistent cookies remain until their expiration date.

  • Security note: Cookies can be protected using flags such as HttpOnly and Secure, and by restricting domain/path and using SameSite settings.

Therefore the correct response is the option that states cookies are stored client-side.

solution: URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator. This is the literal, official name for a URL. Developed by Tim Berners-Lee in 1994, a Uniform Resource Locator is a standardized string of characters that acts as a global address for identifying and locating resources on the World Wide Web.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator
This option confuses the purpose of a URL. A URL locates resources on the web, not specifically source code files. Check if you understand what a URL actually identifies versus file types.

A URL contains a domain name (like google.com) that eventually resolves to an IP address via a DNS (Domain Name System) lookup, but it points to much more than just an IP address. A URL points to a specific resource (like a webpage, an image, or a video file) located at a particular folder path on that server, and it specifies the protocol (like HTTP or HTTPS) used to access it.

A URL has absolutely nothing to do with how files are stored, formatted, or organized on a server's hard drive. title: The first part of complete URL is the needed to
subject: Computer Networks
text: The first part of a complete URL is the ________ needed to access the web resource.
solution:
Concept

A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is a structured address that tells a browser both HOW to communicate and WHERE the resource lives. By the URI syntax (RFC 3986), the very first component of a complete URL is the scheme — commonly called the protocol — which names the communication method (for example http, https, ftp) to be used to reach the resource.

Application

Read a complete URL left to right and identify the leading segment:

  1. Take a concrete URL such as https://www.example.com/page.html.

  2. The portion before ://, here https, is the scheme/protocol. It comes FIRST and tells the browser which communication method to use.

  3. Only after the protocol come the host (www.example.com) and then the path (/page.html).

So the blank — the first part of a complete URL needed to access the resource — is filled by protocol.

Contrast

  • The host's name (the domain such as www.example.com) identifies the server, but it appears AFTER the scheme, not first.

  • A street- or memory-style address is not how a URL's leading component is named; the resource's machine address is resolved later from the host, not stated as the first part.

  • A generic location describes the whole URL's purpose (it locates a resource) rather than its first segment; the leading segment specifically names the access method.

optionFeedback.html: "address" carries a postal/IP sense — a fixed location-identifier you use only after you already know how to reach it. A URL's very first token (before ://) is not this kind of identifier at all; any machine address is resolved later, from the host portion, not from this leading token.

"name" most naturally refers to the host/domain, such as www.example.com — the label people commonly call a website's "name". That token sits after the very first token (before ://) in a URL, so "name" does not correctly label the FIRST part being asked about here.

"location" is literally what the 'L' in URL stands for, but it describes the job of the WHOLE address — locating a resource — not a label for any one token within it. A term describing the entire address cannot correctly name just its very first token.

By the URI syntax, the leading segment of a complete URL (the part before ://, e.g. https) is the scheme, commonly called the protocol; it names the communication method used to reach the resource, which is exactly what the blank asks for.

title: Which one of the following allows the session to continue?

options.html: When the user logs out and is invalidated by the servlet

title: Suppose host also needed to use HTTP to download webpage
subject: Computer Networks
text: Suppose host B also needed to use HTTP to download a webpage with four embedded image. The total number of RTT between the client and the server starting from initiates TCP connection to receive the Fourth object and close connection when using non- persistent HTTP without pipelining_______.
solution:
Answer (corrected): If you count only the four embedded images, the total is 8 RTT. If you include the initial HTML object plus the four embedded images, the total is 10 RTT.

Reasoning:

  • For non-persistent HTTP without pipelining, each object is fetched over a separate TCP connection.

  • Each new TCP connection requires 1 RTT for the TCP three-way handshake and 1 RTT for the HTTP request and for the first byte of the response to arrive. That is 2 RTT per object (handshake + request/response).

Calculations:

  • If counting only the four embedded images: 4 objects × 2 RTT per object = 8 RTT.

  • If including the initial HTML plus the four images: (1 + 4) objects × 2 RTT per object = 10 RTT.

Why the original solution was incorrect:

  • The original counted 3 RTT per file. That overcounts; the correct per-object cost is 2 RTT (one for TCP setup, one for the HTTP request/response).

title: Which FTP transfer mode reduces data size during transmission to
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which FTP transfer mode reduces data size during transmission to improve bandwidth efficiency?
solution:
FTP (File Transfer Protocol, RFC 959) supports three data transmission modes:

1. Stream mode — the file is sent as a continuous stream of bytes, exactly as stored, with no extra processing. This is the default mode.

2. Block mode — the file is sent as a series of data blocks, each preceded by a header that carries a byte count and descriptor codes.

3. Compressed mode — the data is compressed before transmission. It uses run-length encoding: a run of n identical data bytes is replaced by a short two-byte code, and long strings of filler bytes are collapsed into a single byte.

Only the compressed (compression) mode reduces the size of the data during transmission, which increases bandwidth efficiency on large transfers at a small extra CPU cost. Encapsulation, multiplexing and fragmentation are general networking concepts, not FTP transmission modes, and none of them compresses the data.

Hence the correct answer is Compression Mode.

optionFeedback.html: Stream mode is a real FTP transmission mode, but it sends the file as a plain continuous stream of bytes with no compression. Because the data is transmitted exactly as-is, it does not reduce the data size or save bandwidth.

Correct. FTP defines three transmission modes — stream, block and compressed (compression). Compressed mode applies run-length encoding, replacing long runs of repeated or filler bytes with a short two-byte code, so the data size shrinks and bandwidth efficiency improves on large transfers.

There is no FTP transmission mode called 'encapsulation mode'. Encapsulation is the general layering process of wrapping data with headers as it moves down the protocol stack; it adds overhead rather than reducing data size.

Multiplexing is a technique for combining several signals or sessions over one channel; it is not one of FTP's transmission modes. It shares a link among multiple flows but does not compress or shrink the data of a single transfer.

Fragmentation is the splitting of a large packet into smaller pieces to fit a network's MTU; it is not an FTP transmission mode. Breaking data into fragments does not compress it — the total payload stays the same (and headers add a little extra).

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q3

Concept

A network protocol is a standardized set of rules that lets computers communicate. An initialism uses the first letters of the words in its expanded name.

Application-layer protocols provide services directly used by network applications, such as moving files between a client and a server.

Application

In the initialism FTP, F represents File, T represents Transfer, and P represents Protocol. FTP therefore names the application-layer protocol used to transfer files across a network.

Contrast

  • Faster Than Post is an informal comparison about delivery speed.

  • Files To Publish is a phrase about documents selected for publication.

  • Format To Program is a phrase about preparing or formatting material for a program.

Cross-check

The Internet Engineering Task Force specification RFC 959 is titled “File Transfer Protocol (FTP),” which independently confirms the expansion.

Result

FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol.

optionFeedback.html: An initialism is resolved by its established usage in a subject area, and Faster Than Post belongs to an informal comparison about postal-delivery speed.
Initialisms take the conventional term used in their technical field, and File Transfer Protocol belongs to application-layer networking for file exchange.
The expansion of an initialism comes from established domain usage, and Files To Publish belongs to a publishing workflow for releasing documents.
A letter-matching phrase serves as an expansion through established subject usage, and Format To Program belongs to a software-formatting workflow.

title: Which of the following statements best reflects how File Transfer
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following statements best reflects how File Transfer Protocol (FTP) functions at the Application Layer in a network system?

options.html: FTP is mainly utilized for streaming audio and video between devices.
FTP establishes separate connections for commands and data to facilitate file transfer.
FTP secures files during transmission using UDP and built-in encryption.
FTP is primarily used to send emails with file attachments.

solution:
The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) operates at the Application Layer of the OSI model and uses a distinct, dual-connection architecture over TCP to manage file transfers reliably.

Instead of passing everything through a single channel, FTP splits the responsibilities into two separate TCP connections:

  1. Control Connection (Port 21): Used for sending commands and receiving responses (e.g., user authentication, browsing directories, requesting transfers). This connection remains open throughout the entire FTP session.

  2. Data Connection (Port 20 in Active Mode): Created dynamically every time a file transfer or directory listing is actually requested. This connection closes immediately after the data transfer finishes.

optionFeedback.html:
Incorrect.

While FTP transfers complete audio or video files, it does not support real-time media streaming. Protocols like RTSP (Real-Time Streaming Protocol) or HTTP-based streaming (like HLS) are used for that.

Correct.

This out-of-band control mechanism is the defining characteristic of how FTP operates at the Application Layer.

Incorrect

FTP uses TCP for reliable data transfer, not UDP. Additionally, standard FTP lacks built-in encryption; use SFTP or FTPS for secure transfers.

Incorrect

FTP is designed for transferring files between systems, not sending emails. Email transmission uses protocols like SMTP; you should review the primary purpose of each application layer protocol to distinguish their functions.

title: What is the role of DNS? It is best described
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the role of DNS? It is best described as –

options.html: translate a host’s IPv6 address to an IPv4 address
maps a MAC address to an IP address
translate a host’s private IP address to a public IP address
maps a domain name to an IP address

solution:
DNS (Domain Name System) is a hierarchical and decentralized naming system for computers, services, or other resources connected to the Internet or a private network. It translates human-readable domain names (like www.example.com) into machine-readable IP addresses (like 192.0.2.1). This allows users to access websites using easy-to-remember names instead of numerical IP addresses.

हिन्दी उत्तर:

डोमेन नाम प्रणाली (DNS) इंटरनेट या निजी नेटवर्क पर कंप्यूटर, सेवाओं या अन्य संसाधनों के लिए एक पदानुक्रमिक और विकेंद्रित नाम प्रणाली है। यह मानव-पठनीय डोमेन नामों (जैसे www.example.com) को मशीन-पठनीय IP पतों (जैसे 192.0.2.1) में परिवर्तित करता है। इससे उपयोगकर्ताओं को आसानी से वेबसाइटों तक पहुँचने की अनुमति मिलती है, जिसमें आसानी से याद रखे जा सकने वाले नामों का उपयोग किया जाता है, न कि संख्यात्मक IP पतों का।

Step 1: MAC address to IP address mapping is done by ARP, not DNS. Step 2: DNS operates at a higher level and does not deal with MAC addresses.
Step 1: Translating private IP to public IP is the job of NAT, not DNS. Step 2: DNS does not perform address translation for network routing purposes.

title: If Host and starts transmitting at the same time and
subject: Computer Networks
text: If Host B and C starts transmitting at the same time and collision occurs , then which host will receive a collision jamming signal
solution:
Answer: Hosts A, B and C receive the collision jamming signal.

Why: The hub is a Layer 1 repeater that forwards electrical signals to all ports, so it does not separate collision domains. When two hosts on the hub transmit at the same time, their frames collide and the collision (and any jam signal) is seen by every device on that shared medium.

  • Because Hosts B and C are connected to the same hub, the collision is confined to that hub's collision domain and will be received by Hosts A, B, and C.

  • Host D and the router are connected via a switch, which separates collision domains at each port, so they do not receive the hub's collision jamming signal.

  • Therefore the correct set of hosts that receive the collision jamming signal is Hosts A, B, and C.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. A hub creates a single shared collision domain, so a collision between two hosts on the hub is seen by every device connected to that hub, not only Host A. The jamming signal will be received by Hosts A, B, and C.
Incorrect. Host B may be one of the transmitters, but the collision and resulting jamming signal are propagated to all hosts on the hub (Hosts A, B, and C). It is not limited to Host B alone.

Correct. A hub is a Layer 1 device that repeats signals to all its ports and does not separate collision domains. When Host B and Host C collide, the collision (and jam signal) is seen by every host on the hub — Hosts A, B, and C. Devices connected through the switch (Host D and the router) are in a different collision domain and are not affected.

Incorrect. Host D is connected through a switch, which separates collision domains. A collision on the hub is confined to the hub's collision domain (Hosts A, B, and C) and does not propagate to Host D or the router on the switch.

Hubs provide built-in firewall security, while Switches do not

solution: A hub operates at the physical layer and broadcasts all incoming data to every port. A switch operates at the data link layer and intelligently forwards frames only to the destination MAC address.

optionFeedback.html: This option reverses the OSI layer positions. Hubs function at the Physical Layer, while Switches operate at the Data Link Layer. Check your understanding of which network devices correspond to each layer.

This option correctly identifies that hubs broadcast to all ports while switches use MAC addresses for targeted delivery. To verify this, check if the device learns port mappings or simply floods unicast traffic to every connected segment.

Switches operate at the Data Link layer, forwarding packets based on MAC addresses for better efficiency and security.

It forwards data packets based on MAC addresses

solution: A network switch operates at Layer 2 (Data Link layer) of the OSI model. It forwards data packets between devices based on their MAC addresses, ensuring efficient communication within a local network.

optionFeedback.html: This describes a repeater or amplifier function. Switches operate at Layer 2 to forward frames based on MAC addresses, not amplify signals.

This is the function of a Router, not a switch. Routers operate at the Network Layer (Layer 3) and are used to connect entirely different networks together (like connecting your home local network to the global Internet).
A network switch operates at the Data Link Layer (Layer 2) of the OSI model. Its primary job is to connect multiple devices (computers, printers, servers) within the same local area network (LAN).

This is the job of a protocol called ARP (Address Resolution Protocol), not a hardware switch. ARP is a communication protocol used by devices to discover the physical MAC address associated with a known IP address.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q133
subject: Computer Networks
text: In a large enterprise network, which situation most strongly indicates the need for implementing VLANs rather than adding more physical switches ?

options.html: Bandwidth on trunk links is fully utilized
Devices need to be grouped logically rather than physically
The number of broadcast domains must be reduced

solution:
Concept: VLANs (Virtual LANs) let devices be placed into the same logical group -- by function, department, or project -- independent of the physical switch port, floor, or building they are wired into. On a purely physical switch topology, even with many additional switches, a device's group membership is fixed by whichever switch port it happens to be cabled into; moving a device into a different group means either re-patching a cable or reconfiguring that specific port. VLAN tagging (802.1Q) turns group membership into a port/configuration setting that can be reassigned from the switch's management interface without any new cable run, and that setting can be applied consistently across every switch in the trunked fabric.

Application: Checking each situation against this rule:

  1. Devices needing to be grouped logically rather than physically is exactly the situation additional physical switches cannot fix on their own: no matter how many switches are added, a device's group membership stays tied to whichever port it is physically cabled into unless VLANs are configured on the relevant ports (or, under dynamic VLAN assignment, tied to the device's identity) -- something plain physical wiring or extra switch hardware does not provide by itself.

  2. Trunk-link bandwidth being fully used is a link-capacity constraint, resolved by adding physical capacity to that link -- a faster trunk, an extra parallel uplink, or link aggregation -- rather than by any logical-segmentation feature.

  3. Collision domains growing too large is not a persistent problem on a modern full-duplex switched network: each switch port already forms its own separate, single-device collision domain, independent of how many switches or VLANs are configured.

  4. Needing the number of broadcast domains reduced runs the opposite direction from what VLANs do: configuring VLANs splits one flat broadcast domain into several smaller ones, which increases the total count of broadcast domains while shrinking each one's span. Wanting fewer broadcast domains would call for merging domains together, not adding VLAN segmentation.

Cross-check: This lines up with the standard Layer-2 segmentation principle -- VLANs provide logical, configuration-based grouping that is independent of physical wiring, which is the one property plain physical switch hardware cannot replicate by itself. Collision-domain size is already minimized per port on any switched network regardless of switch or VLAN count, and trunk-capacity limits are addressed by adding link capacity; only logical group independence from physical wiring specifically calls for VLANs.

optionFeedback.html: Trunk-link bandwidth utilization is the share of a trunk's total physical capacity being consumed by the combined traffic of every VLAN or subnet carried across that link at a given moment; for the same aggregate traffic, utilization rises as the trunk's available capacity shrinks and falls as more or faster physical capacity is added to that specific link.

Logical device grouping means assigning a device to a functional or departmental group through configuration, independent of the physical port, switch, or wiring closet the device happens to be connected through.

A collision domain is the set of devices whose simultaneous transmissions on a shared medium can produce a frame collision; on a modern full-duplex switch, each individual port already forms its own separate collision domain.

The count of broadcast domains on a network changes with how the Layer-2 topology is partitioned at a routing boundary: splitting one broadcast domain into several smaller ones raises the total count, while merging domains together lowers it.

title: Which of this is not network edge device? Asked in

solution: Network edge devices are host systems that connect to a network and run applications, such as web browsers. These devices operate at the edge of the network and include personal computers, smartphones, and servers. title: Which of the following statements are false?
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following statements are false?

options.html: A bridge uses IP address, while a router uses MAC address
The efficiency of ethernet increases with decrease in propagation delay and decrease in transmission delay
The efficiency of ethernet increases with decrease in propagation delay and increase in transmission delay
Router can connect between a LAN and a WAN

solution:
To determine which statements are false, analyze each option based on networking principles.

Option A: A bridge uses IP address, while a router uses MAC address

A bridge operates at the data link layer and uses MAC addresses to forward frames. A router operates at the network layer and uses IP addresses to route packets. This option incorrectly swaps the functions of bridge and router, making it false.

Option B: The efficiency of ethernet increases with decrease in propagation delay and decrease in transmission delay

Ethernet efficiency is given by the formula: Efficiency = 1 / (1 + 2a), where a = Tp / Tt. Here, Tp is propagation delay and Tt is transmission delay. As Tp decreases and Tt decreases, the value of 'a' decreases, which increases efficiency. This option correctly identifies the relationship between delays and efficiency, making it true.

Option C: The efficiency of ethernet increases with decrease in propagation delay and increase in transmission delay

Using the same formula, Efficiency = 1 / (1 + 2a), where a = Tp / Tt. If Tp decreases and Tt increases, 'a' decreases, which increases efficiency. However, this option incorrectly implies that increasing Tt alone increases efficiency, which is misleading because it ignores the effect of Tp. The statement is false because it misrepresents the relationship between delays and efficiency.

Option D: Router can connect between a LAN and a WAN

Routers operate at the network layer and are designed to connect different networks, including LANs and WANs. This option correctly describes the role of a router, making it true.

Therefore, the false statements are Option A and Option C.

optionFeedback.html: A bridge operates at the data link layer and uses MAC addresses for forwarding. A router operates at the network layer and uses IP addresses. This option incorrectly swaps the roles of bridge and router, making it false.

Efficiency in Ethernet is given by 1/(1 + 2a), where a = Tp/Tt. Decreasing propagation delay (Tp) and transmission delay (Tt) both reduce 'a', increasing efficiency. This option correctly identifies the relationship between delays and efficiency.

Efficiency in Ethernet is 1/(1 + 2a), where a = Tp/Tt. Increasing transmission delay (Tt) reduces 'a', which increases efficiency. However, this option claims that increasing Tt increases efficiency, which is misleading because it ignores the effect of Tp. The statement is false because it implies a direct increase in efficiency with increased Tt without considering Tp.
Routers operate at the network layer and can connect different networks, including LANs and WANs. This option correctly describes the role of a router in connecting LAN and WAN, making it true.

title: Which of the following is NOT true with respect to
subject: Computer Networks
text:
Which of the following is NOT true with respect to a transparent bridge and a router?

(S1) Both a bridge and a router make their forwarding decisions by consulting an address-based table — a bridge its MAC-address table, a router its routing table — rather than forwarding every frame or packet out every port unconditionally, the way a plain repeater would

(S2) A bridge uses IP addresses while a router uses MAC addresses
solution:
Concept: a transparent bridge and a router both do "selective forwarding" instead of blindly repeating every signal, but they differ in OSI layer, protocol data unit, and addressing scheme.

Property

Bridge

Router

OSI layer

Data Link (Layer 2)

Network (Layer 3)

Protocol data unit forwarded

Frame

Packet

Table it builds/uses

MAC address table (learned)

Routing table (from connected, static, and dynamically learned routes)

Address type used to decide forwarding

MAC address

IP address

Applying this to the two statements:

  1. S1 ("Both a bridge and a router make their forwarding decisions by consulting an address-based table — a bridge its MAC-address table, a router its routing table — rather than forwarding every frame or packet out every port unconditionally, the way a plain repeater would"): both devices consult an address-based table as part of deciding how to handle each frame or packet — a bridge checks its learned MAC-address table and applies its forwarding/filtering rules, which include flooding for broadcast, multicast, or not-yet-learned destinations, and a router checks its routing table for the route matching a destination IP. That table-driven decision process — not blind, unconditional repetition the way a plain repeater/hub works — is what both devices do. So S1 is TRUE.

  2. S2 ("A bridge uses IP addresses while a router uses MAC addresses"): this reverses the real pairing from the table above — the bridge is the one that uses MAC addresses, and the router is the one that uses IP addresses. So S2 is FALSE.

Cross-check: since S1 holds, the option claiming both statements are false (“Both S1 and S2”) cannot be right; since S2 fails, the option claiming neither statement is false (“None of the above”) cannot be right either. That leaves exactly one statement as not true.

So the statement that is NOT true is S2 — the one that swaps which device uses MAC addresses and which uses IP addresses.

optionFeedback.html: This combination requires that a transparent bridge floods every incoming frame out every port with no address lookup at all, the way a plain hub or repeater does. Confirm that specific claim — not an assumption about which device sounds more basic — before locking in this combination; it is exactly what the solution's analysis of the first statement checks.

This identifies the addressing claim (S2) as the one that breaks down. In practice, the responsibilities described there are reversed: a bridge builds and consults a MAC address table at the Data Link layer, while a router builds and consults a routing table keyed on IP addresses at the Network layer. The claim that both devices forward selectively, by contrast, describes real behaviour for each — a bridge limits forwarding to the segment holding a learned destination MAC, and a router limits forwarding to the route matching a destination IP — so nothing fails there.

This combination requires both that a bridge floods indiscriminately with no lookup at all, and that the addressing assignment given for each device is wrong. Requiring two independent claims to both fail is a stronger bar than requiring one — confirm each separately against how a bridge and a router actually operate before concluding both fail together; the solution checks each statement in turn.

This combination requires that the addressing assignment given — one device paired with one address type, the other device with the other — is exactly correct as stated, with no swap. Confirm that specific pairing against which OSI layer each device actually operates at (Data Link versus Network), rather than accepting it because it sounds plausible; the solution derives the correct pairing explicitly.

title: Which internetworking devices can separate collision domains
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which internetworking devices can separate collision domains
solution:
Correct answer: Router and Switch.

  • Switch: Separates collision domains per port. Each switch port is its own collision domain, so devices on different switch ports do not contend for the same collisions.

  • Router: Separates collision domains per interface. A router does not forward collisions between interfaces and also separates broadcast domains.

  • Hubs and repeaters: Operate at Layer 1 and extend a single collision domain; they do not separate collision domains.

Summary: The devices that separate collision domains are switches and routers; hubs and repeaters do not.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. A hub is a multiport repeater that operates at Layer 1 and does not separate collision domains — it extends a single collision domain. A switch does separate collision domains per port, but because this option pairs a hub (which does not) with a switch, the option as a whole is not correct.

Incorrect. A switch separates collision domains per port, but a repeater (like a hub) operates at Layer 1 and simply forwards electrical signals, extending the same collision domain. The combination is therefore not correct.

Correct. Both routers and switches separate collision domains: a switch separates collision domains on a per-port basis (each switch port is its own collision domain), and a router separates collision domains on a per-interface basis. Hubs and repeaters do not separate collision domains.

Incorrect. A router does separate collision domains (each router interface is its own collision domain), but a hub does not — a hub/repeater extends a single collision domain. Because the option includes a hub, it is not fully correct.

title: What is the purpose of proxy server in network
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the purpose of a proxy server in a network ?

options.html: Accelerating the rendering of HTML pages
Acting as an intermediary between clients and servers, providing security / performance benefits
Storing and managing session data for web applications

solution:
A proxy server functions as a gateway between an internal network (clients) and the internet (servers). Instead of a client connecting directly to a website, the client sends its request to the proxy server, which then evaluates, modifies, and forwards the request to the destination.

This setup provides several key benefits:

  • Security & Anonymity: It hides the client's actual IP address from the destination server and allows administrators to filter out malicious traffic or block unauthorized websites.

  • Performance (Caching): It can store copies of frequently requested web pages locally. When another user requests the same page, the proxy delivers it instantly without consuming external bandwidth.

  • Load Balancing: It can distribute incoming traffic across multiple servers to prevent system crashes.

optionFeedback.html: While authentication can be a feature of some proxy servers, it is not their primary purpose.
Proxy servers can cache content to speed up access, but they do not directly render HTML pages.

A proxy server functions as a gateway between an internal network (clients) and the internet (servers). Instead of a client connecting directly to a website, the client sends its request to the proxy server, which then evaluates, modifies, and forwards the request to the destination.
This option describes a session store or cache, not the core function of a proxy server.

title: Modem is connected in between telephone line and
subject: Computer Networks
text: A modem is connected in between a telephone line and a ________.
solution:
Concept

A modem (modulator-demodulator) is the device that lets a computer exchange data over an ordinary telephone line. It converts the computer's digital signals into analog tones the phone line can carry (modulation) and converts incoming analog tones back into digital data (demodulation).

Applying it here

The telephone line carries analog signals while a computer works with digital data, so the modem sits exactly at that boundary. One end of the modem faces the telephone line; the other end faces the computer that owns the data. The device on the far side of the modem from the telephone line is therefore the computer.

Cross-check

Trace the data path end to end: computer to modem to telephone line to a distant modem to a distant computer. The modem's local endpoint is always the computer that produces and consumes the data, which confirms the answer.

optionFeedback.html: Network names an abstract interconnected system rather than the concrete piece of hardware a modem physically plugs into; a modem terminates at a single device, not at the system-level concept of a network.
This fits the modem's role: the modem performs modulation and demodulation so that data already in digital form can travel across the analog telephone line and arrive correctly at the other end.

A communication adapter is a generic interface-card category, and the modem is itself the line's communication device; pairing the modem with another communication adapter just describes a second interface, not what sits at the end of the link.
A serial port is merely the physical connector that an external modem may plug into; it is an attachment interface, not the endpoint that produces and consumes the data carried over the line.

title: Which of the following is essential for WAN hardware?
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following is essential for WAN hardware?
solution:
Concept

A WAN (Wide Area Network) connects multiple networks that lie in different geographic locations and that may belong to different network address spaces. Joining two distinct networks requires a device that works at the network layer (Layer 3) — one that reads logical (IP) addresses and decides the best path to forward a packet between networks. That network-layer forwarding-between-networks function is the defining job of a router.

Applying it here

The question asks which device is essential for WAN hardware. Compare the offered devices by the network layer they operate on:

  • Router: a Layer-3 device that forwards packets between separate networks using IP addresses, which is exactly what interconnecting sites across a WAN requires.

  • Bridge and Switch: Layer-2 devices that forward frames using MAC addresses within a single local network; they extend or segment a LAN but do not route between different networks.

  • Firewall: a security device that filters traffic by policy; it controls what may pass but does not itself provide the inter-network forwarding a WAN link needs.

Cross-check

Only the router operates at the network layer and forwards between distinct networks, so it is the device essential to WAN connectivity. The correct answer is Router.

optionFeedback.html: Picking the bridge reflects a Layer-2 mindset: a bridge joins two segments of the same local network by MAC address. It extends a LAN but cannot forward traffic between separate networks across a wide area.
A switch also works at Layer 2, forwarding frames among devices inside one LAN by MAC address. It speeds up local connectivity but has no role in routing between the different networks a WAN spans.

The router operates at the network layer and forwards packets between separate networks using IP addresses. That inter-network forwarding is precisely what links sites across a wide area, which is why it is the device a WAN depends on.

A firewall is a security device that inspects and filters traffic against a policy. It decides what is allowed to pass, but it does not itself provide the inter-network forwarding that a wide-area link needs.

title: Which of the following device is used to connect two
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following device is used to connect two systems, especially if the systems use different protocols?
solution:
Concept: Networking devices operate at different layers of the OSI model, and each layer determines how much of a message a device can understand. A device that must join networks running different protocols has to read and rewrite the data all the way up to the application layer, because the two sides format, address, and encode their messages in incompatible ways. Translating between protocol stacks is therefore an upper-layer job, not a physical- or data-link-layer one.

Applying it here: Connecting two systems that speak different protocols requires full protocol conversion, so the device must operate across all OSI layers. The device that does this is the gateway: it accepts a message on one protocol stack, interprets it completely, and re-encodes it into the other side's protocol so the two otherwise-incompatible systems can communicate.

Why the other devices cannot do this:

  • Hub — a physical-layer (Layer 1) device that simply repeats incoming electrical signals out of every port. It understands no addressing or protocol at all, so it cannot translate between two protocols.

  • Bridge — a data-link-layer (Layer 2) device that forwards frames between segments using MAC addresses. It joins networks that already use the same protocol; it does not convert one protocol to another.

  • Repeater — a physical-layer (Layer 1) device that regenerates and amplifies a weak signal to extend cable distance. Like the hub it has no awareness of protocols and performs no translation.

Cross-check: Order the candidates by OSI layer — repeater and hub at Layer 1, bridge at Layer 2 — and only the gateway reaches up through the application layer, which is exactly where protocol-to-protocol conversion must happen. This confirms the gateway is the device that connects systems using different protocols.

optionFeedback.html: A hub operates at the physical layer (Layer 1), repeating incoming signals to every port without examining their contents. Because it has no awareness of addresses or protocols, it cannot perform any protocol translation between two systems.

A bridge operates at the data-link layer (Layer 2), forwarding frames between segments by MAC address. It interconnects networks that already share one protocol, so it carries data within a single protocol rather than converting one protocol into another.

A gateway operates across all OSI layers up to the application layer, interpreting a message in one protocol and re-encoding it into another. This full protocol translation lets two systems running different protocols exchange data.

A repeater operates at the physical layer (Layer 1), regenerating and amplifying a weakened signal to extend the transmission distance. Because it acts only on the raw signal, it cannot perform any protocol translation between two systems.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q66
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which device forwards IP packets between multiple distinct IP networks?
solution:
Concept

Network devices are distinguished by the addressing information they use and the scope across which they forward traffic.

A router works at the network layer: it reads destination IP addresses and uses a routing table to forward packets from one IP network to another.

Application

The stem asks for a device that connects multiple distinct networks, so the required function is inter-network packet forwarding.

Contrast

  • A switch forwards Ethernet frames between ports within a LAN by using MAC addresses.

  • A hub repeats incoming bit signals to every other port within one shared segment.

  • A router forwards IP packets between distinct networks by using destination addresses and a routing table.

  • A bridge forwards or filters Ethernet frames between LAN segments by using MAC addresses.

Cross-check

When a host sends data to a destination outside its local subnet, it sends the packet to its default gateway; that router selects a route toward the destination network.

Therefore, the required device is a router.

optionFeedback.html: A switch forwards Ethernet frames between ports within a LAN by using MAC addresses.
A hub repeats incoming bit signals to every other port within one shared segment.
A router forwards IP packets between distinct networks by using destination addresses and a routing table.
A bridge forwards or filters Ethernet frames between LAN segments by using MAC addresses.

title: What is the primary function of router in computer network?
subject: Computer Networks
text: What is the primary function of a router in a computer network?

options.html: To connect devices within the same network
To filter incoming traffic based on IP addresses

solution:
Network devices are classified by the OSI layer they operate at and the specific job they perform. A device operating at the data-link layer (Layer 2) forwards frames between ports using MAC addresses within one network -- this is switching. A device operating at the network layer (Layer 3) forwards packets between separate networks using IP addresses and a routing table to select the best path -- this is routing. A device that inspects traffic against a configured rule set to permit or block it -- typically by IP address, port, or protocol -- is performing security/policy filtering, most commonly associated with a firewall or an access-control list.

The question asks for the primary, defining function of a router. Interconnecting separate networks and forwarding data between them based on destination IP addresses is exactly the Layer-3 routing job described above, so "To connect multiple networks together" captures the router's defining role.

Checking this against each of the other listed descriptions:

  • "To connect devices within the same network" describes Layer-2 frame forwarding by MAC address inside one broadcast domain -- a distinct job from forwarding between separate networks.

  • "To filter incoming traffic based on IP addresses" describes a policy-enforcement action -- permitting or dropping packets against a configured rule set. A router can indeed be configured to do this through an access-control list, but that is an optional capability added on top of forwarding; it is the defining job of a firewall, not of the device the question asks about.

  • "More than one of the above" would require at least two of the listed descriptions to each independently capture the primary, defining role. Only the Layer-3 inter-network forwarding description does so: Layer-2 switching within one network is a different device's defining job, and IP filtering is a configured extra rather than a defining role.

  • "None of the above" would require that not one of the listed descriptions names the primary function the question asks about. The Layer-3 description -- forwarding packets between separate networks using destination IP addresses -- does name it, so that condition is not met.

Cross-checking against the OSI model confirms this: any device that makes forwarding decisions purely from a Layer-3 destination IP address, across separate broadcast domains, is by definition performing routing -- confirming that connecting multiple networks together is the router's primary function. This also matches the official answer key for the BPSC TRE 3.0 (Class 11-12) Computer Science paper held on 22 July 2024, from which this question is taken.

optionFeedback.html: Connecting devices within a single network is carried out at the data-link layer, where frames are forwarded between ports using the devices' MAC addresses inside one broadcast domain.

Connecting multiple networks together is carried out at the network layer, where packets are forwarded across separate broadcast domains by examining the destination IP address and consulting a routing table to select the outgoing path.

Filtering incoming traffic based on IP addresses is a policy-enforcement action: each packet's source or destination address is checked against a configured rule set to decide whether to permit or drop it.

This choice asserts that two or more of the listed descriptions each name the single function the stem asks about. Those descriptions cover three separate jobs -- link-layer frame forwarding, network-layer packet forwarding, and rule-based traffic policy -- and one device may perform several of them alongside its one defining job.

This choice asserts that none of the listed descriptions names the function the stem asks about. Those descriptions cover three standard networking jobs -- link-layer frame forwarding, network-layer packet forwarding, and rule-based traffic policy -- each defined by the layer it acts on rather than by any one device.

title: What does the command routerA(config) cons allow you to perform
subject: Computer Networks
text: What does the command RouterA(config)#line cons 0 allow you to perform next?
solution:
Concept: Cisco IOS uses a mode-based CLI: from global configuration mode, the command "line <type> <number>" switches into a separate LINE CONFIGURATION sub-mode for that specific line (console, vty, or aux). Each line type is configured and secured independently — a setting applied under one line type (password, login, timeout) affects only that line, never another.

Application: "cons 0" is the standard IOS abbreviation for "console 0", the router's single physical console port. So RouterA(config)#line cons 0 moves the prompt to RouterA(config-line)#, the configuration sub-mode for that console port. From here, the standard next commands are password <password> followed by login — which is exactly how the console (local terminal) password gets defined and enforced.

Cross-check: Testing the other offered outcomes against the same rule shows none of them fit this sub-mode:

  • Telnet/remote-session access is secured separately, under the VTY lines (e.g. line vty 0 4) — a different line type, not the console line.

  • Halting or restarting the device is a separate top-level operation (e.g. reload); entering a line's configuration sub-mode never changes the device's power or running state.

  • This sub-mode lets you configure how the line behaves; it does not turn the port off or block connections to it.

So among the four offered outcomes, only setting the console password matches what "line cons 0" actually leads to.

optionFeedback.html: This confuses the console line (the physical port on the router itself) with the VTY lines used for remote Telnet/SSH sessions. Different line types are configured separately — securing Telnet access requires entering the VTY lines instead (for example, line vty 0 4), not the console line.
Restarting or rebooting the router needs a separate top-level command (such as reload); entering a line's configuration sub-mode never changes the device's power or running state.

Line 0 is the router's physical console port, so switching into its configuration sub-mode is exactly where the console (local terminal) password gets defined and enforced — the standard next commands are password <password> followed by login.

Switching into a line's configuration sub-mode does not itself disable that line — it puts you in position to adjust ordinary line-level settings (such as its password or session behavior), which is what this classic setup step is for, rather than shutting off access to the port.

title: Which of the following components cannot be directly connected to
subject: Computer Networks
text: Which of the following components cannot be directly connected to a standard USB or HDMI port without the use of an intermediate adapter?
solution: Standard USB and HDMI ports are designed for specific types of connections. USB ports connect devices like keyboards, mice, and storage drives using USB connectors. HDMI ports transmit video and audio signals to displays or projectors. Ethernet cables, however, use RJ45 connectors designed for network ports (LAN). Because the physical connector shapes and signal protocols differ, an Ethernet cable cannot be plugged directly into a USB or HDMI port without an intermediate adapter.

optionFeedback.html: Mice are standard peripherals designed to connect directly via USB, so an adapter is not needed.
Keyboards are standard peripherals designed to connect directly via USB, so an adapter is not needed.
Projectors typically feature HDMI inputs that allow direct connection to computers without adapters.
Ethernet cables typically use RJ45 connectors, which are physically incompatible with USB or HDMI ports without an adapter.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - June 2009 - source row 49
subject: Computer Networks
text: The device which connects dissimilar LANs of different topologies using different sets of communication protocols so that information can flow from one to another is called :
solution:
CONCEPT: Internetworking devices sit at different layers and handle different degrees of dissimilarity between the networks they connect. A gateway is the device that connects networks differing in topology AND in their entire protocol stack — it performs full protocol translation so that data formatted for one network becomes usable on the other.

APPLICATION: The stem describes a device connecting dissimilar LANs of different topologies that also use different sets of communication protocols. This is exactly the gateway's defining role — translating across protocol families between fundamentally different network architectures, not merely extending or switching within one network.

CROSS-CHECK — how the other devices differ:

  • Router: forwards packets between networks at the network layer, but within a common network-layer protocol suite (for example, IP-to-IP); it does not translate between different protocol families.

  • Bridge: works at the data-link layer and joins two segments that use the SAME data-link protocol, extending one logical network — it cannot interconnect networks with differing protocol stacks.

  • Switch: works at the data-link layer inside a single LAN, forwarding frames between devices on that same network by MAC address — it does not interconnect separate networks running different protocols.

Since only a gateway performs full protocol-stack translation between dissimilar networks, that is the correct device.

optionFeedback.html: A router typically selects the best forwarding path using a routing algorithm such as OSPF or RIP, based on metrics like hop count or link cost.
A bridge builds its forwarding table automatically by learning source addresses from observed traffic, a technique known as learning bridging.
A gateway is commonly deployed as a single access point at an organization's network boundary, for example between a local network and the wider internet.
A switch gives each connected device its own dedicated collision domain and bandwidth, unlike devices that share one common transmission medium.
